And he went about among the villages teaching. <sup>7</sup>And he called the twelve and began to send them out two by two, and gave them authority over the unclean spirits. <sup>8</sup>He charged them to take nothing for their journey except a staff—no bread, no bag, no money in their belts— <sup>9</sup>but to wear sandals and not put on two tunics. <sup>10</sup>And he said to them, “Whenever you enter a house, stay there until you depart from there. <sup>11</sup>And if any place will not receive you and they will not listen to you, when you leave, shake off the dust that is on your feet as a testimony against them.” <sup>12</sup>So they went out and proclaimed that people should repent. <sup>13</sup>And they cast out many demons and anointed with oil many who were sick and healed them. <sup>14</sup>King Herod heard of it, for Jesus’ name had become known. Some said, “John the Baptist has been raised from the dead. That is why these miraculous powers are at work in him.” <sup>15</sup>But others said, “He is Elijah.” And others said, “He is a prophet, like one of the prophets of old.” <sup>16</sup>But when Herod heard of it, he said, “John, whom I beheaded, has been raised.” <sup>17</sup>For it was Herod who had sent and seized John and bound him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, because he had married her. <sup>18</sup>For John had been saying to Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.” <sup>19</sup>And Herodias had a grudge against him and wanted to put him to death. But she could not, <sup>20</sup>for Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man, and he kept him safe. When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly. <sup>21</sup>But an opportunity came when Herod on his birthday gave a banquet for his nobles and military commanders and the leading men of Galilee. <sup>22</sup>For when Herodias’s daughter came in and danced, she pleased Herod and his guests. And the king said to the girl, “Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you.” <sup>23</sup>And he vowed to her, “Whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom.” <sup>24</sup>And she went out and said to her mother, “For what should I ask?” And she said, “The head of John the Baptist.” <sup>25</sup>And she came in immediately with haste to the king and asked, saying, “I want you to give me at once the head of John the Baptist on a platter.” <sup>26</sup>And the king was exceedingly sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he did not want to break his word to her. <sup>27</sup>And immediately the king sent an executioner with orders to bring John’s head. He went and beheaded him in the prison <sup>28</sup>and brought his head on a platter and gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother. <sup>29</sup>When his disciples heard of it, they came and took his body and laid it in a tomb. <sup>30</sup>The apostles returned to Jesus and told him all that they had done and taught. <sup>31</sup>And he said to them, “Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while.” For many were coming and going, and they had no leisure even to eat. <sup>32</sup>And they went away in the boat to a desolate place by themselves. <sup>33</sup>Now many saw them going and recognized them, and they ran there on foot from all the towns and got there ahead of them. <sup>34</sup>When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. And he began to teach them many things. <sup>35</sup>And when it grew late, his disciples came to him and said, “This is a desolate place, and the hour is now late. <sup>36</sup>Send them away to go into the surrounding countryside and villages and buy themselves something to eat.” <sup>37</sup>But he answered them, “You give them something to eat.” And they said to him, “Shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give it to them to eat?” <sup>38</sup>And he said to them, “How many loaves do you have? Go and see.” And when they had found out, they said, “Five, and two fish.” <sup>39</sup>Then he commanded them all to sit down in groups on the green grass. <sup>40</sup>So they sat down in groups, by hundreds and by fifties. <sup>41</sup>And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing and broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the people. And he divided the two fish among them all. <sup>42</sup>And they all ate and were satisfied. <sup>43</sup>And they took up twelve baskets full of broken pieces and of the fish. <sup>44</sup>And those who ate the loaves were five thousand men. <sup>45</sup>Immediately he made his disciples get into the boat and go before him to the other side, to Bethsaida, while he dismissed the crowd. <sup>46</sup>And after he had taken leave of them, he went up on the mountain to pray. <sup>47</sup>And when evening came, the boat was out on the sea, and he was alone on the land. <sup>48</sup>And he saw that they were making headway painfully, for the wind was against them. And about the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea. He meant to pass by them, <sup>49</sup>but when they saw him walking on the sea they thought it was a ghost, and cried out, <sup>50</sup>for they all saw him and were terrified. But immediately he spoke to them and said, “Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid.” <sup>51</sup>And he got into the boat with them, and the wind ceased. And they were utterly astounded, <sup>52</sup>for they did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened. <sup>53</sup>When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret and moored to the shore. <sup>54</sup>And when they got out of the boat, the people immediately recognized him <sup>55</sup>and ran about the whole region and began to bring the sick people on their beds to wherever they heard he was. <sup>56</sup>And wherever he came, in villages, cities, or countryside, they laid the sick in the marketplaces and implored him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched it were made well.
6.overview:
Chapter 6 is the widest swing in the Gospel: a village that will not have him, a mission that works, a prophet murdered at a birthday party, a hillside fed until it could eat no more, and a man walking on water in the last watch of the night.

It opens at Nazareth, where the questions asked about Jesus are exactly the right ones — where did this man get these things? what is the wisdom given to him? — and the conclusion drawn is the worst in the book. They knew his trade, his mother, his brothers by name, and the knowing is precisely what stopped them.

Then Mark does something structurally deliberate. He sends the Twelve out (vv. 7–13), interrupts them with thirteen verses on the death of John the Baptist — by far the longest passage in this Gospel about anyone other than Jesus — and only then lets them come back (v. 30). Anyone reading to find out what following costs has just been told, and told at length: the greatest man born of women dies alone in a cellar because a girl danced well and a weak king could not bear to look foolish in front of his officers.

The second half answers the first. The crowd that ruins the disciples' day off is met with compassion rather than irritation, because he sees sheep without a shepherd; five loaves in his hands feed a district with twelve baskets over; and the men who could only do arithmetic are the ones who carry it out to the rows.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — Rejection, Mission, and the Death of John
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Home (vv. 1–6). He goes back to Nazareth and preaches in the synagogue he grew up in, and the village is offended. They know his trade, his mother, his brothers by name and his sisters by sight, and the knowledge is exactly what stops them. Mark records that he could do no mighty work there, and that he marvelled at their unbelief.

The sending (vv. 7–13). Twelve men are sent out in pairs with authority over unclean spirits and instructions to carry almost nothing. They preach repentance, cast out demons, and anoint the sick with oil — and they are sent before they understand very much at all.

The dungeon (vv. 14–29). Then Mark stops the mission dead and tells, at length and out of sequence, how John the Baptist died: a birthday party, a dance, a rash oath, a girl sent to ask her mother, and a head brought in on a serving dish. Herod is not a monster. He is a weak man who liked listening to a preacher and would not be changed by him.

Note where Mark has put that story. He interrupts the sending of the Twelve with a martyrdom, and only then lets them come back. Anyone reading this Gospel to find out what following costs has just been told.
verseByVerse.theology:
Could he not, or would he not? Verse 5 is one of the most startling sentences in Mark — he could do no mighty work there — and it should not be softened into he chose not to. Mark wrote what he wrote.

But read the exception clause, because it settles the meaning: except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them. Whatever the limitation was, it was not a failure of power; he healed people in Nazareth that afternoon. The impossibility is moral, not mechanical. In a village that had decided in advance what he was, mighty works would have been mere spectacle — and Jesus does not do spectacle for people who have already ruled out the conclusion. He had refused exactly that to the Pharisees (8:11–12) and would refuse it to Herod himself (Luke 23:8–9).

Faith is not a mechanism that generates miracles, as though God were a machine and belief the coin. It is the setting in which he ordinarily works, because he deals with persons and not with material. Unbelief does not disable God. It makes his help unwelcome, and he does not force it.

And he marvelled. There are only two things in the Gospels said to have astonished Jesus. He marvelled at the faith of a Roman officer who had no Bible and no upbringing in it (Luke 7:9), and he marvelled at the unbelief of the village that had raised him. The people with every advantage astonished him in the wrong direction.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Herod, who feared John, knew he was a righteous man, protected him from a wife who wanted him dead, was greatly perplexed by his preaching — and heard him gladly. Gladly. He enjoyed it. He came back for more of it.

Now: the most searching portrait in the chapter, because Herod is not a scoffer and never was. He is the rocky ground of chapter 4 given a name and a palace — the word received with real interest, real feeling, even real pleasure, and no root at all. Being moved by a sermon is not being changed by one, and the platter is the proof.

Everything was there in that man except the one thing that matters. He would not repent — and a man who will not repent will eventually have to silence the voice that keeps asking him to. It took a party, a dance and an audience to get it done, but it was decided long before the executioner was sent.

So the honest test is not whether you enjoy good preaching. Herod did. It is whether there is anything the preaching has actually cost you this year.

verseByVerse.quote: He went away from there and came to his hometown, and his disciples followed him. And on the Sabbath he began to teach in the synagogue, and many who heard him were astonished, saying, "Where did this man get these things? What is the wisdom given to him? How are such mighty works done by his hands?
verseByVerse.commentary:
They ask exactly the right questions about Jesus — and stop one honest step short of the answer.

Going home. Mark doesn’t name it: Nazareth, a village of a few hundred where he had lived some thirty years. Everyone in that synagogue had known him since he was small, bought from his workshop, perhaps seen him at Joseph’s funeral; Joseph has vanished from the record by now. And “his disciples followed him”: not a private visit, but a rabbi returning with a following — what a village finds hardest to swallow. (Luke records a visit, probably earlier, when he read Isaiah 61 and said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing,” Luke 4:16–21.)

Astonishment that turns. The same verb used of Capernaum in chapter 1, where it opened into faith. Here it goes the other way, and Mark lets you watch it turn.

The right questions. “Where did this man get these things?” — fair: no one in Nazareth taught him this, and he had no rabbinic training. “What is the wisdom given to him?” — they can hear it is wisdom; they don’t pretend the sermon was poor; and “given” holds half the answer in their own question. “How are such mighty works done by his hands?” — they don’t dispute the miracles either.

Near is not in. A village asking the right questions about Jesus — where does this come from, what is this wisdom, how are these things done — and arriving at the worst answer in the Gospel. One honest step from the truth, and they won’t take it, because the step costs too much. That isn’t only a first-century failure. You can acknowledge that his teaching is extraordinary, his influence inexplicable, that something happened around him ordinary categories don’t cover — and stop there for good, because the next sentence would rearrange your life. These people weren’t fools or liars. They were near. A test: what is the next step you already know you should take with Christ, and won’t?
verseByVerse.note: His hometown is Nazareth.

verseByVerse.quote: Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon? And are not his sisters here with us?" And they took offense at him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Familiarity can blind people to who Jesus really is — yet even his once-unbelieving brothers came to worship him after the resurrection.

The carpenter. The astonishment curdles on one word. The only place in the Gospels where Jesus himself is called a carpenter (Matthew has “the carpenter’s son,” 13:55). The word means a craftsman in hard materials — wood, and in that stony country often stone: doors, roof beams, ploughs, yokes, furniture. For perhaps eighteen years the eternal Son did a trade in a village workshop, and these people had his work in their houses; there were roofs in Nazareth that afternoon he had built. That is the offence: you can’t easily worship a man who fixed your door.

Son of Mary. A Jewish man was normally named as his father’s son, even after the father died. To call a grown man his mother’s son in his own village may well have carried a barb — a whisper that the dates of the wedding and the birth had never quite added up.

Were these Jesus’ real brothers and sisters? The question has divided the church. Rome and the Orthodox, holding that Mary remained a virgin all her life, take them as cousins (Jerome) or as Joseph’s children by an earlier marriage (the Orthodox view). But the words most naturally mean what they say: later sons and daughters of Joseph and Mary, Jesus’ younger half-brothers and half-sisters. Matthew says Joseph “knew her not until she had given birth to a son” (Matthew 1:25), and Luke calls Jesus her “firstborn” (Luke 2:7), a word that waits for others to follow. The more likely reading is the plain one. Mary’s honour isn’t lifelong virginity but that she bore and raised the Son of God, and then mothered his brothers.

What changed his brothers. During his ministry “not even his brothers believed in him” (John 7:5); here they are among the offended, and in chapter 3 they came to take him home as mad (3:21, 31). Then they are in the upper room praying after the resurrection (Acts 1:14). James becomes the pillar of the Jerusalem church and writes as “a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (James 1:1); Judas, in this list, writes Jude. What turns a scornful younger brother into a man who calls his own sibling Lord and dies for it? No one is fooled by a brother. Paul names it in a line: “Then he appeared to James” (1 Corinthians 15:7).

Offended. The root of our word “scandal”: he was a stumbling block, and what they tripped over was that they knew him. That is the warning for anyone raised in a Christian home or a long-attended church. Familiarity doesn’t produce faith; it can produce the opposite — a comfortable, unastonished acquaintance with the most extraordinary Person who ever lived, filed under things you have always known. A test: when did Jesus last astonish you?
verseByVerse.note: “Carpenter” is a general word for a builder or craftsman in wood or stone.

parallels.desc: even his brothers did not believe

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, "A prophet is not without honor, except in his hometown and among his relatives and in his own household." And he could do no mighty work there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them. And he marveled because of their unbelief. And he went about among the villages teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unbelief doesn’t disable God but makes his help unwelcome; Jesus knows the pain of rejection by family, and he keeps going.

Narrowing pain. Probably already a proverb, but notice how it narrows and hurts more as it goes: town, then relatives, then the house he grew up in. And he speaks of himself, with his brothers in the room among the offended.

For the misunderstood at home. If your family think your faith a phase, an embarrassment or a mild derangement — if you dread the Christmas table for the sighs — let this verse do its work. He wasn’t spared it. He was refused in the village where he had been a good neighbour for thirty years, by relatives who could name every brother. And remember where those brothers ended up. Nothing you say to a family member will do what the risen Christ can do to them, and he had to rise from the dead to convince his. Keep praying for yours.

Could he really do nothing? One of Mark’s most startling sentences. Matthew softens it to “he did not do many mighty works there” (Matthew 13:58); Mark says “could not,” deliberately. But the exception settles it: “except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them.” Sick people in Nazareth got up well that day. The limit wasn’t power but something moral. In a place that had already decided what he was, mighty works would have been mere spectacle, and Jesus doesn’t perform. He refuses a sign to Pharisees who demand one (8:11–12) and stands silent before Herod Antipas, who wanted a miracle as one wants a conjuror (Luke 23:8–9).

Faith isn’t a coin in a machine. Faith isn’t a mechanism that produces miracles, as if God were a machine and belief the coin. It is the setting in which he ordinarily works, because he deals with persons, not material. Unbelief doesn’t disable God; it makes his help unwelcome, and he doesn’t force it on a town that has made up its mind.

Two marvels. Twice the Gospels say Jesus was astonished. He marvelled at a Roman officer with no Bible or covenant upbringing who said he need only say the word (Luke 7:9); and here, at the village that raised him and taught him the Scriptures. Those with none of the advantages astonished him one way; those with all of them, the other. A test: are your advantages making you more receptive to him, or less?

He went on. No sulking, long lament, or shaking of Nazareth’s dust. He goes to the next village and keeps preaching. Rejection at home didn’t stop him for a day.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called the twelve and began to send them out two by two, and gave them authority over the unclean spirits. He charged them to take nothing for their journey except a staff—no bread, no bag, no money in their belts— but to wear sandals and not put on two tunics.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ sends ordinary, unqualified disciples on his own authority, in partnership, depending on God and on the hospitality of others.

Sent ones. “Send out” is the verb behind “apostle,” a sent one; here the title begins to mean something. And notice how little they knew. Two chapters ago they asked, “Who then is this?”; before this chapter ends they will fail to understand the loaves. He sends them anyway, with real authority, to preach. If you are waiting to feel qualified before you say anything about Christ, notice that no one in this group was.

Two by two. Never alone. Practical wisdom — a road at night, the risk of accusation, the weight of doing it alone. A legal reason too: “Only on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses shall a charge be established” (Deuteronomy 19:15), and they bear testimony. And it is how the church went on: Paul and Barnabas, Paul and Silas. It also meant each went with a partner he didn’t choose; someone was paired with Simon the Zealot, someone with Matthew the tax collector (cf. Luke 10:1–4).

Authority given. Not developed, innate, or a technique learned by watching. Everything they do runs on borrowed authority — which is why it fails in chapter 9 when attempted out of habit rather than dependence (9:28–29).

Engineered dependence. The list is stripped: no food; no bag (a travelling pack, or possibly a beggar’s collecting bag that would have made them look like the religious hucksters of the day); no money in the belt; one tunic — a second served as the traveller’s blanket, so no change of clothes or bedding. Not asceticism for its own sake but dependence: they eat only if someone feeds them and sleep only if someone takes them in, so the mission can’t be done at arm’s length from the people it is for.

Are missionaries today bound to go without money or provisions? No. This was the instruction for one short mission in Galilee. Later Jesus recalled it — “When I sent you out with no moneybag or knapsack or sandals, did you lack anything?” — and then said things were now different: “let the one who has a moneybag take it” (Luke 22:35–36). The lasting principle is dependence on God and on the hospitality of his people, not a ban on preparation. A test: where are you so self-sufficient in your service that you no longer depend on God or anyone else?

Staff and sandals, or not? A favourite of sceptics: Mark says take a staff and wear sandals; Matthew has Jesus forbid both (Matthew 10:9–10), and Luke says take no staff (Luke 9:3). It dissolves when the verbs are examined. Matthew’s word is “acquire” — don’t procure them; Mark’s is “take,” carry along. One instruction stands behind both: don’t equip yourselves for this journey; don’t go shopping for a new staff or spare sandals, but go as you are, with the stick in your hand and the sandals on your feet. Both forbid the same thing — provisioning — which is the whole point. Matthew forbids the shopping trip; Mark permits the walking stick.
verseByVerse.note: Coins were carried in the belt; the “bag” was a traveller’s pack for supplies.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Whenever you enter a house, stay there until you depart from there. And if any place will not receive you and they will not listen to you, when you leave, shake off the dust that is on your feet as a testimony against them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s messengers must not use people for advancement, and they are responsible for faithful sowing, not for whether people accept the message.

Stay where you are received. Hospitality was owed to travellers, and a visiting teacher with a following would attract offers. The temptation, once established and talked about, was to move up — from the first house to a wealthier host and better room. Jesus forbids it: take the first door that opens and stay behind it.

What it protects. The poor family that risked something to receive them aren’t to be used as a stepping stone and quietly left. And the message: a preacher visibly working his way to the best address in town has already said something about himself that will drown out what he says about Christ. It isn’t obsolete. Every church and ministry has its version of climbing — cultivating the useful people, warmth that rises with a person’s influence. A test: are you warmer to people according to how useful they are to you?

Shaking off the dust. A devout Jew returning from Gentile territory shook the dust off his feet at the border so as not to carry pagan soil into the holy land — a visible gesture everyone could read: what belongs to you stays with you. Doing it on leaving a Jewish village was a shock. It said: you have put yourselves outside; we brought what was ours to bring, and the responsibility now rests with you (cf. Acts 13:51).

Told in advance what to do when it fails. The practical mercy in it. Jesus doesn’t send them expecting a clean sweep. He assumes refusal, names it, and gives them a way to leave that is neither bitter nor guilty. He doesn’t say, try harder, stay longer, keep pressing till they yield. He says: say your piece, and if they won’t have it, go — and don’t carry the town away with you in your shoes.

Sowing, not soil. For anyone who has talked to someone about Christ for years and got nowhere and begun to feel their unbelief is a verdict on your competence: it may be worth examining. But this verse assumes the ordinary case is otherwise — the message was brought faithfully and refused, and the refusal belonged to the hearer. You are responsible for the sowing, never for the soil, and someone who can’t shake the dust off will eventually stop going anywhere at all.
verseByVerse.note: Shaking off the dust was a sign that a town was being left to God’s judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: So they went out and proclaimed that people should repent. And they cast out many demons and anointed with oil many who were sick and healed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heart of their message is a call to turn to God, and the church today is still to pray for the sick, with the elders anointing them in the Lord’s name, trusting God with the outcome.

Turn round. Their message in a few words: “that people should repent” — Jesus’ own opening word (1:15). Repentance isn’t being sorry. Remorse looks at yourself and feels bad; repentance turns round and goes the other way — the mind changed, the road reversed. A direction, not a mood. Not a technique for a better life or a defence of Jesus’ credentials. Turn round.

It worked. The authority of v. 7 proved real in their hands, as the seventy-two later came back astonished at the same thing (Luke 10:17).

What is the oil for? The only place in the Gospels where anointing with oil accompanies healing, and James tells the church to do the same: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord” (James 5:14). It isn’t medicine, though oil was used medicinally (Luke 10:34); these healings aren’t pharmacological. Nor magic; nothing suggests power in the oil. It is a sign: something physical laid on a sick body, saying God is being asked to act here, on this person, now. Oil in the Old Testament set people and things apart for God — kings, priests, the tabernacle. To be anointed is to be claimed as his.

Send for the elders. That is why James can tell an ordinary congregation to do it, and it is a pity many churches have quietly dropped it. If you are seriously ill, the New Testament instruction isn’t to suffer privately and hope someone remembers you in a service, but to send for your elders and ask them to pray over you and anoint you — a concrete thing you are entitled to ask for. And James puts the power where it belongs: “the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up” (James 5:15). The Lord will — not the oil or the elders.

Should we expect healings like these today? These were signs given through the Twelve as they were sent out, part of the apostolic witness (cf. 2 Corinthians 12:12). What continues is what James describes: the elders praying over the sick, with oil as a sign of setting them before the Lord (James 5:14–15). God hears such prayers and sometimes heals, often through ordinary means. But no one is promised that every prayer for healing will be answered with recovery, and when healing doesn’t come, the prayer hasn’t failed. The final healing waits for the resurrection.

Borrowed authority. Mark’s summary is deliberately plain: they preached, cast out, anointed, and people were healed. Twelve men who couldn’t yet answer “Who then is this?” did all that on borrowed authority, because he sent them. A test: is there someone sick you should pray over, or a time you should ask your elders to pray for you?
verseByVerse.note: Olive oil was used as medicine and as a sign of God’s blessing.

parallels.desc: anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord

verseByVerse.quote: King Herod heard of it, for Jesus' name had become known. Some said, "John the Baptist has been raised from the dead. That is why these miraculous powers are at work in him." But others said, "He is Elijah." And others said, "He is a prophet, like one of the prophets of old." But when Herod heard of it, he said, "John, whom I beheaded, has been raised."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Popular opinions about Jesus are respectful but far too small, and an unaddressed guilty conscience keeps its accurate record and torments.

The noise reaches the palace. The mission worked; six pairs covered the district, and word reached Herod. “King” is a courtesy: Herod Antipas was a tetrarch, a Roman-appointed ruler of a quarter, and his ambition to be called king eventually got him exiled. Mark uses the title locals used.

Three verdicts, all too small. John raised; Elijah; a prophet like those of old. Each respectful, each far too small, and each will return almost word for word when Jesus asks his disciples who people say he is (8:28) — and then asks them. The crowd reaches for the biggest category it already has; it never occurs to anyone that a new category might be needed. That instinct hasn’t aged. Ask today and you get the same shape at a lower altitude: great teacher, moral genius, mystic, revolutionary. All respectful, all too small — and all cost nothing. A test: is your Jesus big enough to require something of you?

“Whom I beheaded.” One of the most chilling sentences in the Gospel, because of one word. He could have said “who was beheaded,” or blamed his wife who wanted it, the oath that trapped him, the guests who watched — every excuse was available and he used them all at the time. Alone in his own head months later, it comes out in the first person.

A conscience that keeps the record. Herod has managed this ever since, and the moment he hears of miracles in Galilee his mind goes straight to the man he killed and produces a resurrection to explain it. He isn’t reasoning; he is haunted — a man who can’t hear good news without hearing his own crime in it. Guilt doesn’t fade because unaddressed; it goes underground and comes up sideways, in dreams, irrational fears, the inability to enjoy anything. An unaddressed conscience doesn’t stop working; it stops being useful and becomes a torment. And there is one place where it can be dealt with. Herod had a prophet in his cellar who would have told him where, and he preferred listening to obeying. Now he has a ghost. Is there something you need to bring to Christ rather than keep managing?

A long flashback. Mark now goes back to tell how it happened — thirteen verses, by far the longest account in his Gospel of anything not directly involving Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: “King” Herod is Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee and Perea; his official title was tetrarch.

verseByVerse.quote: For it was Herod who had sent and seized John and bound him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip's wife, because he had married her. For John had been saying to Herod, "It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faithful witness names sin plainly, personally and to a person’s face — and it is costly.

A desert prison. The setting, according to Josephus, is the fortress of Machaerus, a grim hilltop stronghold east of the Dead Sea. The man who baptised thousands in the open Jordan valley, shut in a cell in a desert castle.

The squalid arrangement. Herod Antipas was married. Visiting Rome, he stayed with a half-brother and formed an attachment to his wife, Herodias — also his own niece, a granddaughter of Herod the Great. He came home, put away his first wife (daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas, which later cost him a war and an army), and married Herodias. A man leaves his wife for his brother’s wife, who is also his niece. The law isn’t ambiguous: “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother’s wife” (Leviticus 18:16; cf. 20:21).

He kept saying it. The tense is continuous. Not one outburst Herod overheard; John said it, said it again, kept saying it to the ruler’s face.

A model of faithful rebuke. It is short — one sentence, not a treatise on marriage. It is specific — not a general denunciation of immorality in high places, which costs nothing and changes no one, but this man and this marriage. It is addressed to the man himself, not preached about him in the safety of a crowd that already agreed. And it is about his sin, not his politics; John had no comment on taxes or building projects, only on what Herod would answer to God for. And it cost John his freedom and his head.

When a name is attached. That is always the price of the fourth item. It is safe to denounce sins in general, sins of people not present, sins no one in your circle commits. The moment a name is attached, it becomes expensive — which is why prophets are few and courtiers many. Someone who tells the king only what he can bear isn’t a prophet but staff.

Not a licence for a sharp tongue. John wasn’t rude or indiscriminate; he had words for crowds, tax collectors and soldiers, each fitted to them (Luke 3:10–14). And he said it to the man’s face, repeatedly, risking everything — very different from criticising the powerful at no cost, from a distance, to an audience that will applaud. A test: is there someone you have been talking about whom love requires you to talk to?
verseByVerse.note: Herodias had been married to Antipas’s half-brother; the law forbade marrying a brother’s wife while he lived.

verseByVerse.quote: And Herodias had a grudge against him and wanted to put him to death. But she could not, for Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man, and he kept him safe. When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is possible to respect the truth, be stirred by it and even enjoy hearing it, while refusing to repent — a deeply dangerous condition.

A nursed grudge. She held it against him and nursed it — not a flash of temper but a settled campaign, waiting for its chance (v. 21 calls it “an opportunity”). John’s sentence was aimed at Herod, but it was Herodias who couldn’t live with it, because it named her position: she wasn’t a wife. Every day John lived, that fact lived in the kingdom. When a sin is named, some repent, some argue, and some set out to destroy the one who said it, as if removing the witness would remove the fact. It never does, but it is one of the most reliable human behaviours, and why speaking plainly to power has always been dangerous.

Herod’s portrait. The most searching thing in the chapter, because he isn’t a monster, and everything here is to his credit until it isn’t. “Herod feared John” — not fright at a prisoner but awe, the involuntary respect a slack man feels before a serious one. “Knowing that he was a righteous and holy man” — his assessment is correct. “He kept him safe” — he protected John against his own wife.

Did Herod want John dead or not? Matthew says Herod wanted to put him to death but feared the people (Matthew 14:5). Both are true. Herod’s feelings were divided, as Mark shows: he arrested John, feared him, protected him from Herodias, and listened gladly. A man can want a voice silenced and still be drawn to it.

Perplexed and glad. John’s preaching disturbed him, left him at a loss; the word was getting through; he wasn’t bored. “And yet he heard him gladly.” He sent for him, came back for more — the ruler of Galilee going down into his own prison to listen to the man he had chained, being upset, and returning to be upset again. He enjoyed it.

The most dangerous condition. It looks so much like the real thing. Interest, respect, emotion, protection of the preacher, genuine disturbance of conscience — and no repentance. The one thing John asked for week after week was the one thing Herod wouldn’t do. Herodias stayed. He is the rocky ground of chapter 4 with a name and a palace.

A test. You can love good preaching — seek it, be moved and stirred by it, talk warmly about it afterward — and be, in the settled arrangements of your life, entirely unchanged. Herod would have said he had a high view of preaching. He did. The question isn’t whether the sermon moved you but whether anything in your house is different because of it. Name one thing it has actually cost you this year. A man who won’t repent must eventually silence the voice asking him to; Herod didn’t want John dead, but the logic of unrepented sin runs one way, and it took only a party, a dance and an audience to finish what had been decided long before.

verseByVerse.quote: But an opportunity came when Herod on his birthday gave a banquet for his nobles and military commanders and the leading men of Galilee. For when Herodias's daughter came in and danced, she pleased Herod and his guests. And the king said to the girl, "Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you." And he vowed to her, "Whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pride, the desire to impress others, and careless oaths set a trap that leads to great evil.

A well-timed day. “An opportunity came” — literally a good day, the one Herodias had waited for.

The guest list. Everything turns on it: his nobles (the court), military commanders (the army), and leading men of Galilee (the money and influence). Every man whose opinion Herod cares about, in one hall, on his birthday — the most public night of his year, and by its end a man will be dead.

A squalid dance. Josephus names the daughter Salome; Mark calls her “the girl,” a word for a young girl. We have romanticised this scene, and the reality is squalid. A royal princess didn’t dance at a stag banquet for drunk officers; hired entertainers of low status did. Herodias sent her own daughter to do a dancing girl’s work before her stepfather and Galilee’s whole military command. She was willing to use her child that way to get what she wanted — the measure of the grudge.

A theatrical oath. Three things are wrong with it. It is theatre: Herod performing for the room, buying a moment of admiration with a grand gesture; he doesn’t merely offer but vows, and v. 26 says “oaths,” plural. It is empty: he had no kingdom to give half of; as a tetrarch holding power at Rome’s pleasure, he couldn’t give away a square mile. And it is borrowed: “up to half of my kingdom” is what King Ahasuerus says to Esther (Esther 5:3, 6; 7:2). Every Jew in the hall would catch it, and the echo is unbearable: there the offer was used by a brave woman to save a nation; here, by a girl to fetch a prophet’s head on a plate.

Inflated words. A man who can’t say a small true sentence and can’t stop himself saying a large false one, and in ninety seconds it will have him. The New Testament makes the warning explicit: “let your ‘yes’ be yes and your ‘no’ be no” (James 5:12; cf. Matthew 5:37) — for exactly this reason. Someone who inflates his words to impress a room will one day find himself behind a promise he never meant, before people he can’t bear to disappoint. A test: where do you overpromise to impress?
verseByVerse.note: The historian Josephus names Herodias’s daughter Salome.

parallels.desc: up to half of my kingdom

verseByVerse.quote: And she went out and said to her mother, "For what should I ask?" And she said, "The head of John the Baptist." And she came in immediately with haste to the king and asked, saying, "I want you to give me at once the head of John the Baptist on a platter." And the king was exceedingly sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he did not want to break his word to her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A nursed grudge consumes everything else, and the fear of losing face before others can drive even a reluctant person to terrible evil.

She had to ask. Given an open cheque before the whole court, the girl doesn’t know what she wants and goes out to ask her mother — a child in every sense, and a pointer to where the will in this story lives.

The answer ready. “The head of John the Baptist.” No hesitation; Herodias had the answer ready for months. She asks nothing for herself or the girl — not land, money, jewels or position, though offered half a kingdom. Nothing in the world does she want as much as that voice stopped. That is what a nursed grudge does to a person’s appetites: it eats everything else. Given one unlimited wish, she spends it on a man in a cell who had done her no injury except to tell the truth. A test: what grudge are you feeding, and what is it eating in you?

On a platter. The girl hurries back — “immediately with haste” — pleased to have an answer, and improves on it: “at once,” and “on a platter.” The platter is her own: a serving dish, like those the food is coming round on. In a hall of banqueting men she asks for a head on the crockery. Mark doesn’t comment. This is what becomes of a child raised in that house.

Exceedingly sorry. A strong word, the one used of Jesus in Gethsemane (14:34). Herod’s distress is real; he doesn’t want this. “But because of his oaths and his guests he did not want to break his word.” The whole reason a man is beheaded tonight: his oaths, sworn loudly, twice — he is now the man who said it; and his guests — nobles, officers, the leading men of Galilee, all looking at him, waiting.

Was Herod bound to keep his oath? No. An oath to do evil binds no one; it should be repented of, not carried out. The law made provision for one who had sworn rashly (Leviticus 5:4–6), and Jephthah’s vow stands in Scripture as a warning, not an example. Herod’s real bond was not to God but to the faces around his table. A terrible piety: scrupulous about an oath, murderous about a prophet.

The fear of looking foolish. What he couldn’t face was backing down in front of that room. Not conscience — he had lost that argument and knew John was righteous. Not law — no law allowed executing a prisoner to settle a dinner-party bet. He couldn’t bear to look foolish before people whose opinion he had courted all his life. The most ordinary murder motive in the world, and why this isn’t really about ancient kings. Almost no one does the worst thing they ever do because they wanted to, but because backing out before the watchers was unthinkable: the joke you laughed at, the thing you went along with because the room had turned, the stand you didn’t take because of who would see. Peter is eight chapters from denying Jesus to a servant girl for this reason. “The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe” (Proverbs 29:25). A king with an army was walked into a murder he didn’t want by a girl and a roomful of guests. Where is the fear of others steering you?

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately the king sent an executioner with orders to bring John's head. He went and beheaded him in the prison and brought his head on a platter and gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother. When his disciples heard of it, they came and took his body and laid it in a tomb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faithfulness to God does not guarantee deliverance in this life — but John’s death points to Christ, whose tomb could not hold him.

As long as a walk to the cells. “Immediately the king sent an executioner” — kept on the staff, and everyone knew what for. “He went and beheaded him in the prison.” Mark won’t embellish: no description of the cell, whether John slept, or any last word. A door opening in the dark and a soldier with an order.

The greatest, dying in a cellar. One of the hardest things in the Gospel. This is the man Jesus called the greatest born of women (Matthew 11:11) — the forerunner, the voice in the wilderness, who baptised the Son of God, saw heaven torn open, and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God.” He dies in a cellar, alone, unheard, with no recorded last word, because a girl danced well at a party.

No rescue. The Gospel doesn’t soften it. Jesus was alive and a few days’ walk away, healing strangers, and John — who from that fortress had sent to ask, “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?” (Matthew 11:3) — wasn’t delivered. The answer he got wasn’t “I’m coming to get you” but a message about the blind seeing and the poor hearing good news, and a blessing on the one not offended by him. John died with the question answered and the door still locked.

Faithfulness isn’t a contract with providence. If you are serving God faithfully and things are getting worse, that is in your Bible on purpose and isn’t a sign something has gone wrong. Hebrews knows it: some by faith stopped lions’ mouths and escaped the sword — and others, by the same faith, were sawn in two and killed with the sword (Hebrews 11:33–37). It puts them in one list and calls it all faith. A test: are you trusting God only for deliverance, or for himself whether or not he delivers?

The dish. It comes into the hall, passes to a girl, and she carries it to her mother. Mark stops the sentence there. Herodias has what she wanted; what she does with it we aren’t told.

The one clean act. John’s disciples — powerless, with everything to lose, walking into a Herodian fortress to ask for a headless body — take it and bury it properly. They couldn’t save or avenge him. They could carry him, and did.

Another tomb. Mark’s readers will meet this sentence again in nearly the same words: another righteous man executed by a frightened ruler who knew he was innocent, and friends who took the body and laid it in a tomb (15:45–46). The difference is what came next. Herod’s dungeon kept John. The tomb outside Jerusalem couldn’t keep the One John pointed to — and because it couldn’t, the man in that cell isn’t finally a tragedy. He lost his head for telling a king the truth, and he will see the King.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–56 — The Feeding, the Walking, and the Healings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The rest that never happened (vv. 30–34). The apostles come back full of what they have done, and Jesus's first instruction is not a debrief but a retreat: come away and rest. They get into a boat — and the crowd works out where they are going, runs round the head of the lake on foot, and is waiting when they land. His response to a wrecked afternoon off is compassion, because they were like sheep without a shepherd.

The feeding (vv. 35–44). The disciples do the arithmetic and propose dispersal. Jesus hands the problem back: you give them something to eat. Then he seats a crowd of thousands in ranks on the spring grass, takes five loaves and two fish, and there is more left at the end than there was at the start.

The lake in the fourth watch of the night (vv. 45–52). He sends them off ahead and goes up the mountain alone to pray — and from up there, in the dark, he sees them straining at the oars. He comes to them on the water, and he means to pass by, in the language the Old Testament reserves for God showing himself.

Gennesaret (vv. 53–56). And then a summary paragraph of pure mercy: whole villages carrying the sick out into the marketplaces, and everyone who touched even the edge of his clothing made well.
verseByVerse.theology:
He meant to pass by them (v. 48) is the strangest clause in the chapter, and it is not what it sounds like. He is not trying to overtake them or slip past unnoticed. Passing by is the Old Testament's own vocabulary for God making himself visible.

When Moses asked to see the glory of God, the LORD put him in a cleft of the rock and said while my glory passes by I will cover you with my hand (Ex. 33:22). When Elijah stood at the mouth of the cave, the word was behold, the LORD passed by (1 Kgs. 19:11). And Job, describing the God no man can lay hold of, says he alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea — and then, three verses later, behold, he passes by me, and I see him not (Job 9:8, 11).

Walking on the sea and passing by, in the same sentence, out of the same book. Mark's readers who knew their Scriptures were not being told about a shortcut.

And then, when they scream, he speaks: Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid. The middle phrase is egō eimi — literally I am, the words from the burning bush (Ex. 3:14). It is the ordinary way to say it's me, and in this setting, on that water, from that Person, it is very much more.

Which makes verse 52 the saddest verse in the chapter: they did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened. Mark uses of the Twelve the very word he used of the men in the synagogue who watched a withered hand restored and went out to plan a murder (3:5). Hardness is not a disease of unbelievers only.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: twelve exhausted men doing sums in front of a hungry crowd — two hundred denarii, most of a year's wages, and it still would not be enough — and hearing you give them something to eat.

Now: anyone facing a need that is plainly larger than their resources. The parent who has run out of wisdom. The pastor of a small church looking at a large town. The person asked to care for someone whose needs exceed anything they have.

Jesus is not asking them to solve it. He asks a different question, and it is the practical one: how many loaves do you have? Go and see. Not how many do you need — how many have you got. Go and count it.

Five loaves and two fish is an embarrassing answer to give in front of five thousand people, and it was the right answer, because the multiplication happens in his hands and not in theirs. Bring what you actually have, including how little it is. And notice who ended up carrying the twelve baskets of surplus: the men who had nothing to give, one basket each.

verseByVerse.quote: The apostles returned to Jesus and told him all that they had done and taught. And he said to them, "Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while." For many were coming and going, and they had no leisure even to eat. And they went away in the boat to a desolate place by themselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus cares for his servants’ need for rest, and calls them to stop — especially after success.

Apostles. One of the few places Mark calls the Twelve apostles (cf. 3:14), and exactly the right moment: they have just been sent and come back. And they are full of it — “all that they had done and taught,” probably several talking at once. Demons came out; the sick got up. It worked.

Rest, not strategy. Watch what he does, because it isn’t what a modern ministry would do. No debrief, no strategy session on building momentum, no pressing the advantage at the moment of greatest success. Rest. He doesn’t even say pray, though he will go and do that himself. “Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while.”

Tiredness isn’t a badge. Christians are peculiarly bad at this. There is a way of serving God that treats tiredness as a badge and rest as a shameful concession, and it isn’t in this Gospel. The Lord of the harvest, with a district stirred and more open doors than he could walk through, took twelve effective men out of circulation and sent them to rest.

A measurable diagnostic. “They had no leisure even to eat” — the same detail as 3:20; not a hard week but a pattern. And it is measurable, not vague. Not “Do I feel busy?” — everyone does. Are ordinary human things being squeezed out? Meals eaten standing up. Sleep treated as the flexible item. Days off that became half days and then nothing. When the basics go, something has gone wrong that no fruitfulness justifies, and Jesus treated it as a reason to stop, not a sign of seriousness. A test: which basic — food, sleep, a day off — is God telling you to restore this week?

Rest planned — and ruined. They actually go. The rest was his idea, he arranged it, they obeyed — and in three verses it will be ruined. Planning rest is right, and it will still sometimes be taken from you. What matters is what you do when it is; that is the next verse.

verseByVerse.quote: Now many saw them going and recognized them, and they ran there on foot from all the towns and got there ahead of them. When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. And he began to teach them many things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even when exhausted and interrupted, Jesus is moved to deep compassion, and he is the true Shepherd who feeds his people first with God’s word.

The plan fails. They are seen leaving; someone works out from the boat’s direction where they are heading; word goes along the shore, and people set off round the lake on foot and arrive first. Picture the boat coming in: twelve exhausted men, promised a quiet day, rowing toward an empty shore and seeing, as it comes into view, that it is covered with thousands of people already waiting. Anyone who has needed a day off knows what would rise in the chest.

Compassion in the gut. “He had compassion on them.” He is tired; his plan is destroyed; these are the people he left to escape, and they have chased him round the lake. And he is moved. The word is one of the strongest for pity in Greek, built on the word for the inward organs — moved in the gut. Not a decision to be nice but what happens inside him when he sees them. A test: when interrupted by people’s needs, what rises in you first — irritation, or compassion? Ask him for his.

Sheep without a shepherd. Not a general remark about lostness but a loaded quotation. It is Moses’ prayer for a successor, “that the congregation of the LORD may not be as sheep that have no shepherd” (Numbers 27:17); Micaiah’s vision of Israel scattered after a bad king (1 Kings 22:17); and behind both Ezekiel 34’s denunciation of shepherds who feed themselves, not the flock, and God’s answer: “I, I myself will search for my sheep and will seek them out” (Ezekiel 34:11); “I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep” (Ezekiel 34:15). He isn’t merely sorry for a crowd. He sees the ancient failure — people with no one to feed them — and every one of those texts has an answer, and he is it.

Teaching first. What does compassion produce first? Not loaves or healing, but teaching. A striking order, as in 2:2. Given a hungry, tired, spiritually starving crowd, he gives words first — because the deepest thing wrong with shepherdless sheep is that no one has fed them, and Ezekiel’s complaint is about food. He will reach their stomachs before the day ends; he starts with what they didn’t know they came for.

parallels.desc: not as sheep without a shepherd

verseByVerse.quote: And when it grew late, his disciples came to him and said, "This is a desolate place, and the hour is now late. Send them away to go into the surrounding countryside and villages and buy themselves something to eat." But he answered them, "You give them something to eat." And they said to him, "Shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give it to them to eat?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus gives his people tasks beyond their resources to teach them to reckon on him, not just on arithmetic.

Sensible disciples. Grant them this before watching them fail: they are right about the facts. An empty place, getting dark, thousands with no arrangements made. And their solution is obvious: disperse them while there is light, and let everyone sort himself out.

Reduce the need. The standard shape of religious problem-solving: the need is real, resources insufficient, so reduce the need — send them away. Not callous; they want people fed. It just never occurs to them that the man beside them might be a factor in the calculation — and they have just come back from casting out demons.

“You give them something.” The weight falls on the pronoun. Not fair, and not meant to be. He hands twelve tired men a responsibility plainly, mathematically beyond them, and stands there while they work out what to do. It is one of his settled habits: the command that can’t be obeyed from your own resources. Stretch out your withered hand. Feed this crowd. Make disciples of all nations. Each impossible; each an invitation.

The spreadsheet. “Shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread?” A denarius was a labourer’s day’s wage; two hundred is most of a year’s income, which they don’t have and couldn’t spend in a village at dusk. You can hear the tone: not quite rude, not quite faith — someone showing his working to prove it can’t be done. And it is painful rather than funny: these men had recently cast out demons on borrowed authority, seen a paralytic walk, a leper cleansed, a girl raised, a hurricane muzzled. Standing beside the one who did it all, their response to a catering problem is a spreadsheet.

How normal it is. Before using it as a stick, be honest. Most of us pray about what we already half expect to manage and quietly do arithmetic about the rest. We have a small category for what God might do and a much larger one for what is realistically going to happen, and the second runs our week. Their sum wasn’t wrong; two hundred denarii really wouldn’t have been enough. They were correct, and beside the point, because they left out the only variable that mattered. A test: what need in front of you are you calculating without reckoning on Christ?
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer; two hundred denarii was most of a year’s wages.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "How many loaves do you have? Go and see." And when they had found out, they said, "Five, and two fish." Then he commanded them all to sit down in groups on the green grass. So they sat down in groups, by hundreds and by fifties.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ asks us to bring him what little we actually have, and he is the Shepherd and greater-than-Moses who feeds his people in the wilderness.

Go and count. He doesn’t answer the objection; he asks the practical question. Not “How much do you need?” — that paralysed them. “How many have you got? Go and see.” A method when a need is obviously beyond you: stop calculating the gap; find out exactly what is in your hands, however little, and bring it to him. The gap is his business; the inventory is yours.

Five, and two fish. Five small barley loaves from a boy in the crowd, John tells us — barley was the bread of the poor (John 6:9). The fish small and salted, a relish for bread rather than a meal. An embarrassing thing to report before five thousand hungry people. And the right answer. Christ has never been hindered by the smallness of what is brought to him; he has often been hindered by its being kept back. A test: what small thing are you holding back because it seems too little to matter?

The green grass. Peter’s eye: only Mark mentions the colour. In that country the hills are green for a few weeks in spring after the rains and brown the rest of the year; it tells the season (John says Passover was near) and that someone stood there and remembered what it looked like. It also puts a psalm into the scene: “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures” (Psalm 23:1–2). Mark has just called the crowd sheep without a shepherd. Now the Shepherd sits them on green grass and feeds them.

Hundreds and fifties. From above, the crowd would look like a hillside laid out in rectangles. Not crowd control. This is how Israel was organised in the wilderness: Moses appointed chiefs “of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens” (Exodus 18:25). A crowd seated in hundreds and fifties in a desolate place, about to receive bread from heaven at a leader’s hands, is Israel in the wilderness again — a new exodus, and the one arranging the ranks is greater than Moses, who never made a loaf and only announced that the manna had come.
verseByVerse.note: The groups of hundreds and fifties recall the way Moses organised Israel in the wilderness.

verseByVerse.quote: And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing and broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the people. And he divided the two fish among them all. And they all ate and were satisfied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ provides abundantly through thankful prayer and through his people’s obedient hands, foreshadowing the bread of his own body given for us.

Took, blessed, broke, gave. Four verbs every Christian reader should feel land. You meet them again in an upper room: “he took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to them, and said, ‘Take; this is my body’” (14:22). And at Emmaus two disciples recognise a stranger by the same sequence: “he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them. And their eyes were opened” (Luke 24:30–31). This isn’t the Lord’s Supper, but Mark lays the scenes on top of each other: the one who feeds a hillside with broken bread will be broken himself, and the church has eaten from that ever since.

Thanks before the provision. A Jewish blessing wasn’t said over the food but to God for it: “Blessed are you, LORD our God, King of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth.” He isn’t enchanting the loaves but thanking his Father aloud, over food obviously not enough, before a single extra crumb exists. Gratitude before provision is one of the plainest marks of faith, and easy to test at home: do you thank God for what is in front of you when you can see it won’t stretch?

Multiplied in their hands. Jesus doesn’t distribute; he hands it to the Twelve, who carry it to the ranks on the grass. So the multiplying happened in their hands. Mark doesn’t describe bread swelling. Somewhere between the Lord’s hands and the hundredth row there kept being more — and the carriers were the men who had just proved by arithmetic it couldn’t be done. That is still how he works. He seldom rains provision directly on those who need it; he gives it to his church to carry, and the carriers discover the sufficiency by handing it out. You won’t find out whether there is enough by standing still calculating. You find out on the fourth row. A test: what is he asking you to start handing out before you can see there is enough?

Filled. Emphatic, almost comic: the word for an animal fed to fullness. Not sampled or given a token; thousands ate until they had had enough. They came with no food, chasing a man round a lake, and the day ended with every one full (cf. 2 Kings 4:42–44).

verseByVerse.quote: And they took up twelve baskets full of broken pieces and of the fish. And those who ate the loaves were five thousand men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s provision is more than enough, never wasteful, and reaches far beyond what we start with — yet the crowd misunderstood what kind of King he was.

Nothing wasted. John says the gathering was commanded: “Gather up the leftover fragments, that nothing may be lost” (John 6:12). The one who has just created bread from five loaves won’t have scraps trodden into the grass. Abundance in God’s kingdom never licenses waste. There is no contradiction between believing God’s supply is endless and refusing to be careless with a slice of bread — and the One who made the supply gave the order. A test: does your confidence in God’s provision make you careless, or careful, with what he gives?

Twelve baskets. Twelve disciples, twelve tribes. Each man who went out with an impossible task and a fraction of a loaf comes back carrying a basket he can’t see the bottom of. Do their earlier sum and it comes out backwards: they began with five loaves and two fish and ended with more than they started with, after feeding a town. That is the kingdom’s accounting, and why the sum in v. 37 was the wrong question. “God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work” (2 Corinthians 9:8). The widow of Zarephath, down to a handful of flour and expecting one last meal, found the jar didn’t run out (1 Kings 17:14–16).

Five thousand men. Mark gives the number at the end, almost a footnote, and says “men” — males. Matthew makes it explicit: “besides women and children” (Matthew 14:21). The real figure was far larger, perhaps two or three times. Five thousand men is roughly a Roman legion, more than the population of any Galilean town except Tiberias and Sepphoris — the whole district sitting on the grass at dusk, fed. Because a boy handed over his lunch and twelve men did what they were told with what they had.

Nearly right, entirely wrong. What the crowd didn’t know: John records that they tried to make him king by force that night (John 6:15). They had eaten from his hands and concluded such a man should run the country. Nearly right, and entirely wrong. He hadn’t come to be the kind of king who keeps a nation fed, but to be the bread — and when he said so the next day, most of them left (John 6:66).

verseByVerse.quote: Immediately he made his disciples get into the boat and go before him to the other side, to Bethsaida, while he dismissed the crowd. And after he had taken leave of them, he went up on the mountain to pray. And when evening came, the boat was out on the sea, and he was alone on the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus refused a crown without a cross, and he met success, temptation and crisis alike with prayer.

He made them go. Something is cut short in a hurry, and the disciples plainly didn’t want to leave. John explains: the fed crowd was about to take him by force and make him king (John 6:15). Five thousand well-fed men on a hillside in an occupied country is a rebellion looking for a leader — and twelve disciples who had spent the evening handing out miraculous bread, one a Zealot, were in no state to resist the mood. So he breaks it up: men onto the boat, and the crowd dealt with himself.

A crown without a cross. What he refuses is a crown offered freely, by acclamation, without a cross — the shortcut the devil laid before him in the wilderness (cf. Matthew 4:8–9). He won’t take a kingdom on those terms, because a king who feeds you isn’t the same as a king who saves you.

Prayer with the first free hour. He has had no rest; the retreat was ruined; he has taught for hours, fed thousands, defused a political crisis, and personally dismissed a crowd of that size — a whole evening in a subordinate clause. And with the first free hour he climbs a hill in the dark to pray.

Three prayers alone. The second of three times Mark shows him praying alone, and their placing is the sermon: before dawn at the height of his popularity (1:35); here, on the night the nation tried to crown him; and in Gethsemane, the night they came to arrest him (14:32–39). Success, the offer of glory, the approach of death — handled the same way. That quietly exposes us. Most of us pray hardest at the third kind of moment and hardly at the first two. Prosperity is treated as needing no prayer, and it is the season in which people are most often lost. A test: when things are going well, does your praying increase or fade?

Separated in the dark. A boat somewhere in the dark, a man alone on the mountain. They are separated and can’t see him; night has come down between them. That is how a hard stretch feels from inside the boat — and the next verse changes everything.

verseByVerse.quote: And he saw that they were making headway painfully, for the wind was against them. And about the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea. He meant to pass by them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
While we struggle in the dark, Christ sees and prays for us, comes at his own right time, and reveals himself as God who treads the waves.

He saw them. Perhaps the most comforting clause in the chapter. Middle of the night, he on a mountain ashore, they three or four miles out on the lake (John 6:19). Whatever kind of seeing it was, he watched them the whole time. They didn’t know it. From inside the boat there was only wind, black water, and an empty horizon; every fact available said they were alone.

Tormented rowing. “Making headway painfully” — literally tormented in the rowing, the root of the word for torture. Not a storm threatening to sink them as in chapter 4, but worse in its way: hours of grinding, unrewarded effort. They row and the shore gets no closer. And “the wind was against them” — and they are out there because he sent them. Obedience put them in the wind.

The shape of much Christian experience. You are where he put you, pulling as hard as you can; nothing moves; he seems somewhere else entirely; and it is dark. The verse tells you what you can’t know from inside the boat: he is watching, and was all night, and praying while he watched. Verse 46 has him praying on the mountain; v. 48 has him seeing them from it. Those belong together and are still true: “he always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25). A test: in your long, hard rowing, do you remember who is watching and praying?

The fourth watch. Between three and six in the morning. They set out in the evening and have been at the oars perhaps nine hours. He came not at the first hour when it got hard, nor at midnight, but in the last watch, when men have stopped talking and are simply pulling. He is never early, as we would arrange it. He has never been late.

Passing by. “He meant to pass by them” sounds as though he would leave them to it. He didn’t. “Passing by” is the Old Testament’s language for God making himself visible. To Moses: “while my glory passes by I will put you in a cleft of the rock, and I will cover you with my hand” (Exodus 33:22). At Elijah’s cave: “And behold, the LORD passed by” (1 Kings 19:11). Most exactly, Job says God alone “stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea” (Job 9:8), and three verses later, “Behold, he passes by me, and I see him not” (Job 9:11). Trampling the waves and passing by, in one passage, about God. This isn’t a man taking a shortcut past a struggling boat but a self-revelation: coming to them in the dark on the water, doing what Job says God alone does, in the language of every appearance of God in their Bible. He wasn’t passing them by but passing before them, so they could see who had been watching from the mountain.
verseByVerse.note: The fourth watch was about 3 to 6 a.m. “Pass by” recalls God “passing by” Moses and Elijah to show his glory.

parallels.desc: I will make my goodness pass before you

verseByVerse.quote: but when they saw him walking on the sea they thought it was a ghost, and cried out, for they all saw him and were terrified. But immediately he spoke to them and said, "Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ sometimes comes in ways we first fear, and his comfort rests not on changed circumstances but on who he is — the great “I am.”

A ghost. Of course they cried out. Between three and six in the morning, hours into a headwind, wet, exhausted, frightened — and a figure moving on the water beside the boat. The word is “phantasma,” an apparition; in that world a shape on the sea at night was an omen of death, and every sailor had grown up on such stories.

Coming as what we dread. The fair thing first: the Lord of glory came in the exact form of their worst fear, and they didn’t recognise him. Not stupid — human. The one thing that could save them looked, in the dark, like what was most likely to kill them. That is often how it is. God has a way of coming to his people in the shape of what they most dread. Joseph’s brothers didn’t recognise their salvation in the man who had them arrested. What is bearing down on you out of the dark this year may be the Lord, and you may not know it at the time.

All of them. “They all saw him and were terrified.” Mark rules out one man’s imagination or a trick of light. Twelve men, four of them fishermen who had spent their lives on that water at night, saw the same thing.

His voice first. “Immediately he spoke to them.” The moment they cry out, he speaks — before the wind drops or he gets into the boat. Before anything about their circumstances changes, he tells them who he is. That is still the order in which he deals with frightened people.

“It is I.” Literally “I am.” In ordinary speech, how you identify yourself in the dark: it’s me. But these are the words God gave Moses at the bush — “I am who I am” (Exodus 3:14) — and they run through Isaiah on God’s lips: “I am he. Before me no god was formed” (Isaiah 43:10). Spoken here by a man standing on water, having crossed a sea that Scripture says God alone tramples.

The whole of Christian comfort. In order: “Take heart” — courage now, before anything changes. “It is I” — the reason, and the reason is a Person, not the weather, with the name from the bush. “Do not be afraid” — following only from the middle phrase. No argument: he doesn’t say the wind will drop or the night is nearly over. He tells them who is with them and treats that as enough. It is enough — spoken from the middle of the water they feared. A test: what are you waiting to change before you take heart? Take heart now, because of who he is.
verseByVerse.note: “It is I” can also be heard as the divine name, “I am.”

verseByVerse.quote: And he got into the boat with them, and the wind ceased. And they were utterly astounded, for they did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even devoted disciples can fail to learn from God’s past goodness and grow hardened — yet Christ does not give up on them but comes alongside them.

He gets in. After nine hours of rowing and a night of terror, an almost domestic ending: a man climbs over the side and sits with them, and the wind stops. Mark doesn’t even say he rebuked it. It simply stops, because he is aboard.

A verdict no church would invent. “They did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened.” This is the Gospel’s verdict on the Twelve, from a man whose information came from their chief, circulated while most were alive. And the connection isn’t the one we would expect: the walking on water astonished them because they hadn’t understood the loaves. The bread was the lesson. That afternoon they had carried food from his hands to five thousand and come back with twelve baskets, and drawn no conclusion about who he was. Had they understood the loaves, a man on the water wouldn’t have been a horror; it would have been the same Person doing the same kind of thing.

Past mercies as evidence. God’s past dealings with us are meant to be evidence. A new trouble often knocks us flat because we drew nothing from the last deliverance — relieved, grateful for a fortnight, and filed it as something that happened rather than something we learned about him. A test: what past mercy of God should be shaping how you face today’s trouble?

The word for his enemies. “Hardened” — the same term Mark used of the men in the synagogue who watched a withered hand restored and walked out to plan a murder (3:5). These aren’t enemies but apostles, mid-mission, fresh from casting out demons in his name, described in his opponents’ vocabulary. So hardness isn’t only an unbeliever’s disease, and it doesn’t announce itself. It isn’t disbelief — they believed much. It is the slow loss of the capacity to be affected, the state in which the same truths arrive and produce nothing, in which someone can carry the bread and never taste it (cf. 8:17–21).

Not final. Mark says it without despair, because we know what these men became. The hardening was real and not final. He kept them, taught them, corrected them; was betrayed and denied by them; and after the resurrection fed them breakfast on a beach and sent them out — and the man whose memory this Gospel preserves had denied him three times. He doesn’t give up on hard-hearted disciples. He gets into the boat with them.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret and moored to the shore. And when they got out of the boat, the people immediately recognized him and ran about the whole region and began to bring the sick people on their beds to wherever they heard he was. And wherever he came, in villages, cities, or countryside, they laid the sick in the marketplaces and implored him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched it were made well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Desperate need that sets aside pride reaches Christ, and one person’s testimony can stir a whole region to come to him.

Blown off course. Gennesaret is the fertile plain on the north-west shore, a few miles of rich farmland Josephus praised. They had been sent to Bethsaida (v. 45); the night put them somewhere else, as nine hours against the wind will.

No rest again. The boat touches shore and it starts. Word spreads, and people start carrying — not helping the sick walk but carrying them on their pallets from villages and farms, chasing a moving target: “to wherever they heard he was.” He walks; the beds are carried after him all day by relays of neighbours and relatives. Whole communities mobilised, and not a word about any of them wanting anything for themselves.

In the marketplace. The open square where everything happened — shops, courts, gossip, day-labourers waiting for work — and the sick laid in rows in the middle of it, in public, in everyone’s way. These people have stopped caring how it looks. A desperation that has burned through embarrassment is the only kind that ever gets anywhere with Christ. A test: what is pride or embarrassment keeping you from bringing to him?

The fringe. The tassel every observant Jewish man wore at the corners of his cloak, as a reminder of God’s commandments (Numbers 15:38–39). The request has a one-chapter history: a woman with twelve years of bleeding said, “If I touch even his garments, I will be made well” (5:28), reached from behind, and was healed and called Daughter. Now a province does what she did. That is what one healed woman’s story did when it got out — as one healed madman’s did across the lake (5:20). Mark keeps showing the same mechanism: someone tells what happened to them, and a district comes. Whom could your story bring?

All of them. “As many as touched it were made well.” No qualification, no theology corrected first. Their understanding was thin and probably half superstitious, as hers had been. He doesn’t lecture them about the tassel; he heals them.

Nazareth and Gennesaret. The chapter that began with a village refusing him because they knew him too well ends with strangers running across a plain with beds. Nazareth had every advantage and wouldn’t stretch out a hand; Gennesaret had almost no understanding and grabbed the hem of his coat. The difference isn’t intelligence, opportunity or information. One town thought it already knew him. The other only knew it needed him.
verseByVerse.note: Gennesaret was a fertile plain on the north-west shore of the lake. The fringe was the tassel the law required on a garment.

6.theology:
