Painters have felt it — Raphael’s last work puts the transfigured Christ above and this scene below, the convulsing boy and pointing hands, because they belong in one frame. A great crowd, so public; scribes arguing with the disciples, the professional opponents pressing a failure before everyone. Nine men who promised something and didn’t deliver, a sick child on the ground, and critics in full voice. That was waiting at the bottom of the hill.

The come-down isn’t proof the mountain was false. Peter, James and John had genuinely seen God’s glory. It didn’t exempt them from walking into a shouting match. The conference ends, the retreat finishes, the Sunday that lifted you is followed by a Monday where nothing has changed and something has probably got worse. That isn’t evidence God wasn’t on the mountain. It is the shape of the Christian life, and Mark arranges his Gospel to prepare you. A test: when the high is followed by a low, do you doubt the high?

The crowd runs. They were “greatly amazed” — strong, thrown, the root used of the women at the empty tomb (16:5–6). Why so startled? Mark doesn’t say. Some wonder whether something of the mountain was still on him, as with Moses coming down Sinai; or it was the shock of his arrival at the very moment of public humiliation. The argument stops and everyone runs.

He steps in between. “What are you arguing about with them?” With one question he takes possession of the scene. He doesn’t go straight to the boy, or upbraid the nine before the crowd. By asking, he moves into the middle of the argument, and the scribes are now arguing with him. He steps between his failed disciples and the men attacking them — the first act of the rescue. Whatever he has to say to the nine he will say privately, inside a house, afterwards (v. 28).

verseByVerse.quote: And someone from the crowd answered him, "Teacher, I brought my son to you, for he has a spirit that makes him mute. And whenever it seizes him, it throws him down, and he foams and grinds his teeth and becomes rigid. So I asked your disciples to cast it out, and they were not able."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus meets a desperate parent whom his followers had failed — a picture of chronic suffering that the church couldn’t fix.

Only one not interested in the argument. Not the scribes or disciples, but a man in the crowd, almost anonymous until he speaks. He is the only one present who isn’t interested in the argument.

“I brought my son to you.” “Teacher” — the smallest title in the chapter; he has no theology of who Jesus is. “I brought my son” — he did the one thing he could; he carried the boy here. “To you” — the ache under everything: he came looking for Jesus, Jesus was up a mountain, and he got the disciples instead.

A father’s detail. The boy can’t speak; he has never told his father what it is like. And the father knows the sequence: the seizure, the fall, the foam, the teeth, the stiffening, the body rigid and spent. He has watched it many times.

Illness and the demonic. Two things need care. First, the symptoms are those of severe epilepsy, and Matthew uses the ordinary word for it (Matthew 17:15). Scripture readily distinguishes illness from demonic affliction (1:32–34, where the sick and the demonised are listed separately). This is a specific case in which the two are bound together, and Jesus addresses the spirit because that is what is there. It doesn’t follow — and mustn’t be made to — that seizures, mental illness or disability are generally possession. That inference has done immense harm to suffering people, and the Bible doesn’t license it. If your child has epilepsy, this passage isn’t a diagnosis. Take them to a doctor; that is an ordinary mercy of God.

For those caring for a child who can’t be fixed. Second, this passage is for the father. Years watching his child thrown to the ground, never a conversation with him, lifting him off floors, cleaning him up — and, we will learn, since childhood, with fire and water nearly taking him. If you are caring for someone who can’t be fixed, this man is in your Bible on purpose, and Jesus is about to give him a great deal of time.

“They were not able.” Said quietly, the hinge of what follows. No accusation — not that they refused or did it badly, just the fact. And it has done its damage. He came to the church and the church couldn’t help, and in two verses you will hear what that cost his faith. A test: is there anyone whose faith has been damaged by your failure or your church’s? Pray for them, and bring them to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered them, "O faithless generation, how long am I to be with you? How long am I to bear with you? Bring him to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus grieves deeply over unbelief, yet in the same breath he invites the needy to be brought to him.

Not impatience with a father. The sharpest thing Jesus says in the Gospel, and a hasty reading turns it into impatience with a suffering father, which it isn’t. He “answered them” — plural, addressed to a generation: the nine who failed, the scribes who argued, the crowd who came to watch. Not the father, the one person there doing the right thing.

God’s grief. Not irritation at inconvenience. “How long am I to bear with you?” is God’s language in the wilderness: “How long will this people despise me? And how long will they not believe in me, in spite of all the signs that I have done among them?” (Numbers 14:11; cf. Deuteronomy 32:5, 20). The grief of a God who has done everything and been believed by almost no one — the voice from the mountain, so recently unveiled, now in a valley looking at what unbelief has made of his own disciples.

A shadow of the cross. “How long am I to be with you?” He won’t be with them much longer, and he knows it; six days ago he told them so. A man measuring the time left against the slowness of those he is leaving it with.

“Bring him to me.” The whole character of Christ in four words. The rebuke ends and the rescue begins in one breath. He doesn’t say come back when you have more faith, dismiss the crowd, refuse to act amid unbelief, or make the healing conditional on improvement. He says, bring him here. He is genuinely grieved by faithlessness, and says so hard — and the very next thing he does is call the boy over.

For the ashamed. If you have hesitated to bring something to God because you were ashamed of the state of your faith, this chapter holds a hard word about unbelief and an immediate invitation, spoken by the same voice in the same breath. The rebuke is real; it isn’t a refusal. A test: what have you been holding back from him because you feel your faith is too weak? Bring it today.

parallels.desc: a perverse generation, children in whom is no faithfulness

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought the boy to him. And when the spirit saw him, immediately it convulsed the boy, and he fell on the ground and rolled about, foaming at the mouth. And Jesus asked his father, "How long has this been happening to him?" And he said, "From childhood. And it has often cast him into fire and into water, to destroy him. But if you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus cares for the person as well as the problem, and doubt damaged by others’ failures can still come to him.

His presence provokes it. Since chapter 1, nothing unclean can be near him and stay quiet. And a hard mercy in the timing: the worst seizure happens in front of Jesus. What had happened in fields and houses where no one could help now happens in the one place where something can be done. Mark doesn’t look away: a child on the ground before a crowd.

A question for the father. “How long has this been happening to him?” The most surprising thing in the passage. A boy convulsing at his feet; Jesus can end it in a sentence — he silenced a legion and a hurricane with fewer words. And he asks about the case history. He doesn’t need the information. It is for the father. No one has asked this man anything. He has carried this alone for years and has just been let down before a crowd, and the Son of God stops the whole scene to ask how long it has gone on. That is pastoral care most of us never manage. Faced with a crisis we go straight to the problem. He goes to the person, lets him talk, and the talking is part of the healing. A test: when someone brings you their trouble, do you give them time to tell it?

From childhood. Two words with a life in them: not recent; from when he was small. This father has never known his son well, never heard his voice, never had a normal day.

Fire and water. The open cooking fire in a village floor, the well, the lake — every hearth and water jar a threat for years, and he has pulled his son out often. He hasn’t slept properly in a decade; he can’t leave the boy alone; he has lived expecting catastrophe at any moment. And he knows what he faces: “to destroy him” — not bad luck but intention, watched at work.

“If you can.” The honest condition of many people. He didn’t arrive with that clause. He came looking for the man everyone said could heal, found nine followers who couldn’t, and a public argument — and doubt got in through the crack their failure made. That still happens: people’s confidence in the Lord is regularly damaged by his people — the church that let them down, the Christian who wronged them, the prayer meeting that promised and produced nothing, the leader who fell. They come to Christ afterwards with an “if you can” that wasn’t there before.

“Help us.” “Have compassion on us” — not on him, on us. He has been ill for both of them.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, "'If you can'! All things are possible for one who believes." Immediately the father of the child cried out and said, "I believe; help my unbelief!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The issue is never Christ’s power but our trust, and Jesus accepts honest, mixed faith that brings its doubts to him.

The “if” in the wrong place. Jesus seizes the man’s own two words and hands them back, abrupt, with an exclamation: “If you can!” Not mockery, but refusing to let pass the one word that doesn’t belong. The father attached his “if” to Jesus’ ability, and there is nothing wrong with Jesus’ ability; he has just come down from a mountain where the Father called him his beloved Son.

Not a formula. “All things are possible for one who believes.” This has been made to say something cruel it doesn’t say. It isn’t “believe hard enough and you will get what you want.” That doctrine has crushed many suffering people, told their diagnosis stands because their faith was insufficient. Read on: the boy is healed by a father who says aloud he doesn’t have enough faith. Jesus moves the man’s “if” from one place to another. The question was never whether Christ can, but whether this man will take hold of him. Faith isn’t a force that makes things happen; it is empty hands held out to Someone who has everything (cf. 11:23–24; Hebrews 11:6).

The most honest sentence. “I believe; help my unbelief!” — torn out of a man in crisis, shouted on his knees beside a convulsing child, the crowd watching. Not a considered formulation. “I believe” — he won’t deny the faith he has; it is real, and it brought him here. “Help my unbelief” — he won’t pretend it is more than it is. Having just heard all things are possible for one who believes, instead of manufacturing confidence he tells the truth: there is unbelief in me, I can’t get rid of it, deal with that too. He doesn’t ask for stronger faith in order to qualify; he asks Christ to help the very thing that disqualifies him.

A lifeline. That is why this verse has been the lifeline of honest Christians for two thousand years. Most of us aren’t in one state or the other; we believe and doubt in the same hour about the same thing, affirming every article of the creed and lying awake unable to feel a word of it. The temptation is to sort ourselves out first — work up the required confidence, then pray, as though faith were the entry fee. This man did the opposite and laid both halves at Christ’s feet. And the boy was healed. Jesus didn’t say come back when you are sure. He met the faith that was there, trembling and shot through with doubt, and did what the doubt said he couldn’t.

A test. If your faith this morning is a mess — you believe and can’t feel it, or feel it and can’t hold it — don’t wait for it to improve. Say this man’s sentence. It is in the Bible because God means it to be prayed, and the boy got up.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark records the father’s cry.

parallels.desc: without faith it is impossible to please him

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus saw that a crowd came running together, he rebuked the unclean spirit, saying to it, "You mute and deaf spirit, I command you, come out of him and never enter him again." And after crying out and convulsing him terribly, it came out, and the boy was like a corpse, so that most of them said, "He is dead." But Jesus took him by the hand and lifted him up, and he arose.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s word frees completely and permanently, and his lifting of the boy foreshadows his power to raise the dead.

Before it becomes a show. He sees the crowd swelling and acts — almost certainly wanting this over before it becomes a spectacle, the healing turned show he has avoided all Gospel.

Named precisely. “You mute and deaf spirit.” The father said the boy couldn’t speak; Jesus adds deaf. The thing had shut the child in, sealing both the way words come out and the way they get in.

His own authority. “I command you” — first person, no invocation, formula or higher name; not what the exorcists of that world did, nor what the disciples had done.

Never again. “And never enter him again” — a clause Jesus adds nowhere else in the Gospels. Why here? The father said it had happened since childhood, into fires and water, and the fear in that home wasn’t only that it might happen but that it would keep happening. Jesus doesn’t merely end an episode; he closes the door and tells the father it is closed — as he told the woman, “be healed of your disease” (5:34), a word of permanence for someone who would otherwise wait every morning for it to return. A test: what fear of recurrence do you need to hand to his finished word?

Malicious to the last. It doesn’t go quietly; its last act on the way out is to hurt him as much as it can. The powers of darkness in this Gospel are malicious to the final second, and they always obey.

Like a corpse. Lying still, white, not visibly breathing; most conclude the healer has killed him. Imagine the father in that half-minute: he has prayed the truest prayer of his life, and his son lies on the ground looking dead. God sometimes works this way: the moment before deliverance can look exactly like the disaster you feared. The corpse comes before the rising; Israel was never more trapped than with the sea ahead and chariots behind.

Resurrection words. “Took him by the hand” — as with Peter’s mother-in-law (1:31) and the dead girl (5:41). “Lifted him up” — the verb used of Christ being raised. “He arose” — the verb behind “resurrection.” Mark could have written “the boy got up.” He wrote the two words the church would use for Easter, in the chapter where no one understood the promise of rising (vv. 9–10). Here, before a crowd that has pronounced him dead, the Son of Man takes a boy’s hand and raises him — a small, dusty rehearsal of what he walks to Jerusalem to do for the world. He takes hold of a child everyone has given up on and stands him on his feet.

parallels.desc: he took her by the hand

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had entered the house, his disciples asked him privately, "Why could we not cast it out?" And he said to them, "This kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Spiritual power comes not from technique or past success but from a life of ongoing dependence on God in prayer.

Correction in private. Indoors, afterwards. He never humiliated them in the valley; scribes argued, the crowd watched, nine men failed publicly — and he took over, healed the boy, and said nothing to them until the door was shut. Worth copying by anyone who must correct anyone: the correction is real and coming, but not before an audience. A test: do you correct others privately and gently?

A fair question. “Why could we not cast it out?” Not excuses. They had done this before — given authority over unclean spirits (3:15), they went out and cast out many (6:13). Not amateurs, and they know something has gone wrong they can’t account for.

Not technique or authority. He doesn’t say they used the wrong formula, commanded too weakly, should have laid on hands, or needed another name. No method is withheld. Nor more authority; they had all they needed, never withdrawn.

A life, not a step. “Prayer” isn’t a step they omitted on the day; he is diagnosing a life. If prayer were a component of the procedure, the failure would be a slip. But that collapses at once, because Jesus himself doesn’t pray in this passage; he arrives, asks a question, speaks a sentence, and it is done. What he does here isn’t what he does “very early… while it was still dark” in a desolate place (1:35), all night before choosing the Twelve (Luke 6:12), or in Gethsemane. So prayer here means the posture of a whole life — the settled, daily, unspectacular dependence from which authority actually works.

They stopped depending. These men had succeeded before and come back delighted; demons had obeyed them. Somewhere between that success and this valley, the authority quietly became a possession — something they had, that worked, carried about rather than held moment by moment from the hand that gave it. They didn’t stop believing; they stopped depending. The two are almost impossible to tell apart from inside, until the day the thing doesn’t work.

The drift of every generation. The forms of spiritual ministry deployed without the ongoing communion that gives them power. You can preach, counsel, lead, teach and serve on accumulated competence and be, in the valley, where these nine were. A test: how much of what you do for God this week will be prayed about beforehand — not a sentence before you start, but prayed about as someone who knows he can do nothing? “Apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5) isn’t exaggeration or rebuke but description, and the nine had just proved it.

“And fasting.” Some manuscripts add “and fasting.” The oldest and best don’t, and it was probably added by copyists from the church’s own practice. Jesus’ point is dependence on God in prayer. Fasting is good, and Jesus expected his disciples to fast (Matthew 6:16–18), but it isn’t the secret here.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “and fasting.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–50 — The Second Prediction and the Argument on the Road
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The second telling (vv. 30–32). Walking quietly through Galilee, avoiding notice, Jesus tells them again that he will be delivered up, killed, and rise. Mark adds a devastating detail: they did not understand, and were afraid to ask.

The argument (vv. 33–37). And what they were talking about instead comes out at Capernaum. He asks what they were discussing on the road, and they go silent — because they had been arguing about which of them was the greatest. His answer is to sit down, state the rule (last of all and servant of all), and then pick up a child and hold him.

The complaint (vv. 38–41). John, apparently thinking this a good moment, reports that they stopped a man casting out demons in Jesus's name because he was not one of them. He is told to leave him alone — and that a cup of water given to a disciple will not be forgotten.

The warnings (vv. 42–50). Then the hardest words in the Gospel: a millstone for anyone who trips up a little one, and a hand, a foot and an eye better lost than kept.

The whole section hangs together. Men who have just been told about a cross are arguing about rank, policing the boundaries of their group, and in serious danger of tripping up people smaller than themselves — and it ends with be at peace with one another.
verseByVerse.theology:
"The one who is not against us is for us" (v. 40) seems to collide head-on with whoever is not with me is against me (Matt. 12:30; Luke 11:23), and a reader who notices it deserves an answer.

They are not answering the same question, and that is the whole key. Here the subject is a fellow worker — a man casting out demons in Jesus's name, plainly on Christ's side, who simply does not belong to the disciples' circle; and the lesson is generosity: do not treat an ally as an enemy merely because he is not of your party. There the subject is Christ himself, and the men in view are Pharisees who had just called his works the devil's — open opponents; and the lesson is that toward Jesus there is no neutral ground.

So the two sayings guard two different errors. Toward other Christians serving under a different banner from ours we are far too quick to say against us, and Jesus says: not so — if he is for me, he is for you. Toward the Lord himself we would love to imagine a comfortable middle ground of the undecided, and Jesus says there is none. Read together they are not a contradiction but a pair of fences: be generous about the boundaries of the movement, and uncompromising about the claims of the King.

And a word about the verses your Bible skips. A reader with a King James Bible will find the refrain of v. 48, about the undying worm and the unquenched fire, three times over, at verses 44, 46 and 48. Modern Bibles print it once, at v. 48, and leave 44 and 46 as footnotes. Those two repetitions are a copyist's echo of v. 48 and are not in the earliest manuscripts. Nothing is lost. The sentence stands once, in full force, exactly where Jesus quoted it from Isaiah 66:24.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: twelve men arguing on a road about which of them was the greatest, on the road after being told that their Master would be handed over and killed.

Now: the same argument, conducted with better manners. It runs under a great deal of church life — who was consulted, who was thanked from the front, whose name went on it, who got asked to do the thing you were not asked to do. Nobody says I am the greatest. Everybody knows exactly where they stand in the room.

And notice how Mark exposes it: they kept silent. They would not tell him. Which is the surest sign of all that they already knew it was wrong — you do not go quiet about a conversation you are comfortable with.

Then watch what Jesus does with it, because he does not abolish ambition; he reverses its direction. If anyone would be first — the wanting is allowed to stand — he must be last of all and servant of all. Not last of some. Not servant of the deserving. Of all.

And then he picks up a child, who in that world had no legal standing, no money, no influence and nothing whatever to offer in return — and says that receiving one such is receiving him. The test of greatness in the kingdom is not how you treat the people who can advance you. It is how you treat the ones who cannot do a thing for you, when nobody is watching.

verseByVerse.quote: They went on from there and passed through Galilee. And he did not want anyone to know, for he was teaching his disciples, saying to them, "The Son of Man is going to be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill him. And when he is killed, after three days he will rise." But they did not understand the saying, and were afraid to ask him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cross was God’s handing over of his Son for us, and avoiding hard questions with God leaves room for worse things to fill the silence.

Incognito. He travels unrecognised through his own province, where the crowds first came. The public phase is ending; the Gospel narrows — less crowd, more instruction — and the road turns toward Jerusalem. What remains to do is with these twelve, with little time.

Handed over. The second passion prediction, not a repeat; it has a new and darker word: “delivered” — handed over, given up, betrayed. It is used of Judas throughout, of the priests handing Jesus to Pilate, of Pilate handing him to the soldiers; it runs through the passion like a thread. And here it doesn’t say who does it. Judas will, the priests will, Pilate will — and behind them all, Paul says, God: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). A test: do you see the cross as God giving his Son up for you personally?

Into the hands of men. Not of Rome, the Sanhedrin, or his enemies — men. Humanity in general, which is where the reader stands.

Always the rising too. “They will kill him… after three days he will rise.” Flat and unadorned, and the resurrection attached again. He never mentions the death without the rising.

Afraid to ask. Mark tells the truth about his own leaders: two failures, the second worse. “They did not understand” — forgivable and familiar; the second hearing, and it still won’t go in. “And were afraid to ask him” — not ignorance but a choice. Perhaps because of last time, when Peter raised this and was called Satan before nine witnesses. Perhaps because they suspected they wouldn’t like the answer.

Questions we won’t ask God. A very recognisable state. There are questions Christians decline to ask God — not because they can’t be asked; Scripture is full of bolder ones — but because we half-know the answer, and it would require something. The passage you skip. The subject you never bring into prayer. The area of your life you have agreed with yourself not to discuss with him. Not doubt — doubt at least engages — but avoidance. And see what they do with the silence: they don’t ask about the cross, and fill the walk with an argument about which of them is most important. The unasked question leaves a space, and something always moves into it. What question have you been afraid to ask him?

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Capernaum. And when he was in the house he asked them, "What were you discussing on the way?" But they kept silent, for on the way they had argued with one another about who was the greatest. And he sat down and called the twelve. And he said to them, "If anyone would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
True greatness in Christ’s kingdom is measured by humble service of everyone, not by rank.

A gentle question. He waits until they are indoors; whatever he heard on the road, he says nothing until the door is shut, the same restraint as with the nine. And he doesn’t accuse; he asks.

Silence as confession. “But they kept silent.” They won’t tell him, and the silence confesses, because you don’t go quiet about a conversation you are comfortable with. Happy to have it among themselves on the road; asked to repeat it before him, not one can get the sentence out. A test worth borrowing: would you be willing to repeat aloud to Christ the last conversation you had about someone else — the words, the tone, and why you said it? Most of us have a kind of speech that dies instantly in his presence, and the dying is the verdict.

Rank on the road to the cross. Mark supplies what they wouldn’t: “they had argued with one another about who was the greatest.” The same road on which he had just told them, again, he would be handed over and killed — and the conversation behind him was about rank. An argument, too, with positions and cases made.

How familiar it is. No one in church says, “I am the greatest.” But the argument runs anyway, silently and constantly: who was consulted and who wasn’t, who was thanked from the front, whose name is on it, who was asked to do what you weren’t, who is regarded as sound. It can be conducted entirely without words, and everyone in the room knows the standings.

The lesson staged. “He sat down and called the twelve” — the teacher’s posture; not an aside but a deliberate lesson.

Where the front of the queue is. “If anyone would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all.” It doesn’t condemn the desire; the wanting is allowed to stand. He doesn’t say ambition is wicked; he says where the front actually is. He reverses the direction rather than removing the drive: you want to be first? Go to the back and serve. And the two absolutes make it impossible to soften. “Last of all” — not last of some or modest about your position, but bottom. “Servant of all” — the word for the man who waited at table, with no qualifying clause: not of the deserving, grateful, promising or potentially useful, but of all (cf. 10:43–44; Luke 22:24–27).

Service is measurable. That turns an attitude into something measurable: service of that kind can be looked up in a diary. It is easy to feel humble. It isn’t possible to be a servant in the abstract. A test: whom will you serve this week who can do nothing for you?
verseByVerse.note: Teachers sat to teach.

verseByVerse.quote: And he took a child and put him in the midst of them, and taking him in his arms, he said to them, "Whoever receives one such child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me, receives not me but him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
How we treat people who can do nothing for us is how we treat Christ and God himself.

A child in the middle. Having said it, he shows it. There is a child in the house — perhaps of the household, in what may be Peter’s house — and Jesus stands him in the middle of the circle. The argument was about the highest place; he puts a child at its centre.

What a child meant. We have sentimentalised this beyond recognition, thinking of innocence, wonder and trust. That isn’t what a first-century adult saw. A child had no legal standing, property or voice; children were loved, of course, but they were nobodies. They couldn’t advance, defend or repay you, or add anything to your position. So the lesson isn’t “be innocent like this.” It is: here is a person who can do absolutely nothing for you.

In his arms. Mark alone records it, twice — here and when he takes children in his arms and blesses them (10:16). Peter remembered: while he was explaining greatness to us, he was holding a child. Twelve grown men who had argued about rank, sitting in a circle, and the Lord of glory in the middle with a small child in his arms.

Receiving. The word for welcoming a guest — taking someone in, giving your attention and your table. The standard is exact: not “whoever loves children” but whoever receives — takes trouble over, makes room for — one who has nothing to give back.

The chain. Child, then Christ, then the Father. So the greatness of an act isn’t measured by the significance of the person you did it for, but by who stands behind them (cf. Matthew 10:40; John 13:20).

A test. More searching than a general resolution to be humble: how do you treat people who can’t do a thing for you? The person at church no one seeks out. The elderly relative whose conversation goes in circles. The junior colleague. The child in your own house at the end of a day when you have nothing left. The one whose gratitude you will never hear of. Everyone is attentive to the people who matter to their position. The kingdom’s ranking is worked out entirely on the others — and when you welcome one of them in his name, you have welcomed him, and behind him, God.
verseByVerse.note: Children had little status in the ancient world.

verseByVerse.quote: John said to him, "Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he was not following us." But Jesus said, "Do not stop him, for no one who does a mighty work in my name will be able soon afterward to speak evil of me. For the one who is not against us is for us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christians must not oppose genuine servants of Christ just because they belong to a different group, though no one can be neutral toward Christ himself.

Superb timing. Jesus has just held up a child and said receiving a nobody in his name is receiving him — and John reports stopping someone acting in that name. The only time John speaks alone in this Gospel, and he seems to expect approval; he is a Son of Thunder (3:17).

“Not following us.” The reason, stated with damning clarity. Not “not following you” — the man plainly was, casting out demons in Jesus’ name and succeeding, more than the nine managed in the valley. The objection is to his membership, not his master. He wasn’t in the group.

Sectarianism in a clause. There is a way of caring about the kingdom that has quietly become caring about our part of it — where the first question about a ministry isn’t “Is Christ being preached?” but “Whose is he?” It flourishes among the orthodox and sincere, and produces Christians relieved rather than glad when good work is done outside their circle. A test: are you glad when Christ is served well by people outside your church or tradition?

“Do not stop him.” Flat, immediate. And the reasoning is practical: someone who has just seen the name of Jesus work won’t start slandering it. Whatever is lacking in his understanding or affiliation, he isn’t on the other side, and the evidence is what happened (cf. Numbers 11:26–29, Moses and Eldad and Medad).

For us — or against him? “The one who is not against us is for us” seems to contradict “Whoever is not with me is against me” (Matthew 12:30). They answer different questions. Here the subject is a fellow worker, plainly on Christ’s side, who simply doesn’t belong to the disciples’ circle; the lesson is generosity: don’t treat an ally as an enemy because he isn’t of your party. There the subject is Christ himself, and those in view are Pharisees who had just called his works the devil’s; the lesson is that toward Jesus there is no neutral ground. So the two guard two opposite errors, both alive. Toward other Christians serving under a different banner we are too quick to say “against us” — and Jesus says, if he is for me he is for you. Toward the Lord himself we would like a comfortable middle ground of the undecided — and there is none. Not a contradiction but a pair of fences: be generous about the boundaries of the movement, and uncompromising about the claims of the King.

parallels.desc: whoever is not with me is against me

verseByVerse.quote: For truly, I say to you, whoever gives you a cup of water to drink because you belong to Christ will by no means lose his reward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God notices and rewards the smallest kindness done to his people for Christ’s sake.

Underlined. “Truly” is the amen-formula he keeps for things he wants underlined — and he uses it for a cup of water.

The smallest act. Having widened the boundary to the man outside their circle, he widens it to the smallest imaginable act. He could have said whoever preaches, heals, or gives up his home. He says a drink of water. In a hot country it costs nothing; the well is there, everyone has a cup. The least thing one person can do for another and still be said to have done something — no expense, skill or risk, and no one will ever hear of it. And it won’t be forgotten.

Because you belong to Christ. The whole qualifying clause. Not because the giver was impressive, the act large, or the motive perfectly pure, but because of whose the recipient was. The value isn’t in the water but in the name attached to the person handed the cup — as with the child two verses earlier. Hand a disciple a drink because he is mine, and it goes on the account.

Not lost. The Greek double negative is emphatic: it won’t be overlooked, mislaid, or too small to register. Good news if the service you can give is small and unnoticed, as most Christian work is: meals cooked, lifts given, chairs put out, a message to someone having a bad week, an hour with someone no one else has time for, prayer for people who never learn they were prayed for. None of it will be described from a platform. All of it is on a list.

The list read aloud. One day he will read it, and the people named won’t recognise their own lives: “Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you drink?… as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:37–40). The King of glory keeps a record of cups of water. That is the kind of King he is. A test: what small kindness can you do today for one of his people?

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to sin, it would be better for him if a great millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus treats damaging the faith of weak believers as one of the gravest sins, a solemn warning to anyone with influence over others.

The other end. He has just promised reward for the smallest kindness to his people; now he states what happens at the other end.

The little ones. The child is still in the room, so children are certainly included. But “who believe in me” points wider: the small, the new, the fragile, whose faith is genuine and not yet strong — the recent convert, the person hanging on by their fingernails, anyone whose grip on Christ could be loosened by what you do. “Causes… to sin” is one word: to trip up, put a stumbling block in someone’s path — more than teaching error; anything that makes it harder for a weak believer to keep walking.

A great millstone. His most violent image about anyone. Not the small hand-mill a woman turned in her kitchen, but the upper stone of a village mill an animal walked round to turn — a slab of rock weighing hundreds of pounds no one man could lift. Hung round the neck, and dropped into the sea: no coming up, ever. And the comparison: “it would be better for him.” A violent, hopeless death would be the preferable outcome — drowning like that is the lucky version of what awaits someone who trips up one of his little ones. He doesn’t speak like this of doubters, the confused, the openly immoral, or even his enemies. He speaks like this of people who damage the faith of the small.

For anyone with influence. That makes this the most solemn verse in the New Testament for anyone with influence over someone weaker — many of us. For parents, whose children’s picture of God is assembled largely from what they see at home, and whose faith can be quietly ruined by a father who is one man on Sunday and another on Tuesday. For anyone who teaches or leads in a church, and anyone watched by a younger Christian who thinks well of them.

Ordinary talk. You needn’t preach heresy to trip someone up. It is done with a cynical remark about a fellow believer in front of a new convert; with the running commentary on the church’s failings that a fragile person overhears; with the joke that makes something holy look small. The father in the valley had his faith damaged by disciples who let him down, and came saying “if you can.” Someone put that clause in his mouth. A test: who is watching me who is weaker than I am, and is anything I do making it harder for them? He weighed the answer against a millstone.
verseByVerse.note: The millstone is the heavy upper stone of a mill turned by a donkey.

verseByVerse.quote: And if your hand causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life crippled than with two hands to go to hell, to the unquenchable fire. And if your foot causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life lame than with two feet to be thrown into hell. And if your eye causes you to sin, tear it out. It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than with two eyes to be thrown into hell, 'where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing is worth keeping if it is leading you to destruction; deal radically with sin, because hell is real and Jesus warns of it out of love.

The danger nearest to hand. Having warned about tripping up others, he turns to the likelier danger: yourself. The same verb runs through: what trips others may be your influence; what trips you is nearer. Three examples in order — hand, foot, eye: what you do, where you go, what you look at. Between them, most of the ways a person is ruined.

Not literal — but deadly serious. Is he asking for self-mutilation? No, and not from squeamishness; it wouldn’t work. Chapter 7 settled that nothing outside defiles a man; the trouble comes from the heart (7:21). A man with one hand can still covet; a blind man can still lust. That is why the church has never taken this literally, and pitied the few who did. But don’t soften it to nothing. This is exaggeration in the service of deadly seriousness: nothing in your life is so valuable that it is worth keeping if it is taking you to hell. A hand isn’t a luxury, nor an eye. He chose things you can’t spare. And note the words: the kingdom is “life,” and the alternative, three times, “hell” — the only two categories here.

Make it concrete. Vagueness is how this passage gets neutralised. The hand is what you do. The foot is where you go — the house, the road home past a particular door, the company you keep because it is easier than explaining. The eye is what you look at, and in our generation that is largely one object, in your pocket and lit at midnight. And the surgery isn’t moderation but removal — not “be more careful with it” but “cut it off.” In practice the ruthless, concrete, slightly embarrassing measure: the app deleted rather than managed, the phone that doesn’t come upstairs, the account closed, the friendship stepped back from, the route changed, the arrangement told to another Christian so it can be asked about. Each feels disproportionate. That is the feeling of amputation, exactly what he describes. A test: name the one thing you need to cut off this week, and do it.

Gehenna. The word for hell three times here is Gehenna, a real place: the Valley of Hinnom on Jerusalem’s south side, where apostate Israel burned its own children to Molech — Ahaz and Manasseh did it (2 Chronicles 28:3; 33:6) — and Josiah defiled it so it could never be used so again (2 Kings 23:10); Jeremiah called it “the Valley of Slaughter” (Jeremiah 7:31–32). Jesus takes a place of horror his hearers could walk to in half an hour and makes it his picture of final judgment.

The worm and the fire. The closing line quotes Isaiah’s last verse (Isaiah 66:24), picturing the bodies of those who rebelled against God: the worm doesn’t finish its work; the fire doesn’t go out. This ruin doesn’t end.

The tenderest speaks most of hell. No one in the Bible speaks of hell as often or vividly as Jesus. The tenderest person who ever lived — who held a child while teaching, groaned over a deaf man, thought of a raised girl’s breakfast — won’t let this subject alone. It can’t be dismissed as Old Testament harshness or later invention. It is on the Saviour’s lips three times in six verses, because he means his people not to go there.

Does this teach that punishment is conscious and unending? Some evangelicals hold that the lost will finally be destroyed and cease to exist, noting that the line comes from Isaiah 66:24, where the worm and fire consume the dead bodies of the rebels. But in Jesus’ use the worm doesn’t die and the fire isn’t quenched; it is the punishment, not its victims, that never ends. He sets eternal punishment beside eternal life (Matthew 25:46), and Revelation says “the smoke of their torment goes up forever and ever” (Revelation 14:11). The more likely reading is that the punishment is conscious and unending. It is meant to drive us to the One who bore judgment for all who come to him.

The missing verses 44 and 46. A King James Bible has this refrain three times, at vv. 44, 46 and 48; here the numbers run 43, 45, 47, 48. Those two repetitions are a copyist’s echo of v. 48, absent from the earliest manuscripts, so modern Bibles put them in a footnote. Nothing is lost: the sentence stands once, in full force, where Jesus quoted it from Isaiah.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verses 44 and 46, repeating verse 48. “Hell” renders Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom by Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: their worm shall not die, their fire shall not be quenched

verseByVerse.quote: For everyone will be salted with fire. Salt is good, but if the salt has lost its saltiness, how will you make it salty again? Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every life meets God’s fire, either as judgment or as purifying sacrifice; disciples must keep the distinctiveness that makes them useful, and peace among them flows from each dealing honestly with himself.

Fire and salt. One of Mark’s strangest sentences, puzzled over for centuries, but its two key words open it. Fire is the last word of the previous paragraph, meaning judgment. Salt comes from the altar: “You shall season all your grain offerings with salt. You shall not let the salt of the covenant with your God be missing” (Leviticus 2:13). Salt was rubbed into every sacrifice.

What does “salted with fire” mean? Other readings have been offered: that every believer will be tested by fire (1 Corinthians 3:13); that disciples are to be offered to God like sacrifices seasoned with salt (Leviticus 2:13; Romans 12:1); or that the wicked will be preserved, as salt preserves, in the fire of judgment. The more likely reading keeps the link with the fire of v. 48 and the salt of the sacrifices: everyone meets God’s fire, either as judgment or as the refining of a life given to him. The unrepentant meet the fire that consumes; the disciple, just told to cut off hand and foot rather than perish, meets the fire that purifies — the costly, cleansing fire of a life laid on the altar. Peter writes the same to persecuted Christians: “do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you” (1 Peter 4:12), faith tested by fire being more precious than gold (1 Peter 1:7). A test: in the fire you are facing, are you letting God refine you?

Salt is good. The tone gentles. Salt did two things: it preserved — the only thing between a household and rotten meat — and it seasoned, making food taste of something. Pictures of what a disciple is meant to be: what stops the rot and gives savour.

Salt that has lost its saltiness. The region’s salt wasn’t pure but scraped from the Dead Sea shores, full of other minerals; the salt could leach out, leaving a white powder that looked identical and did nothing, and couldn’t be restored. That is the sober question under the sentence: a Christian who has quietly lost what made him different isn’t obviously distinguishable from one who hasn’t. He looks the same and is in the same place on Sunday; he simply no longer preserves or flavours anything, and there is no procedure for putting it back.

Salt in yourselves, then peace. The chapter’s last line, toward which its second half has been walking. Remember these men: they failed in a valley, were afraid to ask about the cross, argued about which was greatest and wouldn’t admit it, and John stopped a man doing good because he wasn’t one of them. To that group: “be at peace with one another.” And the order is Christian ethics in a sentence. “Have salt in yourselves” first — the inward reality, ruthlessness with your own hand, foot and eye. Peace follows. Peace in a church isn’t produced by managing personalities; it is what happens when a group of people have each dealt honestly with themselves (cf. Colossians 4:6).

Peace he will make. Twelve men wanted to know which was greatest. He held a child, told them to go to the back and serve everyone, warned them about tripping up the little ones, told them to cut off whatever takes them down — and said, now be at peace with each other. He is going to Jerusalem to make that peace at his own cost. Within weeks they will argue about rank again (10:35–41). And on the night he is handed over, he will take a towel and wash every one of their feet.
verseByVerse.note: Salt was added to every sacrifice. Salt from the Dead Sea could have its salt leached out and lose its taste.

parallels.desc: with all your offerings you shall offer salt
let your speech be seasoned with salt

9.theology:
What happened on the mountain? The word is metamorphōthē — transformed. And nothing was added; something was, for a moment, no longer withheld. Set it beside Moses, whose face shone coming down Sinai and had to be veiled (Ex. 34:29–35) — but that light was borrowed and fading, which Paul says is why he covered it (2 Cor. 3:13). Here the light comes from inside; the clothes go white because of what is underneath them. Three men were allowed to see, for a few minutes, what was true of him every day they had walked beside him without noticing.

Who will not taste death? (v. 1) Mark's own arrangement answers it: the very next words are and after six days, and Mark almost never gives intervals. Some standing there would see the kingdom come with power — and six days later, three of them did. Peter confirms the reading himself, citing that mountain as evidence of the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ (2 Pet. 1:16–18). Serious readers have argued for the resurrection, Pentecost, or AD 70, and the instinct behind those is right — the kingdom comes in power by stages — but after six days is not decoration.

Why could the disciples not cast it out? (v. 29) Not a technique, and not a shortage of authority — he had given it and never withdrawn it. Prayer here is not a step they omitted on the day but the posture of a whole life. They had succeeded before; somewhere between that success and this valley the authority had become a possession rather than a gift held moment by moment. They did not stop believing. They stopped depending — and the two are almost impossible to tell apart from the inside until the day it does not work.

And the verses your Bible skips. A King James Bible has the refrain of v. 48, about the worm that does not die, three times, at vv. 44, 46 and 48. Those two repetitions are a copyist's echo of v. 48 and are absent from the earliest manuscripts, which is why modern Bibles footnote them. Nothing is lost: the sentence stands once, in full force, where Jesus quoted it from Isaiah 66:24.
9.examples:
Then: a father who had watched his son thrown to the ground since childhood, pulled him out of fires and out of water, never heard him speak — and who came looking for Jesus, found the disciples instead, and watched them fail in front of a crowd.

Now: the if you can in his prayer was not there when he set out. The disciples' failure damaged his faith in Christ. That still happens exactly the same way: the church that let someone down, the Christian who wronged them, the leader who fell, the prayer meeting that promised and produced nothing. People come to Christ afterwards with a clause in their mouth that somebody else put there — which is worth remembering by anyone whose conduct is watched by a weaker believer, and it is why v. 42 talks about millstones.

And then watch what the man does with the little he has. I believe; help my unbelief! — a shout, not a formulation, from a man on his knees beside a convulsing child. He will not deny the faith he has, and he will not pretend it is more than it is. He asks Christ to deal with the very thing that disqualifies him.

Most of us are not in one state or the other. We believe and doubt in the same hour about the same thing, and the great temptation is to sort ourselves out before we come — to work up the required confidence and then pray, as though faith were the entry fee. This man brought both halves and dumped them at Christ's feet.

And the boy was healed. That is the answer to the prayer and the vindication of it. Jesus does not say come back when you are sure. He meets the faith that is there, trembling and shot through with doubt, and does the very thing the man's doubt said he could not do. So if your faith this morning is a mess, do not wait for it to improve. Say this man's sentence. It is in the Bible to be prayed.

10.title: The Road, the Ransom, and the Beggar Who Followed
10.text: <sup>1</sup>And he left there and went to the region of Judea and beyond the Jordan, and crowds gathered to him again. And again, as was his custom, he taught them. <sup>2</sup>And Pharisees came up and in order to test him asked, “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?” <sup>3</sup>He answered them, “What did Moses command you?” <sup>4</sup>They said, “Moses allowed a man to write a certificate of divorce and to send her away.” <sup>5</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Because of your hardness of heart he wrote you this commandment. <sup>6</sup>But from the beginning of creation, ‘God made them male and female.’ <sup>7</sup>‘Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, <sup>8</sup>and the two shall become one flesh.’ So they are no longer two but one flesh. <sup>9</sup>What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.” <sup>10</sup>And in the house the disciples asked him again about this matter. <sup>11</sup>And he said to them, “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her, <sup>12</sup>and if she divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery.” <sup>13</sup>And they were bringing children to him that he might touch them, and the disciples rebuked them. <sup>14</sup>But when Jesus saw it, he was indignant and said to them, “Let the children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God. <sup>15</sup>Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it.” <sup>16</sup>And he took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them. <sup>17</sup>And as he was setting out on his journey, a man ran up and knelt before him and asked him, “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” <sup>18</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone. <sup>19</sup>You know the commandments: ‘Do not murder, Do not commit adultery, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Do not defraud, Honor your father and mother.’” <sup>20</sup>And he said to him, “Teacher, all these I have kept from my youth.” <sup>21</sup>And Jesus, looking at him, loved him, and said to him, “You lack one thing: go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” <sup>22</sup>Disheartened by the saying, he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. <sup>23</sup>And Jesus looked around and said to his disciples, “How difficult it will be for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!” <sup>24</sup>And the disciples were amazed at his words. But Jesus said to them again, “Children, how difficult it is to enter the kingdom of God! <sup>25</sup>It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.” <sup>26</sup>And they were exceedingly astonished, and said to him, “Then who can be saved?” <sup>27</sup>Jesus looked at them and said, “With man it is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God.” <sup>28</sup>Peter began to say to him, “See, we have left everything and followed you.” <sup>29</sup>Jesus said, “Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or lands, for my sake and for the gospel, <sup>30</sup>who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and lands, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life. <sup>31</sup>But many who are first will be last, and the last first.” <sup>32</sup>And they were on the road, going up to Jerusalem, and Jesus was walking ahead of them. And they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid. And taking the twelve again, he began to tell them what was to happen to him, <sup>33</sup>saying, “See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and the scribes, and they will condemn him to death and deliver him over to the Gentiles. <sup>34</sup>And they will mock him and spit on him, and flog him and kill him. And after three days he will rise.” <sup>35</sup>And James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came up to him and said to him, “Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you.” <sup>36</sup>And he said to them, “What do you want me to do for you?” <sup>37</sup>And they said to him, “Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory.” <sup>38</sup>Jesus said to them, “You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, or to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” <sup>39</sup>And they said to him, “We are able.” And Jesus said to them, “The cup that I drink you will drink, and with the baptism with which I am baptized, you will be baptized, <sup>40</sup>but to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to grant, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared.” <sup>41</sup>And when the ten heard it, they began to be indignant at James and John. <sup>42</sup>And Jesus called them to him and said to them, “You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. <sup>43</sup>But it shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, <sup>44</sup>and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all. <sup>45</sup>For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” <sup>46</sup>And they came to Jericho. And as he was leaving Jericho with his disciples and a great crowd, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, the son of Timaeus, was sitting by the roadside. <sup>47</sup>And when he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out and say, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” <sup>48</sup>And many rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more, “Son of David, have mercy on me!” <sup>49</sup>And Jesus stopped and said, “Call him.” And they called the blind man, saying to him, “Take heart. Get up; he is calling you.” <sup>50</sup>And throwing off his cloak, he sprang up and came to Jesus. <sup>51</sup>And Jesus said to him, “What do you want me to do for you?” And the blind man said to him, “Rabbi, let me recover my sight.” <sup>52</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Go your way; your faith has made you well.” And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him on the way.
10.overview:
Chapter 10 takes the three things people build their lives out of — marriage, children, money — and hands them, one after another, to a man walking to Jerusalem to die.

The Pharisees open with the question that cost John the Baptist his head, and Jesus refuses to argue about grounds for divorce. He goes behind Moses to Genesis: male and female, one flesh, what therefore God has joined together, let not man separate. Then parents bring children and the disciples turn them away, and Jesus is indignant — the only time in Mark that word is used of him, and it is aimed at his own men. Then a rich man runs, kneels, asks the best question in the Gospel, is looked at and loved by the Son of God — and goes home, because there was one thing he would not give.

The second half is a road. Jesus walks ahead with a set face while the twelve follow amazed and the crowd follows afraid, and he tells them for the third time exactly what is waiting: handed over, condemned, given to the Gentiles, mocked, spat on, flogged, killed, raised. James and John's response is to ask for the two best seats — and out of that squabble comes the summit of the Gospel: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.

Then Jericho, and a blind beggar who shouts a messianic title none of the disciples has used, is told to be quiet, shouts louder, throws away the only thing he owns, and follows Jesus up the road. The chapter opened with a rich man who would not follow and closes with a beggar who did.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–31 — Divorce, Children, and the Danger of Riches
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The trap (vv. 1–12). He crosses into Herod's jurisdiction, and the Pharisees immediately ask him about divorce — the question that cost John the Baptist his head. Jesus refuses to argue about grounds and goes behind Moses to Genesis: male and female, one flesh, joined by God.

The children (vv. 13–16). Parents bring their children to be touched, the disciples turn them away as an interruption, and Jesus is indignant — the only time in Mark that word is used of him, and it is aimed at his own men. Then he picks the children up and blesses them.

The rich man (vv. 17–22). A man runs, kneels, and asks the best question in the Gospel. Jesus looks at him and loves him, and asks for the one thing he will not give. He goes away sorrowful, and Mark does not soften the ending.

The impossibility (vv. 23–31). A camel through a needle's eye, disciples asking then who can be saved?, and the only answer there has ever been — with man it is impossible, but not with God.

Three subjects, and one thread running under them: marriage, children, money. The three things people build their lives out of, handled one after another by a man walking to Jerusalem to die.
verseByVerse.theology:
Divorce, and what Mark leaves out. A reader with Matthew open will notice that Mark's version is starker. Matthew twice records an exception — except for sexual immorality (Matt. 5:32; 19:9) — and Mark records none, while adding, for his Roman readers, the case of a wife who divorces her husband.

That is not a contradiction but a difference of purpose. Mark gives the principle in its unguarded, creation-order form, the way a thing is stated when you want its full weight felt. Matthew, writing where the rabbis argued endlessly over grounds, records the one qualification Jesus actually allowed. Paul adds a second — the believer deserted by an unbelieving spouse is not enslaved (1 Cor. 7:15). So the Reformed churches have long recognised two grounds on which the bond may be broken and the innocent party freed: adultery and desertion, and no others.

Mark's silence is not a denial. It is a refusal to lead with the exception — because the moment the exception becomes the headline, hardness of heart starts hunting for a way in. Jesus will not begin where the Pharisees wanted to begin, with the escape clause. He begins with the joining that God himself performs.

And "Why do you call me good?" (v. 18) is not Jesus denying that he is good or that he is God — and note that he never withdraws the word or corrects the man for using it. He holds it up to the light. The young man has tossed off Good Teacher as easy flattery. Jesus stops him: do you know what you are saying? Goodness in the full sense belongs to God alone. So either you should not have called me good — or, if the word is right, you must reckon with who I am. It is not a denial of his deity but a door held open to it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a man who ran, knelt, asked the right question, had kept the commandments since boyhood, was looked at and loved by the Son of God — and went home.

Now: he is the most alarming figure in the Gospel precisely because there is nothing wrong with him. He is not a Pharisee, not a hypocrite, not hostile. He is sincere, moral, eager and respectful, and he is the one person in Mark who meets Jesus, is loved by him, and walks away.

And notice what stopped him. Not an argument. Not doubt. One thing he would not hand over.

So the question the passage actually asks is not am I a good person? — he was, by every visible measure. It is: what is the one thing? What would you be unable to say yes to, if Christ named it tonight? For this man it was money, and Jesus went straight to it, because a rival throne is always specific.

The test is not hypothetical either. Most people know the answer within a few seconds and then spend a while explaining why that particular thing is different. He went away sorrowful, which means he knew exactly what he was refusing. Mark records no second visit.

verseByVerse.quote: And he left there and went to the region of Judea and beyond the Jordan, and crowds gathered to him again. And again, as was his custom, he taught them. And Pharisees came up and in order to test him asked, "Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The question was a political and rabbinic trap, asked entirely from the man’s side — and Jesus is about to bring the forgotten wife into view.

Galilee behind him. He won’t return; everything from here runs toward Jerusalem. He goes “beyond the Jordan” — Perea, the eastern strip, which like Galilee was ruled by Herod Antipas. He has walked into the jurisdiction of the man who beheaded John the Baptist, and the next thing he is asked about is divorce.

His custom. “Again, as was his custom, he taught them.” The whole ministry in one sentence: they came, and he taught.

A loaded question. Mark gives the motive first: “to test him.” First, it was politically lethal. John had told Herod Antipas his marriage to his brother’s wife was unlawful, and it cost him his head (6:17–29); Herod’s fortress was in this very region. Answer strictly, and a repeat is likely — and they know it.

A live dispute. Second, everyone knew the sides. Moses permitted divorce if a man found “some indecency” in his wife (Deuteronomy 24:1), and the argument turned on that phrase. The school of Shammai said it meant unfaithfulness only. The school of Hillel said almost anything — the rabbis’ own examples include spoiling a dish, and one teacher allowed divorce if a man found someone prettier. The question is designed to make him take sides where every answer loses someone.

Nobody mentioned the wife. Third, the part we feel least: “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?” is asked entirely from the man’s side. In that world the initiative was almost always his; a woman put away had no property, standing, or much future. They are debating the limits of a man’s freedom to dispose of a person. No one has mentioned the wife. Jesus is about to. A test: when you think about a hard question in marriage, whose interests do you think of first?
verseByVerse.note: “Beyond the Jordan” is Perea, the land east of the river, ruled by Herod Antipas — who had imprisoned John for his marriage. Rabbis debated the grounds for divorce.

verseByVerse.quote: He answered them, "What did Moses command you?" They said, "Moses allowed a man to write a certificate of divorce and to send her away." And Jesus said to them, "Because of your hardness of heart he wrote you this commandment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s regulation of divorce was a concession to sin to limit damage, not a statement of what he wants — and asking “how far may I go?” is usually the wrong question.

Commanded, or allowed? He answers with a question, and the verb is precise: “What did Moses command you?” They correct him without realising they have conceded the argument: “Moses allowed.” Not commanded — permitted. And they are right. No commandment in the law tells anyone to divorce. Deuteronomy 24 regulates a practice already happening, and the regulation is protective. The certificate was the woman’s document: written proof she had been released and wasn’t an adulteress, without which she could be accused and destitute for life. Moses wasn’t opening a door but limiting the damage on the other side of one already open.

Hardness of heart. The phrase used of the Pharisees in the synagogue (3:5), and close to what Mark said of the disciples (6:52; 8:17): a heart thickened until it can’t feel. So the legislation exists because of a defect in the people it was given to. It isn’t a description of what God wants, but damage limitation for a world where men will put their wives out whether or not it is permitted, so that at least she leaves with a paper in her hand.

“For you.” Sharp: “he wrote you this commandment.” Not us, not Israel: you. The concession was granted to people like you, for hardness like yours, and you have turned it into an entitlement and come asking how far it extends.

Permitted is not intended. A distinction we constantly lose in reading Scripture. The Bible regulates polygamy, slavery, warfare and divorce; it commends none of them, and in each case the regulation restrains a fallen practice rather than laying down a blueprint. Reading a concession as an endorsement is exactly the mistake in this conversation.

The wrong question. “Is this allowed?” is often the wrong question, and nearly always asked by someone who has already decided what they want. Someone who genuinely wants to please God doesn’t begin by fixing the outer boundary of what he can get away with. That is the Hillel question, and Jesus won’t answer it. A test: in what area are you asking “how far may I go?” rather than “what does God want?” He goes back further than Moses, to a garden.
verseByVerse.note: A certificate of divorce freed a woman to remarry.

verseByVerse.quote: But from the beginning of creation, 'God made them male and female.' 'Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.' So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Marriage is God’s own work, built into creation, a real union of one flesh — to be guarded faithfully, not treated as an arrangement that lasts while it works.

From the beginning. The most important move in the passage. Asked about Deuteronomy, he goes to Genesis; asked about the rules for ending a marriage, he goes to what a marriage is. And he treats Genesis 1 and 2 as God’s own word about how people were made, deeper and earlier than the Mosaic regulation.

Male and female. “God made them male and female” (v. 6, quoting Genesis 1:27). Marriage isn’t a human invention societies happened to adopt and may therefore adapt. It is built into how people were made — before any law, culture, or the fall.

Leave and hold fast. Genesis 2:24 has two verbs. “Leave” — a public, decisive break with the strongest tie a person has had. Marriage begins with a departure, and a marriage where one party has never really left home, emotionally or practically, will feel that fault line for decades. “Hold fast” — to be glued or welded, used of clinging to God himself (Deuteronomy 10:20); not a mood but a decision renewed regardless of how the week has gone.

One flesh. “So they are no longer two but one flesh” — Jesus’ own comment on the text. A fact, not an ideal to aim at: two people have been made a single unit, and the union is real whatever either feels on a given morning. That is why ending a marriage is never merely administrative. You can’t separate one flesh without tearing something, and everyone who has been through it knows that in their body long before they can say it (cf. Ephesians 5:31).

God joined. “What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.” The weight is in the two agents. God joins — not the couple, officiant, registrar or guests. In every genuine marriage, including those between people who never gave him a thought, there is a divine act, and the two are dealing with something they didn’t make. Man didn’t do the joining, so isn’t competent to undo it.

For the married. This verse is mainly about how you regard the marriage you are in. Not an arrangement that continues while it works, but something God did. That changes the bad days — the year going wrong, the stretch where you feel nothing, the first thought that you might have made a mistake. The question then isn’t “Is this still working?” but “What did God join, and what am I doing to keep it?” Marriages are rarely separated by one decision but by a thousand small permissions — the conversation not had, the resentment kept, the friendship at work that becomes where you feel understood. “Let not man separate” is a command about all of that, addressed to the person in the mirror. A test: what small permission do you need to withdraw this week?

parallels.desc: male and female he created them

verseByVerse.quote: And in the house the disciples asked him again about this matter. And he said to them, "Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her, and if she divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s standard for marriage applies equally to husband and wife, the wronged spouse is truly sinned against — and Christ’s forgiveness reaches every broken marriage.

They asked again. A public statement, then a private question; those who ask get the fuller answer. They ask again, because it landed as startling; the disciples were as taken aback as anyone: “If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is better not to marry” (Matthew 19:10).

Named as adultery. Two things would startle a Jewish ear. First, the act is called adultery. Under the rabbinic system a properly executed divorce ended the marriage, and a man who remarried had done nothing wrong; the certificate had cleared him. Jesus says the certificate doesn’t touch what God joined.

“Against her.” Second, astonishingly, the wrong is done against her. In Jewish law adultery was an offence against a husband; a man couldn’t commit adultery against his own wife. Jesus names the woman as the one sinned against. In a conversation that began with men debating a man’s freedom to dispose of a person, with no mention of the wife, he puts her at the centre and calls her the wronged party. Wherever the gospel has gone, that has followed: the raising of women’s dignity where Christianity spread starts here, in a house in Perea, with a rabbi telling twelve men a discarded wife has been sinned against.

No double standard. “If she divorces her husband” — a clause only in Mark. Under Jewish law a woman normally couldn’t initiate divorce; under Roman law she could, and did, as Herodias had (6:17). Mark writes for the church at Rome, where women had legal options no Galilean woman had, and includes the sentence that applies to them. The standard is the same both ways; no allowance for the husband denied to the wife.

Is there then no ground at all for divorce? Mark gives the principle without qualification, but he isn’t the only witness. Matthew records the exception, “except for sexual immorality” (Matthew 19:9), and Paul adds desertion by an unbelieving spouse: “the brother or sister is not enslaved” (1 Corinthians 7:15). Some Christians hold there are no grounds at all, only separation; others allow divorce for many reasons. The more likely reading is that adultery and desertion are real grounds, and in those cases the innocent party is free to remarry. That isn’t a list of loopholes; even then reconciliation is better where possible.

What of those who divorced on other grounds and remarried? The sin is real and should be confessed. But a second marriage, once made, is a marriage, and the answer isn’t to break it, which would add another sin (cf. Deuteronomy 24:1–4). Christ forgives the repentant, and they are to live faithfully where they now are (cf. 1 Corinthians 7:10–11).

For the divorced reader. For the reader already divorced, perhaps remarried, reading these sentences with a sinking heart: the standard hasn’t moved, and it would be no kindness to pretend so; a church that lowers it to seem gentle only makes grace unnecessary. But hear this clearly. No sin named here is beyond the blood of Christ, and no marriage so broken — your fault, another’s, or a tangle of both — that grace can’t make something new of what remains. The gospel meets you not in the marriage you should have had but in the life you actually have, with a Saviour who came “to give his life as a ransom for many” (v. 45), the divorced among them. Repent where you must, receive what he freely gives, and walk forward forgiven.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish law did not allow a wife to divorce her husband, but Roman law did; Mark’s wording covers both.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were bringing children to him that he might touch them, and the disciples rebuked them. But when Jesus saw it, he was indignant and said to them, "Let the children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is angered when anyone, especially the small and unimportant, is kept from him, and his kingdom belongs to those who come as children.

Bringing children. Parents, presumably; Luke’s word suggests some were infants (Luke 18:15). It was ordinary to bring a child to a respected rabbi for a blessing. That is all they ask: put your hand on him.

Rebuked. A strong verb, used of rebuking demons and of Peter rebuking Jesus. They didn’t gently discourage; they told them off. And by ordinary measures their reasoning was sound: the Master is on the road to Jerusalem, has taught all day, has just handled a hostile delegation, is tired, and there is a queue of adults with real questions. Children aren’t a priority; someone must manage the diary. The second time in two chapters they have tried to control access to Jesus (9:38). Something in religious people gravitates toward the door.

Indignant. Mark alone records it, the word he uses of the ten furious with James and John (v. 41). Not mild disapproval: Jesus was angry, with his own disciples, because children were being kept from him. The Son of God, days from the cross, visibly angry because someone turned away a queue of toddlers. If you have wondered whether the small and unimpressive matter to Christ, this settles it. What angered him wasn’t the interruption but the gatekeeping.

Do not hinder. The word the Ethiopian used: “What prevents me from being baptized?” (Acts 8:36). Who hinders children now? Rarely deliberately. It is done by treating them as a distraction to manage until they are old enough to matter: the church with no room for them, the family where faith is discussed but never with them, the parent too tired at bedtime and always will be. No one rebukes anyone; the children simply don’t get brought. A test: what one thing will you do this week to bring a child to Christ?

To such. “To such belongs the kingdom of God” — not “to these.” Not that children are automatically in and adults not, but that the kingdom belongs to people of this kind, and v. 15 says what kind.

Does this passage support baptizing infants? Many Christians think so, reading “do not hinder them” as a word about bringing children into the covenant community and giving them its sign. But no one is baptized here. Jesus blesses the children; he doesn’t baptize them, and the point he draws is about receiving the kingdom like a child (v. 15), with empty hands. The more likely reading is that baptism belongs to those who have come to faith, while the children of believers are brought to Christ in prayer and teaching from the start.

What of children who die young? Scripture gives no age of accountability and no formula. Some believe all who die in infancy are saved, others only the children of believers; the safest course is to say no more than Scripture says. But it gives good ground for hope: David expected to go to his son (2 Samuel 12:23), and the One who took children in his arms is the Judge who will do right (Genesis 18:25).
verseByVerse.note: Children had little status in the ancient world.
