verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it." And he took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kingdom is received only as a gift, with the empty-handed dependence of a child, and Christ welcomes the small with tender love.

A condition. The amen-formula, and stated negatively, so it is a condition, not a compliment: no one enters any other way.

What about a child? Not innocence. Children aren’t morally blank; anyone who has raised one knows selfishness needs no teaching, and David says he was “brought forth in iniquity” (Psalm 51:5). Not simplicity of mind either, as if faith required us to stop thinking; this is the Lord who told a scribe to love God with all his mind. It is dependence. A small child owned nothing, earned nothing, contributed nothing. He didn’t negotiate for dinner; he was fed. He didn’t qualify for his place in the family; he was born into it. Everything came as a gift from someone bigger, and he took it without embarrassment. That is how the kingdom is received — the opposite of how everything else in life is acquired.

Hard for competent adults. Every other sphere rewards the self-sufficient — the one who earns it, manages it, deserves it, brings something to the table. Here the qualities that recommend you everywhere else disqualify. “Receive” is the only verb on offer. It explains the rest of the chapter: a child comes with empty hands and is welcomed; a rich man comes with full ones and can’t get in. A test: are you still trying to bring something to qualify, or have you received the kingdom as a gift (cf. Matthew 18:3)?

In his arms. He doesn’t merely permit them; he picks them up. The rare verb, “to fold in the arms,” occurs twice in the New Testament, both in Mark: here and in 9:36. Peter remembered both times — a fisherman in Rome decades later telling a church that the Lord of glory didn’t pat children on the head; he gathered them up. The parents asked for a touch; he gave an embrace and a blessing, one child at a time, on a road going up to Jerusalem, while grown men wished he would get on.

Those hands. He laid his hands on them — the hands that took a dead girl by the hand (5:41) and lifted a convulsing boy (9:27), and which within weeks would be nailed down, unable to hold anyone at all.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he was setting out on his journey, a man ran up and knelt before him and asked him, "Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?" And Jesus said to him, "Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An eager, sincere seeker still thinks of salvation as something to earn, and Jesus challenges him to reckon with who Jesus really is.

Everything right. He ran — a grown man of standing (Matthew says young, Luke a ruler) running on a public road, undignified in that culture, and he didn’t care. He knelt, in the dirt, before an itinerant teacher. And he asks the best question anyone asks in this Gospel. The Pharisees ask about divorce law and signs; the disciples about seats and greatness; he asks how to be saved. Hold that before the passage turns hard, because its point is nearly always missed by making him a villain. He isn’t. He is eager, humble, urgent, morally serious, and asking the right thing. If he walked into your church you would thank God for him.

The crack in the question. “What must I do to inherit?” An inheritance is precisely what no one does anything for; you receive it because of who you are in the family. He has joined the language of gift to the language of achievement, and doesn’t notice. The child two verses ago received; this man wants to know the price.

Was Jesus denying he is good — or God? “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone” has been seized on for centuries as if he were denying his goodness or deity. He is doing neither, and he never withdraws the word or corrects the man for using it. He holds it up to the light. “Good Teacher” wasn’t a normal address; the rabbis didn’t use it. It is flattery — warm, sincere and cheap, the compliment paid to a respected figure on the way to asking a favour. Jesus stops him: do you know what you just said? Goodness in the full sense belongs to God alone. That leaves two possibilities, and the man never works out which he is in: either you shouldn’t have called me good and have come kneeling to the wrong person, or the word is right and you must reckon with who stands before you. Not a denial of his deity but a door held open to it. He came asking what he must do; the deeper question, which he never reaches, is “Who is this?”

Compliment or confession? A hard test for how we talk about Jesus. It is possible to say very warm things about him and mean very little — wonderful, loving, good, the greatest teacher who ever lived — paying a compliment rather than making a confession. He can stop someone mid-sentence and ask whether he knows what he is saying. A test: when you praise Jesus, do you mean that he is God?
verseByVerse.note: Matthew says he was young, Luke that he was a ruler. Jesus does not deny his goodness; he asks the man to think about what he is saying.

verseByVerse.quote: You know the commandments: 'Do not murder, Do not commit adultery, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Do not defraud, Honor your father and mother.'" And he said to him, "Teacher, all these I have kept from my youth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law is a mirror to show us our need, but this sincere man treats it as a checklist and doesn’t see his own heart.

The mirror. “You know the commandments.” He begins where the man began — “What must I do?” — and goes to the law, not because keeping it saves anyone, but because it is the mirror the man needs to look into.

Only the second table. Do not murder, commit adultery, steal, bear false witness, defraud; honour your parents — all about how you treat others (cf. Exodus 20:12–16). Not one of the first four commandments: no other gods, no idols, the Name, the Sabbath. Deliberate, a trap set gently. The man’s problem will turn out to be a first-table problem — a rival god — and Jesus recites only the commandments he can pass, and waits.

“Do not defraud.” One item isn’t among the Ten. It appears elsewhere in the law: “You shall not oppress your neighbor or rob him. The wages of a hired worker shall not remain with you all night until the morning” (Leviticus 19:13) — withholding what is owed, especially to a labourer; it may stand for the tenth, against coveting. Jesus slipped it in, the one commandment a wealthy landowner in that world was most likely to break and least likely to notice: the sin of the account book, not the bedroom. He is probed kindly at the point of his danger, and feels nothing. A test: is there anything you owe someone — wages, payment, a debt — that you have been quietly holding back?

“All these I have kept.” Two things, pulling opposite ways. It isn’t contested; Jesus doesn’t say “no you haven’t,” and next he looks at him and loves him. Taken as most would take it — an upright, observant, decent man since boyhood — it was probably true. And it is the most self-condemning sentence in the chapter. Someone who has genuinely understood any commandment doesn’t talk like this. It isn’t the language of a man who has looked into the law and seen his own face, but of one treating it as a checklist and waiting for the remaining item.

Something to add? He dropped “Good” — “Teacher” now; something in the first exchange registered. And he still assumes something is missing that can be added, that the account is nearly balanced and one more entry will do it. What he is about to be shown isn’t an extra item but that the whole account belongs to Someone else.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus lists the commandments about one’s neighbour; “do not defraud” is not one of the Ten in so many words; it may stand for the tenth, against coveting (cf. Lev 19:13).

parallels.desc: the second table of the Ten Commandments

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus, looking at him, loved him, and said to him, "You lack one thing: go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me." Disheartened by the saying, he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ lovingly exposes whatever rival god holds our heart, and refuses to lower the cost of following him — because a cheaper offer would leave our idol in place.

He loved him. Only Mark records it — one of the tenderest half-sentences in the Bible. “Looking” is a fixed, held gaze, not a glance. And “he loved him”: the only place in this Gospel where Jesus is said to love a particular individual. Everything hard that follows must be read inside that. These aren’t cold words, but those of a man who looked at this eager, moral, self-deceived young person and was moved with love.

One thing. “You lack one thing” must have been a relief for two seconds: a single outstanding item. Then the item.

Is this required of every Christian? No, and the Gospels settle it. Peter kept his house in Capernaum. Zacchaeus gave away half and was told salvation had come to his house (Luke 19:8–9). Joseph of Arimathea was rich and remained so, and his money bought the tomb. Jesus issues this command to no one else in the New Testament. It isn’t a universal rule but a scalpel, going to one man’s one thing. A test: what is your one thing — the thing you would find hardest to give up for Christ?

A first-table problem. The demand exposes a first-table problem with a second-table instruction. He had passed the list about neighbours; Jesus now finds out in one sentence whether he has another god, and the answer comes back at once.

A trade, not asceticism. Jesus doesn’t tell him to be poorer but to trade — treasure on earth for treasure in heaven, the better end of any bargain offered a human being. And the real prize isn’t the treasure: “come, follow me.” He is invited to join the Twelve. He is the only person in Mark personally called by Jesus who says no (cf. Philippians 3:7–8).

Sorrow that isn’t repentance. “Disheartened” — his face fell, the word for a darkening sky. And he goes. The sorrow is real; he isn’t angry or scoffing. He knows exactly what he refuses and refuses it anyway, miserably. There is sorrow over the cost of obedience that never obeys, and he is its portrait.

They had him. “For he had great possessions” — flat, last, without comment, and exactly the wrong way round. He didn’t have great possessions. They had him.

He let him go. Jesus doesn’t call after him, soften the terms, offer a smaller figure, or suggest they discuss it over a meal. The Son of God, who loved him, watched him walk away and let him go. That is love that won’t lie to you. A love that lowered the price would have been crueller — sending him home comfortable, idol intact, thinking himself safe. Mark records no second visit: a man walking down a road with everything he came for still in his hands.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark notes that Jesus looked at him and loved him.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus looked around and said to his disciples, "How difficult it will be for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!" And the disciples were amazed at his words. But Jesus said to them again, "Children, how difficult it is to enter the kingdom of God! It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wealth makes self-reliance feel natural, but no one can enter the kingdom by human power — and by world standards most of us are rich.

For those staying. He watches the man go, then turns to the Twelve. What follows isn’t aimed at the departing figure but at the men staying.

Why they were staggered. In the Old Testament prosperity often signals God’s favour — Abraham, Job, Solomon — and popular theology concluded a rich man is a blessed man. Practically, too: a rich man can afford generosity, keep the law scrupulously, endow a synagogue, give alms, has leisure to be devout. If anyone would make it, surely he would. Jesus says the opposite, and the ground moves.

For everybody. He says it again, without the qualification: “how difficult it is to enter the kingdom of God!” Verse 23 was about the wealthy; v. 24 about everyone. The rich man’s case isn’t a special category but the general human case with the difficulty made visible. And he begins, “Children” — affectionate, the only time in Mark — opening the hardest thing in the chapter as a father would.

Meant to be impossible. The largest animal anyone handled, the smallest hole anyone used. Two softenings have circulated for centuries; lay both aside. One says the “Needle’s Eye” was a small Jerusalem gate a camel could squeeze through if unloaded and kneeling. There is no evidence such a gate existed; the story appears only in the Middle Ages, and it turns the saying into encouraging advice — with a bit of humility and less baggage you can just manage — the opposite of the point. The other suggests “cable” for “camel,” the Greek words being similar; the manuscripts don’t support it, and a ship’s rope won’t go through a needle either. He meant impossible. The disciples’ reaction shows they heard it so, and he doesn’t correct them.

We are the camel. Before filing this under other people’s problems, be honest about who is reading. Anyone with a home, a change of clothes, food not in question this week, and medical care within reach is, by every measure the world has known and most it knows now, rich. This isn’t a passage about bankers. It is the camel and the needle, and we are the camel (cf. 1 Timothy 6:9–10, 17). A test: what are you trusting for security that only God can give?
verseByVerse.note: The camel was the largest animal in the land; the picture is deliberate exaggeration. The idea of a gate called “the Eye of the Needle” is a much later invention.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were exceedingly astonished, and said to him, "Then who can be saved?" Jesus looked at them and said, "With man it is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can save himself, but God can and does save the helpless.

The right question. “Exceedingly astonished” — stronger than before. And their question is exactly right; here the disciples reason perfectly. If the man with every visible advantage — money, morality, eagerness, a clean record since boyhood — can’t get in, nobody can. They see the difficulty isn’t one of degree; it isn’t that the rich have further to walk, but that the door admits no one under their own power. And it isn’t academic: these men have left everything, as Peter will say. If wealth can’t buy entry, neither can renunciation, and they have just worked that out.

He looked at them. Mark keeps showing Jesus’ eyes: he looked at the rich man and loved him (v. 21), looked around at the disciples (v. 23), and now fixes his gaze on them before the most important sentence in the passage.

Impossible with man. We habitually take it as exaggeration. Not difficult, not unlikely without help, not achievable by the exceptionally devout — impossible, with the full force of the camel and the needle. No one has ever saved himself, contributed to it, met God halfway, or made himself a better prospect — not the rich man with his record, not Peter with his boat, not you. So the disciples’ question has one answer, and it isn’t the poor, humble or hard-trying. It is: nobody — unless God does it.

But not with God. The whole of Christianity in the turn (cf. Genesis 18:14). The impossibility is real and total, and God’s to solve, and he has solved it. That demolishes the most popular religious sentence in English, “God helps those who help themselves.” It isn’t in the Bible and is the reverse of this verse. God saves those who can’t help themselves, which is everyone.

By a death. How? Not left in the air. The man saying it is on the road to Jerusalem, and in eighteen verses says why: “to give his life as a ransom for many” (v. 45). The impossibility isn’t overcome by changing the requirements but by a death.

The correct assessment. If you have looked honestly at yourself and concluded you have no business in the kingdom of God, you have understood v. 27 better than most. That is the correct assessment; Jesus made it first, and then said the four words that answer it: “but not with God.” A test: are you resting on anything you have done, or only on what God has done in Christ?

parallels.desc: is anything too hard for the LORD?

verseByVerse.quote: Peter began to say to him, "See, we have left everything and followed you." Jesus said, "Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or lands, for my sake and for the gospel, who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and lands, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life. But many who are first will be last, and the last first."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ gives his followers a new family in the church now, along with suffering, and eternal life later — yet sacrifice earns no ranking in his kingdom.

“We have left everything.” “Began to say” is delicate, as if Peter started the sentence and thought better of finishing it. Peter all over: honest, blurted, not quite right. Having watched the rich man fail, heard about the camel and that it is impossible, what comes out is: we did, though. A real question underneath — Matthew has it plainly: “What then will we have?” (Matthew 19:27) — and not wholly unworthy: they left boats, nets, a business, a home, a family. But it is the wrong question two verses after “with man it is impossible.” He is doing arithmetic again.

A generous answer. Jesus doesn’t rebuke him; he answers generously, with an amen-formula. The list — house, brothers, sisters, mother, father, children, lands — is everything a man in that world had. And “for my sake and for the gospel” isn’t incidental: loss as such isn’t commended; Christians aren’t called to abandon families as a spiritual achievement. What is in view is what following him costs when it costs something.

A hundredfold now. He repeats the list: a hundredfold, the extravagant yield of the sower parable (4:8, 20), and “now in this time,” not only in heaven. What is he promising? Not a hundred houses for one, but the church. Leave your family for Christ and you are given families — a hundred homes where you are welcome, a hundred mothers, brothers, sisters. That is what happened: Paul greets a woman in Rome as “his mother, who has been a mother to me as well” (Romans 16:13); the early church was a network of homes and tables belonging to unrelated people (cf. Acts 2:44–47). And it is one of Christ’s few promises testable this month: the believer with no family never alone at Christmas; the convert cut off by relatives with more people praying for him than he can count. If your church isn’t that for someone, this verse is an indictment before it is a comfort. A test: whom could you be a brother, sister or mother to this week?

With persecutions. One item missing from the first list is added: persecutions, set among the blessings, unemphasised, as one of the things received. No one left persecutions behind; everyone is given them. The most honest recruiting sentence ever spoken, and why this promise can’t be mistaken for a prosperity scheme. The hundredfold comes with trouble in the same parcel.

First and last. A warning aimed at the man who said “we have left everything.” The kingdom isn’t a league table with the earliest and most sacrificial at the top. Having left most doesn’t put you first — and by the chapter’s end James and John will ask for the top seats and the ten will be furious (cf. Matthew 20:16).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–52 — The Road to Jerusalem, the Ransom, and Bartimaeus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Walking ahead (vv. 32–34). Mark gives us a picture worth stopping over: a road going up to Jerusalem, Jesus striding out in front, and behind him a group that is amazed and a crowd that is frightened. Then he tells them, for the third and most detailed time, exactly what is waiting — handed over, condemned, given to the Gentiles, mocked, spat on, flogged, killed, raised.

The request (vv. 35–45). And immediately James and John ask for the two best seats. The other ten are furious, which is not righteous indignation but competition. So Jesus lays down the law of his kingdom — the great one is the servant, the first is the slave — and grounds it in himself: he came to give his life as a ransom for many.

Jericho (vv. 46–52). The last miracle before Jerusalem. A blind beggar shouts a messianic title that none of the disciples has yet used, is told to be quiet by the crowd, shouts louder, throws away the only thing he owns, and follows Jesus up the road to the cross.

The chapter opened with a rich man who would not follow and closes with a beggar who did.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mark 10:45 is the theological centre of this Gospel, and every word repays weighing.

A ransom — lytron — was the price paid to set a captive free: the sum laid down to buy a slave out of bondage or a prisoner off the block. Jesus says his own life is that price.

And a ransom is a substitute — one thing given instead of another. He does not merely die for our benefit; he dies in our stead, the many going free because the One is handed over.

Behind it stands Isaiah 53, where the Servant poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many, and by his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous (Isa. 53:11–12). That word many rings through the prophecy, and Jesus claims it as his own errand.

And to whom is the price paid? Not, as some early teachers imagined, to the devil, as though Satan held a rightful claim. The debt is owed to the justice of God — and God, in the person of his Son, pays it himself.

Here, then, is why he came. Not first to teach, or to heal, or even to model servanthood, though he did all three. To die in the room of sinners who could never buy themselves back. Nineteen verses earlier the disciples asked then who can be saved? and were told with man it is impossible, but not with God. This is how.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the same question — What do you want me to do for you? — asked twice in fifteen verses.

It is put to James and John in verse 36 and to a blind beggar in verse 51. Mark has done that deliberately, and the two answers are the whole chapter.

James and John ask for glory. They open with a blank cheque — we want you to do for us whatever we ask — and then name the two best seats in the kingdom. They get a redirection and a warning.

Bartimaeus asks for mercy, and then for sight. He gets exactly what he asks for, immediately.

Now: the question is still being asked, and most of us answer it more like the brothers than the beggar. The blank-cheque prayer — do what I have decided — dressed up religiously. The request framed around position, comfort, and being noticed.

And notice what makes Bartimaeus's answer better. It is not humility as a technique. He asked for the thing he actually needed, from someone he had correctly identified, having first asked for mercy rather than a favour. He had no credentials, no standing, and no way of repaying anybody — which is precisely the child of verse 15, arriving at the other end of the chapter with nothing in his hands.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were on the road, going up to Jerusalem, and Jesus was walking ahead of them. And they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid. And taking the twelve again, he began to tell them what was to happen to him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus went to the cross deliberately, leading the way — and he still goes ahead of his people in every fearful path.

Up to Jerusalem. Literally as well as idiomatically: Jerusalem stands over three thousand feet above Jericho, the road climbing steeply through the wilderness. Every Jew said “up” to Jerusalem regardless of the compass.

Out in front. One of the great pictures of the Gospel, painted in a few words: “Jesus was walking ahead of them.” Not led, not carried along by events or swept toward Jerusalem by a movement out of hand, but setting the pace, everyone behind. Luke: “he set his face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51). Isaiah, in the Servant’s voice: “I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame” (Isaiah 50:7). Whatever else the cross was, it wasn’t something that happened to him. He walked to it, faster than the men following.

Amazed and afraid. Two groups, two reactions. “They were amazed” — the Twelve; something in the way he walked frightened them; they had never seen him like this. “Those who followed were afraid” — the pilgrims and hangers-on further back, catching the atmosphere without understanding it. One man striding ahead with a set face, a cluster of disciples staring after him in alarm, and a straggle of frightened people behind.

He is in front. A picture of the Christian life, often exactly like this: stretches where following Christ plainly costs something, where you don’t understand what is happening, and where the honest description of your state is amazed and afraid. And the one thing the picture gives you is the one thing that helps: he is in front. Not waiting at the destination or sending instructions from afar, but on the road, going first, and nothing is coming that he hasn’t already walked into. A test: in the fearful stretch you are walking, are you keeping your eyes on him ahead of you?

Told again. He takes them aside a third time and tells them again, in more detail than ever, because they haven’t understood the first two. He won’t let them arrive in Jerusalem without having been told.
verseByVerse.note: Jerusalem stands high in the hills; one always went “up” to it.

verseByVerse.quote: saying, "See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and the scribes, and they will condemn him to death and deliver him over to the Gentiles. And they will mock him and spit on him, and flog him and kill him. And after three days he will rise."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus went knowingly to every humiliation of the cross, as the suffering Servant, and always with the promise of resurrection — though his disciples heard only what they wanted.

The fullest prediction. The first (8:31) named the rejecting parties; the second (9:31) added the handing over; this one gives the sequence step by step. “Delivered over to the chief priests and the scribes” — handed over again. “They will condemn him to death” — a verdict from the Jewish authorities. “And deliver him over to the Gentiles” — handed over a second time, and new: Israel’s leaders will pass their own Messiah to the pagans. It also says what kind of death: the Sanhedrin’s penalty was stoning; only Rome crucified. “Gentiles” means cross, without the word.

Gratuitous contempt. “Mock him and spit on him, and flog him and kill him” — four verbs, every one fulfilled in Mark 15: the purple robe and thorns, the spitting, the scourging, the crucifixion (15:15–20). Mocking and spitting aren’t needed for an execution; Rome could kill efficiently. The contempt is gratuitous, and he names it in advance — walking toward it knowing not only that he would die but that he would be humiliated first. The Servant said it centuries before: “I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting” (Isaiah 50:6). A test: when you suffer contempt for Christ, do you remember he walked into it first, for you?

Always the rising. “After three days he will rise” — on the end of every prediction. He never mentions the death without the resurrection, and the disciples never mention the resurrection.

Hearing only “glory.” Put it beside what comes next. He has described condemnation, handing over to pagans, mocking, spitting, whipping and execution, and two of his closest friends respond, with no interval, by asking for the best seats. They heard “glory” and nothing else — the third telling, and the third time they took only what they wanted. Before condemning them, admit the mechanism. We do it constantly with Scripture: the promise received, the cost skipped; the comfort taken, the command left; a sermon on the cross followed by a conversation about lunch. The disciples aren’t another species. They are us, with better excuses, since at least they had never seen a resurrection.
verseByVerse.note: This third prediction is the fullest, naming the Gentiles, mocking, spitting and flogging.

parallels.desc: I gave my back to those who strike

verseByVerse.quote: And James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came up to him and said to him, "Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you." And he said to them, "What do you want me to do for you?" And they said to him, "Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even devoted disciples can seek glory and position while ignoring the cross, and can pray as though asking God to endorse what they have already decided.

Two of the three. On the mountain of transfiguration, in the room when the girl was raised, soon taken deeper into Gethsemane — and the Sons of Thunder (3:17), and it shows. Matthew says their mother made the request (Matthew 20:20). Both presumably true: she asked, they stood there, and Mark, from Peter, puts responsibility where the ten put it (v. 41). No one was fooled about whose idea it was.

A blank cheque. “We want you to do for us whatever we ask of you.” Not a question but a request to agree before the question is put — a blank cheque signed in advance, how a child approaches a parent when he already knows the answer is no. The same move comes in respectable clothing: praying that isn’t asking but informing, a decision already taken, brought to God for endorsement rather than judgment. “Lord, bless what I have determined to do.” Reverent words; a blank-cheque transaction. A test: is there a decision you are asking God to bless rather than to judge?

“What do you want me to do for you?” He won’t sign the cheque; he makes them say it aloud. And mark the question: Jesus will ask it again, word for word, of a blind beggar (v. 51). Two very different people, and their two answers are the point of the chapter.

The top two seats. “Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory.” A king’s right and left were the realm’s two highest places — prime minister and second-in-command. Not asking to be useful, but for the top two positions in the government of the universe — both, so they have already decided the other ten aren’t getting them.

Admirable and deaf. Something almost admirable is buried in it: they believe him. Just told he will be spat on and killed, they still ask about his glory — a genuine conviction that this man will reign, more than the crowd had. But it sits on a deafness hard to credit: he named the stages of his execution, and they took away “after three days he will rise” and made a seating plan.

The real right and left. Notice where he is while they ask: on a road, going up, walking ahead, toward the day when there will indeed be a man on his right and a man on his left in his glory — two thieves, and the glory a cross (15:27).
verseByVerse.note: To sit at a king’s right and left was the place of highest honour.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, or to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?" And they said to him, "We are able." And Jesus said to them, "The cup that I drink you will drink, and with the baptism with which I am baptized, you will be baptized, but to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to grant, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Following Christ means sharing his suffering, God graciously declines prayers we don’t understand, and places in his kingdom can’t be grasped by asking or earning.

“You do not know what you are asking.” Not “you shouldn’t have asked” or “how dare you,” but gently: you have no idea what you just requested. The first mercy in the passage, and one we should want. God doesn’t grant our prayers according to our understanding of them. If he did, most of us would have been destroyed years ago by things we asked confidently. There is much to thank him for in the prayers he has declined. A test: what prayer of yours are you now glad he didn’t answer as asked?

The cup. In the Old Testament, regularly the cup of God’s wrath: “in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine… and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs” (Psalm 75:8; cf. Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). The word he will use face down in Gethsemane: “Remove this cup from me” (14:36).

The baptism. Not water but being overwhelmed: “all your breakers and your waves have gone over me” (Psalm 42:7; cf. Luke 12:50). So he asks: can you be drowned in what is about to drown me? Can you drink what I will drink?

“We are able.” Instantly, with no idea what they agreed to — as Peter will at the supper (14:31). But what is right in it: they mean it. Not cynics; they think they can and want to, and their loyalty is genuine, just standing on nothing.

A prophecy fulfilled. “The cup that I drink you will drink” isn’t sarcasm but prophecy, and it came true. James was the first of the Twelve killed, put to the sword by Herod Agrippa about a decade later (Acts 12:2). John outlived them all and was exiled to a penal island “on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus” (Revelation 1:9), writing the Bible’s last book as an old man in trouble. They asked for thrones and were promised suffering, and got it, and didn’t fall away. It doesn’t end badly for them.

Not his to grant. Not a denial that he is God, but the Son speaking of the ordered work of the Trinity, where allotting places belongs to the Father — the same submission shown in Gethsemane. He doesn’t say the seats don’t exist, but that they aren’t his to hand out on request. And they are “prepared”: a divine allocation already made, not open to lobbying. You can’t secure a place in God’s kingdom by asking, deserving, arriving early, or knowing the right person — great relief for anyone who has felt they were losing a race they didn’t want to run.
verseByVerse.note: The “cup” is the Old Testament picture of God’s judgment poured out; “baptism” pictures being overwhelmed by suffering. James was later killed by Herod Agrippa.

parallels.desc: the waters have come up to my neck
I have a baptism to be baptized with

verseByVerse.quote: And when the ten heard it, they began to be indignant at James and John. And Jesus called them to him and said to them, "You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ forbids worldly power-seeking in his church and redirects ambition into humble, measurable service of everyone.

Furious. The word used of Jesus when children were turned away (v. 14), meaning just what it looks like. Mark doesn’t say why, because he needn’t. Not theological grounds — no one says, “How could you, when he has just told us he will be killed?” They are angry because two men made a move for what all twelve wanted, and got there first. They had argued about this in chapter 9 and been given a child and a lesson; nothing took. The ambition went underground and surfaced as outrage at someone else’s — the usual form in religious company. Almost no one says “I want to be the greatest”; many are quietly annoyed when someone else is treated as though they were. A test: whose recognition quietly annoys you?

All twelve. He calls them all, not dealing separately with James and John or taking the ten’s side. The disease is general and the treatment given to the whole group.

The world’s model. “Those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them.” Rome is the model: authority running downward as pressure, greatness measured by how many must do what you say. And a barb in “those who are considered”: their eminence is general opinion, what everyone agrees to call them.

“It shall not be so among you.” Among the most disobeyed words in the New Testament. Not advice but a flat prohibition on importing the world’s model of authority into the church — and church history is largely the story of ignoring it, in cathedrals and small congregations alike, wherever someone discovered that a position in the things of God could make others smaller (cf. Luke 22:24–26).

Servant, then slave. Two rungs, the second lower. “Servant” is the one who waited at table, who has a role and can go home at day’s end. “Slave” has no going home — no time of his own, no rights, no choice about whom he serves. Again the ambition isn’t forbidden — “whoever would be great.” He doesn’t say stop wanting to matter; he redirects the wanting and gives it a road, and the road runs downward (cf. 9:35).

Measurable. You can’t be a servant in general. Service happens to particular people at particular times and shows up in a diary and a bank statement. And “slave of all” removes the last escape — choosing whom to serve: the interesting, the grateful, the influential, those who will notice. All — including the ten furious with you and the two who went behind your back. A test: whom will you serve this week who will never thank you?

verseByVerse.quote: For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the heart of Mark’s Gospel: the King entitled to all service became the servant and died in the place of sinners to pay the price of their freedom — and every call to serve rests on that.

The summit. It arrives as a “for.” He has just told them to go to the bottom, and this is the reason: not a principle but a Person, and what he is walking toward.

Even the Son of Man. No modest title. In Daniel 7 one like a son of man comes with the clouds and is given “dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him” (Daniel 7:14). In Daniel the whole world serves him — and he says he came not to be served. The one figure in Scripture entitled to universal service arrived and declined it.

To serve. He did, visibly, through this whole Gospel. But here the word has a particular weight, because he is about to say what the serving cost.

A ransom. A word from the marketplace, not the temple: the price paid to free a captive, laid down to buy a slave out of bondage or a prisoner off the block. A price is named, and the currency is his life.

In the place of. “For many” uses a Greek word meaning “in the place of” — one thing given instead of another, as a substitute steps into a queue. He doesn’t merely die for our benefit; he dies in our stead. The many go free because the One is handed over. Behind it stands Isaiah 53, read aloud in every synagogue: “he poured out his soul to death… yet he bore the sin of many, and makes intercession for the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12). “Many” tolls through the prophecy, and Jesus claims it as his errand.

Does “for many” mean that Christ died only for some? The phrase comes from Isaiah 53, where the Servant bore the sin of many, the great number set against the one. Many Christians read it as simply “all”; Reformed Christians read it as the definite people for whom his death actually paid. The more likely reading is the second, since a ransom paid sets the captive free (cf. 1 Timothy 2:5–6). But his death is sufficient for all and offered to all, and no one who comes to him is turned away.

To whom is the ransom paid? Some early teachers imagined it was paid to the devil, as though Satan held a rightful claim God had to buy out. He doesn’t; he is a thief with stolen goods (3:27), and God owes him nothing. The debt is owed to God’s own justice — and God, in the person of his Son, pays it himself. So there is no drama between an angry Father and a reluctant Son; it is one God resolving in himself what could be resolved no other way.

Why he came. Not first to teach, though he taught as no one has; not first to heal, though he emptied villages of illness; not even to model servanthood, though he just did. He came to die in the place of sinners who could never buy themselves back. Nineteen verses ago they asked, “Then who can be saved?” and he said, impossible with man, possible with God. This is how: not by lowering the requirement but by a payment.

In a squabble about seats. And notice where the sentence is placed: not in a sermon on the atonement but as the closing argument in a quarrel about the best seats. Twelve men jostling for position, and he settles it by telling them he will be sold for their freedom (cf. Philippians 2:5–8). Everything asked of you in the Christian life rests on that. You aren’t told to serve because service is noble, but because the One who owned everything went to the bottom and stayed there until it killed him — and bought you on the way down. A test: whom will you serve today because he served you?
verseByVerse.note: A ransom was the price paid to free a slave or captive.

parallels.desc: he bore the sin of many

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Jericho. And as he was leaving Jericho with his disciples and a great crowd, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, the son of Timaeus, was sitting by the roadside. And when he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out and say, "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!" And many rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more, "Son of David, have mercy on me!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A blind beggar sees who Jesus is more clearly than those around him, asks only for mercy, and refuses to be silenced — a model of faith that won’t give up.

The last city. Jericho, last before the climb: fifteen miles up through the wilderness to Jerusalem, Passover days away, the road thick with pilgrims.

A named man. “Bartimaeus… the son of Timaeus.” Almost no one healed in this Gospel is named — not the leper, paralytic, man among the tombs, or woman with the bleeding. This man is named in Aramaic and translation, with his father. The likeliest reason: the church knew him. He was still around when Mark wrote, or well remembered — a signed piece of testimony.

One blind man or two? Matthew mentions two blind men, and Luke places the healing “as he drew near to Jericho” (Luke 18:35). Mark names the one the church knew; he doesn’t say there was only one. And in Jesus’ day there were two Jerichos, the old site and Herod’s new town nearby, so one could be leaving one and approaching the other. The accounts don’t contradict.

By the roadside. His whole life in one phrase: going nowhere, beside the road while everyone else walks up it. He can see nothing; he has only a crowd’s noise and a name passed down the line, and acts on it at once.

Son of David. One of the most significant sentences in Mark. A messianic title — God’s promise to establish David’s son’s throne forever (2 Samuel 7:12–16), the shoot from Jesse, the king who is coming — and not used once so far in this Gospel. Not by crowds, Pharisees, or the Twelve; Peter said “you are the Christ” and was told to keep quiet. A blind beggar shouts it in public, before hundreds, days before Passover. Everyone in this chapter who can see has misunderstood him: the rich man called him Good Teacher and went home; James and John asked for thrones. The man who can see nothing names him rightly first time.

Mercy. Not “heal me,” not yet, but mercy — what you ask with no claim of any kind, resting only on the character of the one asked. The rich man asked what he must do; James and John asked for what they thought they had earned; the beggar asks for mercy, and is the only one in the chapter who gets exactly what he came for. A test: when you pray, do you come asking for mercy, or presenting your claims?

Louder. “Many rebuked him” — the word the disciples used on the parents (v. 13). He is an embarrassment: a distinguished rabbi on a solemn pilgrimage, and a beggar bawling at him. “But he cried out all the more.” He has nothing to lose and knows it — blind, destitute, in the dust, with one chance — and respectable disapproval doesn’t trouble him. For anyone quietly discouraged from coming to Christ — by a family that finds it excessive, a church that made them feel they didn’t fit, the sense of being too much, too messy, too late: the crowd told this man to be quiet, the crowd was wrong, and Jesus stopped for the shouting.
verseByVerse.note: Jericho lay about 15 miles north-east of Jerusalem, near the Jordan. Bartimaeus means “son of Timaeus.” “Son of David” is a title for the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus stopped and said, "Call him." And they called the blind man, saying to him, "Take heart. Get up; he is calling you." And throwing off his cloak, he sprang up and came to Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On his way to the cross Jesus stops for one person, his call changes how others treat the outcast, and true faith leaves everything to come to him.

Jesus stopped. Perhaps the loveliest words in the chapter. Consider what they interrupt: the road to Jerusalem; he has walked ahead with a set face (v. 32), three times foretelling the mocking, spitting, flogging and killing at the top of that hill; a crowd around him, Passover ahead, a cross at week’s end. And he stops in the road because a blind man is shouting. The Son of God on his way to die halts the procession for one beggar everyone else was trying to silence. Nothing in his life was ever too urgent for a person.

“Call him.” He doesn’t go over; he tells those who were silencing him to fetch him. Deliberate: the crowd that hindered is made the crowd that brings.

The same voices. “Take heart. Get up; he is calling you.” Thirty seconds ago they told him to be quiet; now they encourage him. Nothing has changed except that Jesus stopped — and the moment he took an interest, so did they. A warning for anyone in church: the person you find embarrassing, inconvenient, too loud or needy may be the one Christ is calling. Be careful whom you shush. A test: who in your church have you quietly written off?

The cloak. Mark’s specific details suggest an eyewitness, and the cloak is the one to stop on. A beggar’s cloak was his equipment: spread on the ground to catch coins, his bed at night and shelter from cold, the one possession the law protected — taken in pledge, it had to be returned by sundown (Exodus 22:26–27). Literally everything he owned. And he flings it aside in the road, blind, with no idea where it lands or whether he will find it again.

Two ends of one chapter. A rich man asked to give up his possessions for Christ went away sorrowful, because he had many. A blind beggar, asked for nothing, threw away the only thing he had because it might slow him down. One had much and wouldn’t let go of any; one had one thing and didn’t think twice. A test: what are you holding that is slowing you down from coming to him?

He sprang up. The verb means to leap: a blind man jumping up and moving toward a voice, not knowing how far it is or what is in the way. He heard “he is calling you,” and that was enough.
verseByVerse.note: A beggar’s cloak was spread to collect coins and was also his covering at night.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, "What do you want me to do for you?" And the blind man said to him, "Rabbi, let me recover my sight." And Jesus said to him, "Go your way; your faith has made you well." And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him on the way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faith that asks Christ for mercy is answered, and true healing leads straight into following him on the road to the cross.

The same question. Word for word what he asked James and John (v. 36); Mark does it deliberately, and the two answers say everything. They opened with a blank cheque and asked for the top seats; this man is asked the same and the difference is total. And Jesus asks at all, though it could hardly be more obvious what a blind beggar wants. He won’t do things to people over their heads; he lets the man say it in his own words — a dignity no one had shown him in years.

The one thing he needs. One clause, no preamble. And Mark keeps his word, “Rabbouni” — a warmer form, something like “my Master,” found elsewhere only on Mary Magdalene’s lips at the empty tomb (John 20:16). Note what he doesn’t ask for: not money, which he had begged for all his life and which would solve his immediate problem; not compensation or position. Sight — which would end his livelihood and make him start again at whatever age he was. He asks for the thing that will cost him his old life. A test: are you willing to ask Christ for what will change your life, not just ease it?

Just a sentence. No touch, spittle or second attempt, unlike the man at Bethsaida (8:22–25). “Your faith has made you well” — what he said to the woman who touched his cloak (5:34); something more than eyesight has happened. And faith is located rightly: not in the quality of his theology, though he got the title right, nor his persistence, though he had plenty. Faith saves because of whom it takes hold of, and this man took hold of the Son of David with both hands and wouldn’t be shouted down.

His way became Christ’s way. “Go your way” — he is free: to go home, find his cloak, start a life, tell Jericho. And he doesn’t go his way. He goes Christ’s. Given freedom and eyes in one breath, he uses both to get on the road to Jerusalem behind the man who healed him. “On the way” in this Gospel is never just geography; it is the road to the cross the disciples have walked amazed and afraid. He is the last person healed in Mark before the passion — the only one named, who names Jesus rightly, throws away all he owns, and ends walking up the hill with him (cf. Isaiah 35:5).

The chapter’s two ends. It began with a wealthy, moral, eager man who asked the right question, was looked at and loved, and went home with everything he came with. It ends with a blind beggar in the dust with one cloak, who shouted until heard, threw the cloak away, asked for mercy, and followed Jesus to Jerusalem. That is the kingdom from inside, as Jesus said in v. 15 when he picked up a child: those who get in come with nothing and simply receive.

parallels.desc: the eyes of the blind opened

10.theology:
Divorce, and what Mark leaves out. Matthew twice records an exception — except for sexual immorality (Matt. 5:32; 19:9) — and Mark records none, while adding, for his Roman readers, the case of a wife who divorces her husband. Not a contradiction but a difference of purpose: Mark gives the principle in its unguarded, creation-order form, the way a thing is stated when you want its full weight felt; Matthew, writing where the rabbis argued endlessly over grounds, records the one qualification Jesus allowed. Paul adds a second — the believer deserted by an unbelieving spouse is not enslaved (1 Cor. 7:15). So the Reformed churches have long recognised two grounds on which the bond may be broken and the innocent party freed: adultery and desertion, and no others. Mark's silence is not denial but a refusal to lead with the exception — because the moment the exception becomes the headline, hardness of heart starts hunting for a way in.

"Why do you call me good?" is not a denial that Jesus is good or that he is God, and he never withdraws the word or corrects the man for using it. He holds it up to the light. Good Teacher was easy flattery; Jesus stops him and asks whether he knows what he is saying. Either the word should not have been used — or it is right, and the man must reckon with who is standing in front of him. A door held open, not a door shut.

And v. 45 is the theological centre of Mark. A ransom (lytron) is the price paid to buy a captive out of bondage. The word rendered for is anti — in the place of, one thing given instead of another — so he does not merely die for our benefit but in our stead. Behind it stands Isaiah 53, where the Servant poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many (Isa. 53:12), that word many tolling through the prophecy and claimed here by Jesus as his own errand. And the price is not paid to the devil, as some early teachers imagined — he is a thief with stolen goods (3:27) and God owes him nothing. The debt is owed to the justice of God, and God in the person of his Son pays it himself.
10.examples:
Then: the same question asked twice, fifteen verses apart. What do you want me to do for you? — to James and John (v. 36), and to a blind beggar (v. 51).

The brothers open with a blank cheque — we want you to do for us whatever we ask — and name the two best seats in the kingdom. Bartimaeus asks for mercy, and then for sight.

Now: most of us pray more like the brothers than the beggar. The blank cheque dressed up religiously — a decision already taken, brought to God for endorsement rather than judgement. The request framed around position, comfort, and being noticed.

And note what actually makes Bartimaeus's answer better. Not humility as a technique. He had correctly identified who was passing — Son of David, a messianic title not one of the disciples had yet used out loud — and he asked for mercy, which is what you ask for when you have no claim of any kind and the only ground of the request is the character of the one you are asking.

And then there is the cloak (v. 50). A beggar's outer cloak was his equipment: spread on the ground to catch coins, his bed at night, his shelter, and the one possession the Law protected (Ex. 22:26–27). It was everything he owned. He flung it aside, blind, with no idea where it landed, because it might slow him down by four seconds.

Set that against the man at the start of the chapter, asked to give up his possessions and going away sorrowful because he had a great many. One had much and would not let go of any of it; one had a single thing and did not think about it twice. Mark put them at opposite ends of the same chapter on purpose.

11.title: Leaves Without Fruit
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when they drew near to Jerusalem, to Bethphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent two of his disciples <sup>2</sup>and said to them, “Go into the village in front of you, and immediately as you enter it you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it. <sup>3</sup>If anyone says to you, ‘Why are you doing this?’ say, ‘The Lord has need of it and will send it back here immediately.’” <sup>4</sup>And they went away and found a colt tied at a door outside in the street, and they untied it. <sup>5</sup>And some of those standing there said to them, “What are you doing, untying the colt?” <sup>6</sup>And they told them what Jesus had said, and they let them go. <sup>7</sup>And they brought the colt to Jesus and threw their cloaks on it, and he sat on it. <sup>8</sup>And many spread their cloaks on the road, and others spread leafy branches that they had cut from the fields. <sup>9</sup>And those who went before and those who followed were shouting, “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! <sup>10</sup>Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David! Hosanna in the highest!” <sup>11</sup>And he entered Jerusalem and went into the temple. And when he had looked around at everything, as it was already late, he went out to Bethany with the twelve. <sup>12</sup>On the following day, when they came from Bethany, he was hungry. <sup>13</sup>And seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, he went to see if he could find anything on it. When he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs. <sup>14</sup>And he said to it, “May no one ever eat fruit from you again.” And his disciples heard it. <sup>15</sup>And they came to Jerusalem. And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold and those who bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. <sup>16</sup>And he would not allow anyone to carry anything through the temple. <sup>17</sup>And he was teaching them and saying to them, “Is it not written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it a den of robbers.” <sup>18</sup>And the chief priests and the scribes heard it and were seeking a way to destroy him, for they feared him, because all the crowd was astonished at his teaching. <sup>19</sup>And when evening came they went out of the city. <sup>20</sup>As they passed by in the morning, they saw the fig tree withered away to its roots. <sup>21</sup>And Peter remembered and said to him, “Rabbi, look! The fig tree that you cursed has withered.” <sup>22</sup>And Jesus answered them, “Have faith in God. <sup>23</sup>Truly, I say to you, whoever says to this mountain, ‘Be taken up and thrown into the sea,’ and does not doubt in his heart, but believes that what he says will come to pass, it will be done for him. <sup>24</sup>Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours. <sup>25</sup>And whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father also who is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses.” <sup>27</sup>And they came again to Jerusalem. And as he was walking in the temple, the chief priests and the scribes and the elders came to him, <sup>28</sup>and they said to him, “By what authority are you doing these things, or who gave you this authority to do them?” <sup>29</sup>Jesus said to them, “I will ask you one question; answer me, and I will tell you by what authority I do these things. <sup>30</sup>Was the baptism of John from heaven or from man? Answer me.” <sup>31</sup>And they discussed it with one another, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’ <sup>32</sup>But shall we say, ‘From man’?”—they were afraid of the people, for they all held that John really was a prophet. <sup>33</sup>So they answered Jesus, “We do not know.” And Jesus said to them, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.”
11.overview:
After ten chapters of hushing everyone who worked out who he was, Jesus stages a public claim to the throne — and does it on a borrowed donkey's foal, exactly as Zechariah said the king would come. The crowd throws down cloaks as they did for Jehu, spreads leafy branches cut from the fields, and shouts the Passover psalm at him: Hosanna — save now. They are right about who he is and wrong about what he came to do, and by Friday the road is empty.

Then he goes into the temple, looks around at everything, and leaves, because it is late.

What he does the next morning is therefore not a loss of temper. He had seen all of it the night before, slept on it, and walked two miles back. And Mark wraps the temple inside a fig tree to tell you what it means: a tree in full leaf and no fruit, cursed on the way in; the tables overturned; and on the third morning the tree dead to its roots. Israel's worship that week was magnificent from a distance. He came near, and found leaves.

Out of the dead tree comes the great teaching on faith, prayer and forgiveness. And the chapter ends with the Sanhedrin asking the right question — by what authority? — and being handed one question in return that would have led them home, and spending it instead on a calculation about the crowd.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — The Entry, the Fig Tree, and the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The entry (vv. 1–11). After nine chapters of silencing everyone who worked out who he was, Jesus stages a public claim to be king — and does it on a borrowed donkey's foal, exactly as Zechariah said. The crowd sings the Passover psalm at him. Then he walks into the temple, looks around at everything, and goes out to Bethany because it is late.

The tree (vv. 12–14). The next morning, hungry, he goes to a fig tree in full leaf and finds nothing on it — and Mark adds the detail that makes the whole thing intelligible: it was not the season for figs. He curses it, and the disciples hear him.

The temple (vv. 15–19). And then he does to the temple what he has just done to the tree. Tables over, seats over, the traffic stopped — and two verses of Scripture that between them tell the leadership exactly what their house has become.

The lesson (vv. 20–26). Next morning the tree is dead to the roots, and out of that comes the great passage on faith, prayer and forgiveness.

Mark has wrapped the temple inside the fig tree deliberately. The tree is the temple: leaves and no fruit, an advertisement with nothing behind it, and it is finished.
verseByVerse.theology:
Was it fair to curse a tree for having no figs out of season? The objection is old and it deserves a proper answer, and the answer turns on the leaves.

A Palestinian fig produces its fruit before or alongside its leaves, not after. In early spring the branches put out small green knobs — the paggim — which are edible, and a hungry traveller ate them. The leaves follow. So a tree standing in full leaf is making a claim: there is fruit here.

The main harvest was months away, which is exactly why Mark tells us it was not the season for figs. He is not embarrassed by the detail; he supplies it, so that no reader can mistake this for agricultural pique. Nobody was owed a crop. What the tree owed was consistency with its own appearance, and it had none.

And then look where Mark has put it. He splits the story in two and wedges the temple between the halves — curse (vv. 12–14), temple (vv. 15–19), withered (vv. 20–21). It is his habitual sandwich, and it is never accidental. The tree interprets the temple.

Israel's worship at that moment was in full leaf: the courts crowded, the sacrifices running, the festival packed, the money changing hands. From a distance it looked like the healthiest religion in the world. He came near, looked around at everything (v. 11), found nothing, and the next morning both the tree and the temple were under sentence.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a den of robbers — the phrase everybody quotes and almost nobody reads properly.

A robbers' den is not where the robbery happens. It is the cave they retreat to afterwards, where they divide the takings and feel perfectly safe. That is the charge, and Jeremiah, whom Jesus is quoting, spells it out: Will you steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely... and then come and stand before me in this house, which is called by my name, and say, 'We are delivered!' (Jer. 7:9–11).

Now: the accusation is not primarily about commerce in church buildings. It is about using religion as a safe house — going out into the week, doing what you do, and coming back on Sunday to feel delivered.

That is a test anyone can run. Does your churchgoing make you more uncomfortable about the way you conduct your business, or less? If a man can hold a grudge for eleven years, cut corners at work, be cold at home — and find that an hour on Sunday settles his conscience without changing any of it, then he has not been worshipping. He has been using the den.

And note where the tables were standing. The trading filled the Court of the Gentiles, the one place a non-Jew was permitted to pray — which is why Mark alone keeps Isaiah's full phrase, for all the nations. The arrangement that made the insiders comfortable had physically evicted the outsiders, and nobody had noticed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they drew near to Jerusalem, to Bethphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent two of his disciples and said to them, "Go into the village in front of you, and immediately as you enter it you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it. If anyone says to you, 'Why are you doing this?' say, 'The Lord has need of it and will send it back here immediately.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus now openly stages his entry as Israel’s humble, peaceful King foretold by Zechariah — and he asks for what is ours, and returns it.

A loaded place. The Mount of Olives is the ridge east of the city across the Kidron, looking straight down onto the temple platform — and where Zechariah says the LORD will stand when he comes to fight for his people: “On that day his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives” (Zechariah 14:4). He approaches from the one direction the prophets marked.

The secret is over. For ten chapters he has walked everywhere, and been to Jerusalem before; this once he sends for transport. Everything about the entry is staged deliberately. After nine chapters of silencing demons, hushing the healed and telling disciples to say nothing, he makes a public, unmistakable claim before a Passover crowd. He has decided the hour.

A king on a donkey. A colt — a young donkey — and every Jew knew the text: “Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey” (Zechariah 9:9). The next verse has the LORD cutting off chariot and war horse. A conqueror rode a horse; a king coming in peace rode a donkey, as Solomon rode his father’s mule to his coronation (1 Kings 1:33). The animal is a sermon: he claims the throne and says what kind of king he is in one gesture. They will get the first half and miss the second.

Never ridden. Not incidental. An animal put to sacred use had to be unworked: the red heifer “on which a yoke has never come” (Numbers 19:2), the cart for the ark drawn by cows never yoked (1 Samuel 6:7). This colt is set apart for holy use.

One animal or two? Matthew mentions a donkey and her colt (Matthew 21:2); Mark and Luke only the colt, the animal Jesus rode. Matthew adds the mother because Zechariah’s prophecy names both (Zechariah 9:9). To mention more isn’t to contradict.

“The Lord has need of it.” Foreknowledge or prior arrangement? Mark doesn’t say; either fits — he shows Jesus knowing thoughts (2:8) and making practical plans (3:9). What is certain is that the two are given a password and told it will work. And the password is striking. The Lord of glory, who made the animal, asks for its use and promises to send it back. He doesn’t seize; he requests and returns. That is how he deals with what is yours — the money, the house, the car, the spare room, the evenings. He has every right to take, and he asks — and nothing lent to him has ever failed to come back larger than it went. A test: what does the Lord need of yours this week?
verseByVerse.note: Bethphage and Bethany were villages on the Mount of Olives, just east of Jerusalem. An animal never ridden was fit for a sacred purpose.

parallels.desc: a heifer on which a yoke has never come

verseByVerse.quote: And they went away and found a colt tied at a door outside in the street, and they untied it. And some of those standing there said to them, "What are you doing, untying the colt?" And they told them what Jesus had said, and they let them go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Obedience goes with nothing but Christ’s word and finds it holds, and ordinary unnamed people serve him by giving what they own.

Exactly as he said. They went, they found, they untied — Mark’s flattest confirmation, his way of underlining it. And precise: “tied at a door outside in the street.” Someone remembered where the animal stood and told it to Peter.

A fair question. “What are you doing, untying the colt?” — fair to ask two strangers untying your donkey. Mark’s restraint is almost comic and entirely believable; no one in a village stands by while their livestock walks off. They repeated the sentence they were given, and the objection evaporated.

Nothing but the word. The disciples had no documents, no owner’s permission to produce, no explanation to satisfy anyone — only a sentence they were told to say, and it was enough. A fair picture of much Christian obedience: you go with the word you were given into a situation you can’t control, and find that it holds. A test: what has God told you to do that you are waiting to understand fully before you obey?

The anonymous givers. Someone let their animal go — unnamed, probably unknown, handing property to two strangers on the strength of a sentence on the most significant morning of the year, and the King rode into his city on it. A whole class of such people runs through this Gospel, all anonymous: the man who lent the upper room, the owner of the boat, whoever gave the demoniac a cloak, someone’s five loaves and two fish. None named; each in the story because something they owned was asked for and they didn’t say no.

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought the colt to Jesus and threw their cloaks on it, and he sat on it. And many spread their cloaks on the road, and others spread leafy branches that they had cut from the fields.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd hails Jesus as king and liberator, rightly recognising who he is but wrongly expecting what he came to do.

A quiet miracle. No saddle, so the disciples use their cloaks — the second time in two chapters a cloak is thrown down before him (10:50). And an unremarked miracle: an animal never ridden, in a noisy festival crowd, with a man on its back for the first time, and nothing happens. It carries him. The one creature in Jerusalem that week that did exactly what he wanted was a donkey.

A coronation gesture. Cloaks on the road isn’t mere enthusiasm but protocol. When Jehu was proclaimed king, “every man of them took his garment and put it under him on the bare steps, and they blew the trumpet and proclaimed, ‘Jehu is king’” (2 Kings 9:13). Putting your cloak in the dirt for a man to ride over says: this is my king, and I will spend something to say so. And a cloak wasn’t cheap — the garment the law protected, a man’s covering and often his bedding. They lay down what they own for him to walk on.

Palms for a liberator. John says palm branches (John 12:13), hence Palm Sunday — and palms had been a national symbol since the Maccabees drove out the Greeks two centuries before; they later appeared on the coins of the Jewish revolts against Rome. Cloaks for a king; palms for a liberator. It is political.

Right about who, wrong about what. The ache under the scene: they are right about who he is and wrong about what he came to do. The liberator they welcome rides toward an execution, and within days a crowd in this city will shout for it. That isn’t only first-century enthusiasm. You can be thrilled about Jesus, sing loudly, spend something on him, and expect an entirely different Christ from the one actually coming — one who will sort out your circumstances, vindicate your side, and deliver you from what you want delivering from. The cloaks were sincere; by Friday the road was empty. A test: are you welcoming Christ as he is, or as you want him to be?
verseByVerse.note: Spreading cloaks on the road was a gesture of homage to a king.

parallels.desc: your king, mounted on a donkey

verseByVerse.quote: And those who went before and those who followed were shouting, "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David! Hosanna in the highest!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They cry for salvation to the right person at the right hour, but they want rescue from Rome while he comes to save them from something far worse.

A procession. Those before and those behind: a column with him in the middle and noise from both ends.

Hosanna. Hebrew, and not the general shout of praise we make it: “save, we pray” — a cry for help addressed to God. It comes from Psalm 118, the last of the Hallel psalms sung at Passover; every pilgrim on that road had been singing it all week.

He who comes. “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” — the next line of the psalm (Psalm 118:26). Originally a greeting to pilgrims arriving at the temple gates; now sung at one man on a donkey, and “he who comes” has become a title for the Messiah, as John asked from prison: “Are you the one who is to come?” (Matthew 11:3). And Jesus will quote this psalm back at the temple authorities within days: “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (12:10; Psalm 118:22). He is listening to what they sing.

A dangerous shout. “Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David!” goes beyond the psalm to say what they mean: the restoration of David’s monarchy, a real throne in this city, under Roman occupation, at Passover — when Jerusalem swelled to several times its size and the governor came up from Caesarea with extra troops precisely because this was the week riots started. An enormously dangerous thing to shout.

Heard and answered. “Hosanna in the highest!” — let heaven itself hear. And the terrible irony: they shouted the right word. “Save, we pray” was the right request, to the right person, at the right hour. They had no idea what they asked. They wanted saving from Rome; he had come to save them from something worse, and the salvation they shouted for would be accomplished by Friday afternoon in a way that would empty this road. He heard the prayer and answered it, and almost no one who prayed it recognised the answer. A test: when you cry to Christ to save, are you willing for him to save you his way?
verseByVerse.note: “Hosanna” means “save, we pray,” and had become a shout of praise.

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: And he entered Jerusalem and went into the temple. And when he had looked around at everything, as it was already late, he went out to Bethany with the twelve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord inspects his house before he acts, and his judgment is considered and deliberate, never a fit of temper.

The temple. Where the procession was heading all along — not the palace, fortress or governor’s residence. As Malachi said: “the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple… But who can endure the day of his coming, and who can stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire” (Malachi 3:1–2).

He looked around. One of the most quietly ominous sentences in the Gospel. He walked the courts and inspected them: the traders, tables, coins, birds in cages, the traffic across the Court of the Gentiles — the whole arrangement, seen by the one person present who knew what the building was for. And he said nothing.

A deliberate anticlimax. The crowd has called him king, the palms are on the road, the city is full; every expectation says something is about to happen. He looks round the temple, notices the time, and leaves for supper in a village two miles away.

Considered, not provoked. So what he does next day isn’t a loss of temper. He had seen it all the night before, walked out, slept on it, walked two miles back in the morning, and then overturned the tables — not a man provoked beyond endurance but a considered act, decided in advance, done deliberately. That is what makes it judgment rather than temper.

Before God acts, God looks. The inspection itself is the warning. He came down to see the city and tower at Babel (Genesis 11:5), went down to see whether Sodom was as bad as its outcry (Genesis 18:21), and the risen Christ walks among the lampstands saying to church after church, “I know your works” (Revelation 2–3). He still does this — walks round and looks at everything, the church and the person reading this. Not a glance but a survey; and what he does about it is decided quietly, never in a temper. A test: if he looked around your life today, what would he see?
verseByVerse.note: Bethany was about two miles east of Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: On the following day, when they came from Bethany, he was hungry. And seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, he went to see if he could find anything on it. When he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs. And he said to it, "May no one ever eat fruit from you again." And his disciples heard it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This acted parable pronounces judgment on Israel’s showy but fruitless temple worship — and warns against religion that has leaves but no fruit.

He was hungry. Easy to skim: the Son of God, walking two miles into the city before breakfast, wanting something to eat — as Mark shows him asleep in a storm and hungry on a road.

How a fig tree works. He sees leaves from a distance, and the objection people raise dissolves once you know the tree. A Palestinian fig puts out fruit before or alongside its leaves. In early spring the branches produce small green knobs, edible if unremarkable, which a hungry traveller ate; the leaves come with them. So a tree in full leaf makes a claim: there is something here.

Not the season. Mark’s own clause is the key, not an embarrassment, there so no reader mistakes this for pique over breakfast. No one was owed a crop; the main harvest was months off, and Jesus knew it. What the tree owed was consistency with its own advertisement — the only tree on that road claiming something, and the only one with nothing.

Did Jesus not know there would be no fruit? He went to the tree as a man looking for fruit, and that was the point of the acted parable: he came to Israel looking for fruit and found only leaves. It was a deliberate sign, not a mistake.

A sign, not a tantrum. The only destructive miracle in the Gospels, done to a tree — telling us it is a sign, not a punishment. He who healed on a hundred roads doesn’t blast people; he curses a plant, once, before witnesses, for a reason. “And his disciples heard it”: said aloud, deliberately, to be remembered — and in seven verses Peter will remember.

The tree is the temple. Mark splits the story and wedges the temple into the gap: the curse (vv. 12–14), the temple (vv. 15–19), the withered tree (vv. 20–21). His habitual sandwich, never accidental; the halves interpret each other. Israel’s worship that week was in magnificent leaf: Herod’s temple one of the wonders of the ancient world, the courts packed, sacrifices from dawn, priests busy, money moving. From the road it looked like the healthiest religion on earth. He came near — “looked around at everything” (v. 11) — and found nothing but leaves. And the fig was Israel’s own image: “Like the first fruit on the fig tree in its first season, I saw your fathers” (Hosea 9:10); “there are no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree” (Jeremiah 8:13). A prophet’s acted parable, like Jeremiah’s and Ezekiel’s, carried out on the building forty years later, when not one stone was left on another (13:2).

Leaves and fruit. The tree wasn’t condemned for being fruitless in season but for advertising. Leaves are what others can see — attendance, vocabulary, a reputation for soundness, the Bible on the table. Fruit is what is actually there. He isn’t in the distance any more; he comes near, and looks. A test: what fruit would he find in your life if he looked closely today?
verseByVerse.note: Leaves on a fig tree normally promise early fruit. The fig tree was a prophetic picture of Israel.
