parallels.desc: no figs on the fig tree

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Jerusalem. And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold and those who bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. And he would not allow anyone to carry anything through the temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He clears the court that was meant for Gentiles to pray, judging a religion that had crowded out the outsider and exploited the poor.

What he didn’t attack. Not the sacrificial system: the animals were needed; God commanded the sacrifices, and pilgrims came from Egypt, Babylon, Rome and Asia, unable to drive a lamb a thousand miles. Not money-changing as such: the temple tax had to be paid in Tyrian silver, the region’s reliable coinage, and Roman coins bore the emperor’s image and a divine title. Somebody had to change money.

Where it happened. The offence was where it all was, and what it had become. The trading filled the Court of the Gentiles, the vast outer court — the one part of the temple a non-Jew could enter. Beyond it stood a low barrier with notices in Greek and Latin warning that any foreigner who passed had himself to blame for his death. So the one square yard of God’s house available to the nations had become a livestock market and a currency exchange. A God-fearing Greek or Ethiopian come to pray had to stand among the cattle pens, coin tables and pigeon cages, in the noise.

Did Jesus cleanse the temple once or twice? John puts a cleansing at the start of Jesus’ ministry (John 2:13–22); Mark puts this one in the last week. Some think John moved the event for theological reasons. But the two accounts differ in what Jesus says and what follows, and the abuse was the kind that would return. The more likely reading is that there were two cleansings, one at the beginning and one at the end.

The pigeon-sellers. Mark singles them out because pigeons were the poor person’s sacrifice: “if he cannot afford a lamb, then he shall bring… two turtledoves or two pigeons” (Leviticus 5:7; cf. 12:8) — the offering Mary and Joseph brought when they presented Jesus in this building (Luke 2:24). Those were the tables where the poorest worshippers were handled, at a reportedly outrageous mark-up, and it is those seats that go over. A test: does anything in your church make it harder for the poor or the outsider to come to God?

He stopped the traffic. Only Mark records it. The great court was apparently used as a shortcut across that quarter of the city, people carrying goods through. The rabbis themselves later forbade using the Temple Mount as a thoroughfare. So for part of that day one man stood in the outer court of God’s temple and wouldn’t let anyone walk through carrying anything. Everything stopped — no trading, changing, carrying or shortcuts — and for the first time in years a Gentile could have stood in that court and prayed. He cleared the room for the people no one thought about.
verseByVerse.note: The trading happened in the outer court, the only place Gentiles could pray. Pigeons were the sacrifice the poor could afford. Money-changers exchanged coins into the currency accepted for the temple tax.

parallels.desc: pigeons for those who cannot afford a lamb

verseByVerse.quote: And he was teaching them and saying to them, "Is it not written, 'My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations'? But you have made it a den of robbers." And the chief priests and the scribes heard it and were seeking a way to destroy him, for they feared him, because all the crowd was astonished at his teaching. And when evening came they went out of the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s house is for all peoples, and religion that becomes a hiding place for unrepentant sin stands condemned.

A lesson. Mark’s word is “teaching”: tables on the floor, birds loose, and he gives a lesson grounded in two texts.

For all the nations. Isaiah 56:7, and its context decides everything. Isaiah 56 is God’s promise about the outsider — the foreigner joined to the LORD and the eunuch, the two categories excluded from the assembly under the old arrangements (Deuteronomy 23:1–8). God will bring them to his holy mountain, make them joyful in his house, accept their offerings, “for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.” Matthew and Luke both quote this verse and stop before the final phrase. Mark keeps it: “for all the nations.” The Gospel written for Gentiles in Rome preserves the clause about the Gentiles — the clause that condemns what the court had become. The trade hadn’t merely cluttered the temple; it had evicted the very people the verse was about.

A den of robbers. Jeremiah 7:11, quoted constantly and almost always misunderstood. A robbers’ den isn’t where the robbery happens but where thieves retreat afterward, count the takings, sleep soundly and feel safe. Jeremiah makes it explicit: “Will you steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely, make offerings to Baal… and then come and stand before me in this house, which is called by my name, and say, ‘We are delivered!’—only to go on doing all these abominations? Has this house… become a den of robbers in your eyes?” (Jeremiah 7:9–11). The accusation isn’t doing business in church but using God’s house as a safe house — living as they pleased and coming here to feel delivered.

A test. The mechanism hasn’t changed. Does your churchgoing make you more uncomfortable about how you conduct the rest of your week, or less? Someone who can hold a grudge for eleven years, sharpen his invoices, be cold to his wife, and find that an hour on Sunday settles his conscience without altering any of it hasn’t been worshipping. He has been using the den.

Urgent now. The chief priests and scribes “were seeking a way to destroy him.” Decided long ago (3:6), but now urgent, because he has touched the temple — their institution, authority and income. “For they feared him, because all the crowd was astonished at his teaching.” Fear and the crowd’s devotion made a public arrest impossible; they will need the night and someone on the inside.

Out of the city. He leaves again, as the night before. He won’t sleep in Jerusalem this week until the night they come for him.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark keeps “for all the nations” from Isaiah’s words.

parallels.desc: a house of prayer for all peoples

verseByVerse.quote: As they passed by in the morning, they saw the fig tree withered away to its roots. And Peter remembered and said to him, "Rabbi, look! The fig tree that you cursed has withered." And Jesus answered them, "Have faith in God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The withered tree confirms the judgment Jesus spoke, and his disciples are to respond not with fascination but with faith whose object is God himself.

Withered from the roots. The third morning, the same road, the tree dead — not wilted or dropping leaves, but “withered away to its roots,” killed from the bottom up in under a day, from the part no one sees. Matthew, compressing, says it withered at once (Matthew 21:19); Mark, following the days, gives two mornings: the disciples walked past twice, and the second time it was a dead stick. And they had heard him say it.

“Rabbi, look!” You can hear the man: no reflection, just pointing. And in a Gospel from Peter’s preaching, he tells it against himself as usual: I saw a dead tree and got excited about the tree. He missed what it was for. The withering isn’t the point; the temple is, and he walked past that twice as well. A test: are you more fascinated by the signs than by what God is saying through them?

“Have faith in God.” A surprising reply: Peter says the tree is dead, and Jesus says have faith in God. He doesn’t explain the sign — that this will happen to the nation, though it will (13:2). He turns to what the disciples are to do with what they have seen. They watched a word spoken to a tree, and the tree obeyed. They will be sent into a world where they must speak and pray, against things far more immovable than a fig. So: have faith in God.

Faith in a Person. Literally “have faith of God” — faith whose object is God. Not faith in faith, nor in the power of your own believing, a modern superstition and a cruel one. Faith in God — a Person who hears, decides, and is good. That distinction governs the next two verses, among the most abused in the Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, whoever says to this mountain, 'Be taken up and thrown into the sea,' and does not doubt in his heart, but believes that what he says will come to pass, it will be done for him. Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ calls his people to bold, believing prayer for great things — offered to a wise Father, not used as a technique to force God’s hand.

This mountain. They stood somewhere specific: the road from Bethany crosses the Mount of Olives, looking across at the temple mount and, on a clear day, toward the Dead Sea. “This mountain” may well be the hill the temple stood on, just pronounced fruitless, with the sea in view. And moving mountains was a proverb; the rabbis called a teacher who solved impossible problems “an uprooter of mountains” — the immovable obstacle, shifted.

What it plainly says. Don’t soften it first. Jesus means his people to pray with enormous boldness, ask for things far beyond their resources, and expect God to act. Most of us aren’t in danger of presumption but of praying for nothing much, in case nothing happens. The point of the mountain is that it is too big, and he tells them to say so aloud. A test: what “mountain” have you stopped asking God to move?

Does enough faith guarantee what we ask? No. It isn’t a mechanism by which enough certainty compels God. That reading turns prayer into a technique and God into a force, and the rest of the Bible refutes it — most decisively the man saying it. Within days, in a garden a few hundred yards away, this same Jesus will ask his Father to remove the cup and add, “Yet not what I will, but what you will” (14:36). The cup doesn’t pass. If unqualified confidence always secured the request, that prayer is unintelligible. He didn’t lack faith; he trusted his Father enough to leave the answer with him. Paul asked three times about his thorn and was told no, and given something better (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). And John, who heard this saying, wrote the qualifier into his letter: “if we ask anything according to his will he hears us” (1 John 5:14).

For those who asked and didn’t receive. You are the person this passage most often wounds: your faith was very likely not the problem, and blaming it only adds a second grief to the first. Prayer that moves mountains is real, and you should ask for mountains to move. But it is prayer to a Father, not an incantation aimed at a force. A good Father sometimes gives what we didn’t ask because it is better, and withholds what we begged for because his love sees the whole of a story we see only the middle of.

Believe boldly, trust deeply. Ask for great things (cf. Matthew 17:20; James 1:6). And trust him enough to want his will more than your own, knowing his no, when it comes, is as wise and kind as the yes you hoped for.

parallels.desc: faith like a grain of mustard seed
ask in faith, with no doubting

verseByVerse.quote: And whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father also who is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unforgiveness blocks prayer; those who truly grasp God’s forgiveness let go of grudges against others — though full reconciliation waits for repentance.

The obstruction. Having said a believing person can move a mountain, he names what will stop him, without a pause: straight from “whatever you ask in prayer” to “forgive.” Unforgiveness is presented as the great obstruction in the pipe.

Every time. “Whenever you stand praying” — standing was the ordinary posture for prayer, so this is the daily occasion, every time you pray.

Anything against anyone. Every word widens it. “Anything” — not only large injuries but the slight, the exclusion, the remark, what was said about you at work. “Against anyone” — no exception for family, for the one who never apologised, who doesn’t know they did it, or for the dead. And the initiative is wholly yours: no clause about them repenting first or being sorry. You stand to pray, find something in your hand, and put it down.

Not earned. “So that your Father… may forgive you” can be read as though pardon is earned by pardoning, which would overturn the gospel. It isn’t that. No one is forgiven because they forgive; we are forgiven because a ransom was paid (10:45). But the two can’t be separated in practice: “forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32); and the servant forgiven ten thousand talents who then seized a colleague by the throat over a small debt (Matthew 18:23–35). Someone who has grasped what he was let off doesn’t hold small debts against others. If he does, the question isn’t whether he forfeited his forgiveness but whether he ever understood it.

A name. Here many prayer lives quietly die. There is a name — you thought of it reading this: the person you would rather not pray for, the situation you have decided is unresolvable, the grudge carried so long it has become furniture and no longer feels like sin. Jesus doesn’t tell you to feel differently about them but to let it go, in prayer, deliberately, now — and again whenever it comes back, because it will. A test: whom do you need to forgive before you pray tonight?

Must I forgive someone who hasn’t repented? Jesus also says, “if he repents, forgive him” (Luke 17:3). Both are true, because forgiveness has two parts. The first is in your heart before God: letting go of the grudge and the wish for revenge, and handing the case to him. That is commanded here, whether or not the other person repents. The second is the restored relationship, which waits for repentance, as God’s own reconciliation with us does. So a believer wronged by someone unrepentant, even an abuser, mustn’t nurse bitterness, but isn’t required to pretend nothing happened, to trust where trust hasn’t been earned, or to return to danger.

The missing verse 26. The numbers run 25, then 27. Older Bibles print v. 26 — “But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive your trespasses” — which modern ones footnote. Those words aren’t in the earliest manuscripts of Mark; a scribe seems to have written them in the margin from Matthew 6:15, where they belong, and a copyist took the margin for the text. Nothing is lost: the truth stands plainly in v. 25, and Jesus teaches it in Matthew (Matthew 6:14–15).
verseByVerse.note: Jews commonly prayed standing. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 26: “But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive your trespasses.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The challenge. They come back into the city and the full weight of the establishment is waiting: chief priests, scribes and elders — the three constituencies of the Sanhedrin, which is to say the supreme court of Judaism has sent a delegation to meet him in the temple courts.

Their question is the right one and the only one: by what authority are you doing these things? A man has stopped the temple trade, halted the traffic across the courts, and is now teaching daily on the premises. Somebody has to ask who authorised it.

The counter-question. Jesus offers to answer if they will answer one of his: was John's baptism from heaven or from man?

It is not evasion, and it is not a debating trick. John's commission was the same kind as his own — direct from God, without institutional sanction — so anyone who can assess the one can assess the other.

The calculation. And Mark lets us listen in while they work out what to say, which is the most damning thing in the chapter: they weigh both answers by what each will cost them, and the question of what is actually true never comes up.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why does Jesus refuse to answer? It looks at first like a rabbinic sparring move, and it is much more than that.

He is not withholding truth from honest enquiry — he has never once done that in this Gospel. He explained the parables privately to anyone who stayed and asked (4:10, 34); he answered a scribe who asked about the greatest commandment and told him he was not far from the kingdom (12:34); he answered the rich man who ran and knelt (10:17-22).

What he refuses is to give an answer to men who have already demonstrated they will not deal honestly with an answer. They have John's case in front of them — a prophet the entire nation recognised — and they cannot bring themselves to say publicly what they think about him, because both possible verdicts are expensive.

And that is a settled principle, not a mood: do not give dogs what is holy, and do not throw your pearls before pigs (Matt. 7:6). He will stand silent in front of Herod, who wanted a miracle for entertainment (Luke 23:9), and largely silent before Pilate.

So the withdrawal of light is itself a judgement — and a merciful one, because more truth given to a man determined to reject it only deepens the guilt of the rejecting.

And note what their answer costs them. We do not know is a lie, spoken publicly by the highest religious authority in Israel, about the most famous prophet of their own generation. To protect their position they declared themselves incompetent — and having done so, they had no ground left from which to judge anybody's authority, including his.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: If we say, "From heaven," he will say, "Why then did you not believe him?" But shall we say, "From man"? — and they were afraid of the people.

Read the deliberation again and notice what is missing from it. Two options are weighed. Each is assessed for consequences. And at no point does anybody in that huddle ask: which of these is true?

That question is simply absent. These are the most religiously educated men in the nation, standing in the temple, discussing a prophet's commission — and truth is not one of the factors.

Now: the mechanism is not first-century and it is not confined to unbelievers. It is the standing temptation of any institution, church or person with more to lose from the truth than from avoiding it.

It is the doctrine quietly not preached because of who would leave. The sin not named because of who is in the family. The question about your own life you have never taken to God because you already know roughly what the answer costs.

And it ends the way it ended here: not in a lie you tell somebody else, but in we do not know — a shrug that feels like humility and is in fact a decision. They walked away with their positions intact and no answer at all, and it is the last conversation they have with him before they arrest him.

verseByVerse.quote: And they came again to Jerusalem. And as he was walking in the temple, the chief priests and the scribes and the elders came to him, and they said to him, "By what authority are you doing these things, or who gave you this authority to do them?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s highest council asks a fair institutional question, but Jesus’ authority comes from no human channel — only from God.

Back again. The third entry into the city in three days; he keeps returning to the building he has judged. Not outside making speeches, but inside, walking about, teaching, entirely at home. He overturned the tables yesterday and is back this morning, behaving as though the place belongs to him — which, he has said, it does: “my house” (v. 17).

The Sanhedrin. Chief priests (the Sadducean temple aristocracy), scribes (legal experts, largely Pharisaic), and elders (lay heads of leading families) — the full composition of Israel’s supreme court. Not a heckler, but an official delegation.

A reasonable question. He has interfered with the national temple, halted a licensed trade, stopped the thoroughfare, and is teaching in the courts. Someone in that position should be asked who authorised him. It is the correct institutional response; if a stranger did the same in any church today, the elders would rightly ask.

Authority through channels. The second half reveals how they think: “who gave you this authority?” In their world authority came through channels — ordained, trained, appointed, licensed. The question assumes a name must stand behind him: a school, a rabbi, a body. And no one gave it to him. That has been the issue since chapter 1, when the crowd said “he taught them as one who had authority, and not as the scribes” (1:22). The scribes’ authority was derived, cited, borrowed from a higher court. His isn’t derived from anything.

No answer in their terms. So the question has no answer in their terms. There is only one name to give, and if he says it plainly here, in the temple, days before Passover, the week ends at once. So he doesn’t answer. He asks. A test: do you recognise Christ’s authority over your life as coming straight from God, or do you treat his words as one opinion among many?
verseByVerse.note: The chief priests, scribes and elders together made up the Sanhedrin, the ruling council.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "I will ask you one question; answer me, and I will tell you by what authority I do these things. Was the baptism of John from heaven or from man? Answer me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John, like Jesus, had authority straight from God, and honestly answering about John would have led them to the truth about Christ.

A fair bargain. Answering a question with a question was ordinary in rabbinic debate — method, not rudeness — and he offers a fair deal: one question, and he will give them what they came for. He isn’t dodging. If they answer honestly they will have answered their own question, which is why they won’t.

Heaven or man. “From heaven” is a reverent way of saying “from God” without the name. A stark question with no third option: was John’s commission divine, or was he acting on his own? “Answer me” — he presses; it isn’t a rhetorical flourish.

A genuine parallel. Not a trick. John had no institutional standing: no office, school, ordination, or temple post — though as a priest’s son (Luke 1:5) he could have had one. He appeared in the desert, preached, baptised, and was recognised by a whole nation as a prophet, his authority directly from God without a human channel. Exactly the kind of authority Jesus has, and exactly what the delegation refuses to consider. So: you have already had one case like mine; what did you conclude? If they can assess John, they can assess him. If they can’t assess John — dead a year or two, his ministry witnessed by the whole country — they have disqualified themselves as judges of anyone’s commission.

A mercy too. More than logic. John’s whole ministry pointed at Jesus: “After me comes he who is mightier than I” (1:7). Anyone who honestly settled John’s authority would be carried straight to the answer about Christ. Jesus handed them the one question in the world that would have led them home, and they are about to spend it on a calculation about crowd management. A test: is there a question God keeps putting to you that, answered honestly, would lead you closer to Christ?
verseByVerse.note: “From heaven” means from God.

verseByVerse.quote: And they discussed it with one another, saying, "If we say, 'From heaven,' he will say, 'Why then did you not believe him?' But shall we say, 'From man'?"—they were afraid of the people, for they all held that John really was a prophet. So they answered Jesus, "We do not know." And Jesus said to them, "Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When self-protection rather than truth drives our answers, we shut ourselves off from further light.

Inside the huddle. Mark lets us listen as Israel’s supreme court, in the temple, works out what to say — the most damning paragraph in the chapter.

They knew. “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’” They see it at once. No confusion about what John’s ministry meant; concede he was sent by God, and they stand condemned for ignoring him. So they had already decided about John and knew it was indefensible. They aren’t weighing evidence but managing an exposure.

Both roads closed. “But shall we say, ‘From man’?” — Mark breaks off their sentence to give the reason, as if the calculation were too naked to write: “they were afraid of the people, for they all held that John really was a prophet.” Josephus confirms how deeply John was revered and that Antipas was widely blamed for his death. One road costs credibility; the other safety.

Truth not a factor. What is missing is the point. Two options considered, each assessed for consequences, and no one asks: which is true? The most religiously trained men in the nation, in God’s house, discussing whether a prophet was sent by God — and truth doesn’t enter the discussion. That is what institutional self-preservation does to a mind, and it isn’t a first-century disease. It tempts any church, board or person with more to lose from the truth than from avoiding it: the doctrine not preached because of who would leave; the sin not named because of whose family it is in; the question about your own life you have never put to God because you already know roughly what the answer would cost. A test: is there a question you avoid because of what the true answer would cost?

“We do not know.” A public lie by Israel’s highest religious authority about the most famous prophet of their generation — and the perfect lie, because it sounds like humility; it is what a careful man says. It is also a confession of incompetence: having declared themselves unable to judge John’s commission, they have destroyed their standing to judge his. People still use that sentence this way. Agnosticism can be an honest condition, and God is patient with it. But it can also be a position taken because it is cheapest — never saying yes or no, keeping every door open by walking through none.

Light withdrawn. “Neither will I tell you.” He keeps the bargain exactly. Not petulance but judgment, and the chapter’s most sobering thing: withdrawing light from someone who has decided against it is itself a terrible mercy; more truth given to a person determined to reject it would only deepen the guilt. They leave with positions intact and no answer. It is their last real conversation with Jesus before the arrest — and the next time they ask him directly who he is, at night in the high priest’s house, he will answer fully, and they will tear their clothes and condemn him (14:61–64). He was never unwilling to tell them. He waited for the hour when the answer couldn’t be turned into anything else — and that hour was a cross.

11.theology:
Was it fair to curse a tree out of season? The answer turns on the leaves. A Palestinian fig produces its fruit before or alongside its leaves, not after — in spring the branches put out small edible knobs, the paggim, and a hungry traveller ate them. So a tree in full leaf is making a claim. Mark's clause it was not the season for figs is not an embarrassment but the key: he supplies it so no reader mistakes this for pique over a missed breakfast. Nobody was owed a crop. What the tree owed was consistency with its own advertisement, and it had none.

And the placement is the interpretation. Mark splits the story and wedges the temple into the gap — curse, temple, withered — his habitual sandwich, never accidental. The fig tree was Israel's own image for itself (Hos. 9:10; Jer. 8:13), and the sentence pronounced here is carried out on the building in 13:2.

A den of robbers (Jer. 7:11) is the most misquoted phrase in the chapter. A robbers' den is not where the robbery happens; it is the cave they retreat to afterwards, where they feel safe. Jeremiah spells it out at the temple gate: Will you steal, murder, commit adultery... and then come and stand before me in this house, which is called by my name, and say, 'We are delivered!' The charge is not commerce in church. It is using religion as a safe house.

And v. 17 keeps a clause the other Gospels drop. Matthew and Luke both quote Isaiah 56:7 and stop before the final phrase; Mark keeps for all the nations — the Gospel written for Gentiles preserving the clause about Gentiles. Isaiah 56 is God's promise about the foreigner and the eunuch, the two categories explicitly excluded under the old arrangements; and the trading filled the Court of the Gentiles, the one place a non-Jew could stand. The arrangement had physically evicted the very people the verse was about.
11.examples:
Then: whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours — a promise that has been made to carry a weight it was never meant to bear.

What it does say: pray with enormous boldness, ask for what is far beyond your resources, expect God to act. Most of us are not in danger of presumption. We are in danger of praying for nothing much in case nothing happens, and the whole point of the mountain is that it is too big.

What it does not say: that sufficient certainty compels God. That reading makes prayer a technique and God a force, and it is refuted most decisively by the man saying it — within days, in a garden a few hundred yards away, he asks his Father to remove the cup and adds yet not what I will, but what you will (14:36), and the cup does not pass. If unqualified confidence always secured the request, that prayer is unintelligible. Paul asked three times about the thorn and was told no (2 Cor. 12:8–9); John, who heard this saying, wrote in the qualifier himself — if we ask anything according to his will he hears us (1 Jn. 5:14).

Now: to the reader who asked and did not receive — your faith was very likely not the problem, and blaming it only adds a second grief to the first. Believe boldly, ask for great things, and trust him enough to want his will more than your own, knowing that his no, when it comes, is as wise and as kind as the yes you hoped for.

And note what he says next (v. 25), with no pause: whenever you stand praying, forgive. Having promised that a believing man can move a mountain, he immediately names the thing that blocks the pipe. There is a name — you thought of it while reading this — and the instruction is not to feel differently, but to put it down, deliberately, now, and again whenever it comes back.

12.title: The Beloved Son and the Widow’s Two Coins
12.text: <sup>1</sup>And he began to speak to them in parables. “A man planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a pit for the winepress and built a tower, and leased it to tenants and went into another country. <sup>2</sup>When the season came, he sent a servant to the tenants to get from them some of the fruit of the vineyard. <sup>3</sup>And they took him and beat him and sent him away empty-handed. <sup>4</sup>Again he sent to them another servant, and they struck him on the head and treated him shamefully. <sup>5</sup>And he sent another, and him they killed. And so with many others: some they beat, and some they killed. <sup>6</sup>He had still one other, a beloved son. Finally he sent him to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’ <sup>7</sup>But those tenants said to one another, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.’ <sup>8</sup>And they took him and killed him and threw him out of the vineyard. <sup>9</sup>What will the owner of the vineyard do? He will come and destroy the tenants and give the vineyard to others. <sup>10</sup>Have you not read this Scripture: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; <sup>11</sup>this was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?” <sup>12</sup>And they were seeking to arrest him but feared the people, for they perceived that he had told the parable against them. So they left him and went away. <sup>13</sup>And they sent to him some of the Pharisees and some of the Herodians, to trap him in his talk. <sup>14</sup>And they came and said to him, “Teacher, we know that you are true and do not care about anyone’s opinion. For you are not swayed by appearances, but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? Should we pay them, or should we not?” <sup>15</sup>But, knowing their hypocrisy, he said to them, “Why put me to the test? Bring me a denarius and let me look at it.” <sup>16</sup>And they brought one. And he said to them, “Whose likeness and inscription is this?” They said to him, “Caesar’s.” <sup>17</sup>Jesus said to them, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” And they marveled at him. <sup>18</sup>And Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection. And they asked him a question, saying, <sup>19</sup>“Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies and leaves a wife, but leaves no child, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother. <sup>20</sup>There were seven brothers; the first took a wife, and when he died left no offspring. <sup>21</sup>And the second took her, and died, leaving no offspring. And the third likewise. <sup>22</sup>And the seven left no offspring. Last of all the woman also died. <sup>23</sup>In the resurrection, when they rise again, whose wife will she be? For the seven had her as wife.” <sup>24</sup>Jesus said to them, “Is this not the reason you are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God? <sup>25</sup>For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven. <sup>26</sup>And as for the dead being raised, have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush, how God spoke to him, saying, ‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? <sup>27</sup>He is not God of the dead, but of the living. You are quite wrong.” <sup>28</sup>And one of the scribes came up and heard them disputing with one another, and seeing that he answered them well, asked him, “Which commandment is the most important of all?” <sup>29</sup>Jesus answered, “The most important is, ‘Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. <sup>30</sup>And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.’ <sup>31</sup>The second is this: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no other commandment greater than these.” <sup>32</sup>And the scribe said to him, “You are right, Teacher. You have truly said that he is one, and there is no other besides him. <sup>33</sup>And to love him with all the heart and with all the understanding and with all the strength, and to love one’s neighbor as oneself, is much more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.” <sup>34</sup>And when Jesus saw that he answered wisely, he said to him, “You are not far from the kingdom of God.” And after that no one dared to ask him any more questions. <sup>35</sup>And as Jesus taught in the temple, he said, “How can the scribes say that the Christ is the son of David? <sup>36</sup>David himself, in the Holy Spirit, declared, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet.”’ <sup>37</sup>David himself calls him Lord. So how is he his son?” And the great throng heard him gladly. <sup>38</sup>And in his teaching he said, “Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes and like greetings in the marketplaces <sup>39</sup>and have the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts, <sup>40</sup>who devour widows’ houses and for a pretense make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation.” <sup>41</sup>And he sat down opposite the treasury and watched the people putting money into the offering box. Many rich people put in large sums. <sup>42</sup>And a poor widow came and put in two small copper coins, which make a penny. <sup>43</sup>And he called his disciples to him and said to them, “Truly, I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the offering box. <sup>44</sup>For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on.”
12.overview:
This is the last day Jesus ever taught in the temple, and it is one long interrogation. Three delegations come at him in turn, each with a question designed to finish him, and by verse 34 nobody dares ask him anything at all.

He opens by answering the challenge they refused to answer, with a story. A vineyard is planted at great expense, leased out, and the owner sends for his share — and the tenants beat one servant, humiliate another, kill a third, and go on doing it. Then, having nobody else, the owner sends a beloved son, which in this Gospel is a phrase that has twice come out of heaven. They recognise him, kill him, and throw him out of the vineyard. Mark says the leaders understood the parable perfectly — and went away to arrange the arrest.

Then the traps: a coin with Caesar's face on it, and a riddle about a woman with seven husbands. He answers the first in sixteen words that have shaped Christian political thought ever since, and the second from a single present-tense verb in the burning bush.

Then one honest scribe asks a real question and is told he is not far from the kingdom of God. And the chapter ends with Jesus sitting down opposite the treasury, watching people give, and calling his disciples over to look at a widow putting in two of the smallest coins in the empire — everything she had to live on, three days before he did the same.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–27 — The Tenants, Caesar’s Coin, and the Resurrection
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The parable (vv. 1–12). They asked by what authority he acts, and refused to answer his question. So he tells them a story about a vineyard, and it is the least veiled parable he ever told: an owner, a run of beaten and murdered servants, and finally a beloved son. They understood it perfectly — Mark says so — and went away to arrange the arrest.

The coin (vv. 13–17). Pharisees and Herodians together again, opening with flattery and closing a trap with two jaws: endorse the tax and lose the crowd, oppose it and be reported for sedition. He asks for a coin, asks whose face is on it, and gives an answer nobody has improved on.

The riddle (vv. 18–27). Then the Sadducees, with a seven-husbands puzzle designed to make resurrection look absurd — and he answers them from the one part of the Bible they accepted, out of a single present-tense verb.

Three challenges from three different quarters, all in one day, all of them designed to end him — and by verse 34 nobody dares ask him anything else.
verseByVerse.theology:
Render to Caesar (v. 17) cuts in two directions at once, and both must be held.

On one side, a real obligation. Jesus does not say the tax is illegitimate or that a man of God may treat the government as an enemy to be defied. The coin is Caesar's; give it to him. Paul draws the same line plainly: the governing authority is God's servant for the ordering of society, so pay your taxes, keep the law, honour the office (Rom. 13:1–7; 1 Pet. 2:13–17). Christianity is not anarchy, and a faith that despises all earthly authority has not understood this verse.

On the other side, the obligation is bounded. Caesar may claim the coin; he may not claim the soul. The image on the denarius marks what is his; the image of God stamped on the man marks what is God's — and what is God's, Caesar must never be given.

So the same verse that tells you to pay the tax tells you where obedience stops. The moment the state demands what belongs to God alone — worship, or the violation of God's clear command — the Christian renders to God and not to Caesar. We must obey God rather than men, the apostles answered the very Sanhedrin that plotted this trap (Acts 5:29). It is the fault line the martyrs died on: they would pay any tax Rome levied and pray for its emperor, but they would not drop the pinch of incense that called Caesar Lord, because that title was God's.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the Sadducees, and the ground Jesus chooses to fight them on.

They were the aristocratic priestly party who ran the temple — wealthy, powerful, politically pragmatic — and they held that only the five books of Moses carried full authority. They also say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit (Acts 23:8).

Which is why Jesus does not answer from the obvious places. He could have quoted Daniel — many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake (Dan. 12:2) — or Isaiah 26:19, and they would simply have waved those books away. Instead he beats them on their own chosen ground, reaching into the Torah, into the burning bush that every priest knew by heart, and finding the resurrection in a present-tense claim: I am the God of Abraham. Not was. Abraham has been dead four hundred years and God speaks of him in the present tense.

Now: he does not merely win the argument. He wins it inside the fence they built themselves, proving that the hope they denied was lying all along in the only Scriptures they would accept.

And note the diagnosis he gives first: you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. Those are the two ways to go wrong, and they are still the two. Some err because they do not know the text; some because they know the text and have quietly decided what God is not able to do.

verseByVerse.quote: And he began to speak to them in parables. "A man planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a pit for the winepress and built a tower, and leased it to tenants and went into another country. When the season came, he sent a servant to the tenants to get from them some of the fruit of the vineyard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The vineyard is Israel, the owner is God, and the tenants are its leaders — and everything God gives us is a tenancy, held for him and owing him fruit.

A story for the men who wouldn’t answer. “To them” — the delegation that has just refused to answer his question about John (11:33). They wouldn’t answer him, so he tells them a story, the least veiled parable he ever told; verse 12 says outright that they understood it.

Isaiah’s vineyard. The first sentence is a quotation, and every man listening knew it: “My beloved had a vineyard on a very fertile hill. He dug it and cleared it of stones, and planted it with choice vines; he built a watchtower in the midst of it, and hewed out a wine vat in it” (Isaiah 5:1–2). And Isaiah says what it means: “For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:7). Before a single character acts, the delegation knows the story is about them.

A costly investment. Each detail is money spent: a fence against animals, a tower for a watchman, a press cut out of rock. This isn’t a man who threw seed at some ground. He has prepared the place thoroughly before anyone else touches it — as God did for Israel, and does for every person he places somewhere.

Tenants, not owners. Then he leaves, and the arrangement is ordinary: absentee landlords commonly leased land to tenant farmers, who worked it and paid part of the crop as rent. The tenants own nothing. They have the use of something valuable that someone else built, on the understanding that its fruit isn’t finally theirs. That is the position of Israel’s leaders — and of everyone given anything by God: a church, a family, a gift, a life. None of it is freehold. The parable turns on the difference between a tenant and an owner, and on what happens to someone who forgets which he is. A test: what are you treating as yours that God has only lent you?

A modest request. “When the season came, he sent a servant… to get from them some of the fruit.” Not all of it; the agreed share, when it was due. He has every right, and he asks.
verseByVerse.note: The setting echoes Isaiah’s song of the vineyard, where the vineyard is Israel. Absentee landlords commonly leased land to tenant farmers.

verseByVerse.quote: And they took him and beat him and sent him away empty-handed. Again he sent to them another servant, and they struck him on the head and treated him shamefully. And he sent another, and him they killed. And so with many others: some they beat, and some they killed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is Israel’s history with God’s prophets — and above it, the astonishing patience of a God who keeps sending.

Escalation. Mark makes us watch it four times over, worsening each time. The first servant beaten and sent back with nothing — a message as much as an assault: there will be no rent. The second “struck… on the head and treated… shamefully” — injured and publicly humiliated. The third killed. Then Jesus stops counting: “so with many others: some they beat, and some they killed.” The pattern never changed.

The servants are the prophets. “My servants the prophets” is God’s own phrase for them: “I have persistently sent all my servants the prophets to them, day after day” (Jeremiah 7:25). And the treatment is the record. Jeremiah was beaten and put in the stocks by the temple’s chief officer (Jeremiah 20:2) and lowered into a muddy cistern (Jeremiah 38:6). Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned “in the court of the house of the LORD” on the king’s orders (2 Chronicles 24:20–21). Micaiah was struck and imprisoned (1 Kings 22:24–27). John the Baptist lost his head at a party (6:27). Stephen will say it to this same council and die for it: “Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute?” (Acts 7:52).

An owner who keeps sending. But the story isn’t mainly about the tenants. After the first beating any landlord in that room would have gone to law or come with force. This one sends another man, and another, and after a murder, more. The absurdity of the parable — the tenants must have thought him a fool — is the owner’s patience.

Still someone at the gate. That is God’s history with his people, and with you. The astonishing thing here isn’t human wickedness, which anyone could predict. It is that after the beating, the humiliation and the killing, there is still someone else at the gate. A test: how many messengers has God sent you that you have sent away empty-handed? The next verse says who is left.

parallels.desc: they mocked the messengers of God

verseByVerse.quote: He had still one other, a beloved son. Finally he sent him to them, saying, 'They will respect my son.' But those tenants said to one another, 'This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.' And they took him and killed him and threw him out of the vineyard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is foretelling his own death: God sends his only Son, and his own people’s leaders kill him knowingly, wanting God’s world without God.

No one left but a son. “He had still one other.” The servants are spent; the owner has come to the end of what he had, and what remains isn’t another employee. “A beloved son” — and the parable stops being about someone else, because twice already in Mark that phrase has come out of heaven: “You are my beloved Son” at the Jordan (1:11), “This is my beloved Son; listen to him” on the mountain (9:7). Now, in a parable, before the men arranging his death, he tells them who he is and what they are about to do.

The cost of sending. “They will respect my son” isn’t naive; it is what any reasonable man would think — a servant can be brushed aside, the heir is the owner in person. And a listener would feel the cost: this man knows what these tenants do to those he sends, and he sends his son. “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32).

They knew him. “This is the heir.” That is the horror of the parable and of Good Friday: they don’t kill the son by mistake but because they know who he is. And their reasoning is every rebellion against God stated honestly: “the inheritance will be ours.” Get rid of the heir and keep the estate. It is the serpent’s offer — you will be like God — and the logic of sin, which is finally about ownership, not pleasure. A test: where do you want God’s gifts but not God’s rule?

Thrown out. “They took him and killed him and threw him out of the vineyard” — one sentence, no adjectives. To leave a body unburied was the ultimate contempt. And Mark’s readers knew the Son was in fact rejected and put outside: led out of the city and crucified there — “Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12). He stands in the temple describing his own murder, in the third person, to the men who will commit it.
verseByVerse.note: “Beloved son” echoes the Father’s voice at the baptism and transfiguration.

verseByVerse.quote: What will the owner of the vineyard do? He will come and destroy the tenants and give the vineyard to others. Have you not read this Scripture: 'The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord's doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s leaders will lose their stewardship, and the Son they reject God will raise to be the foundation of his people.

He answers his own question. “What will the owner of the vineyard do?” He asks and answers it himself — unusual for him, and leaving no ambiguity.

Destroy the tenants. Within forty years Jerusalem was besieged and burned, the temple destroyed, and the priestly aristocracy that ran it gone. He will describe it in the next chapter (13:2).

Give the vineyard to others. The harder half, and it has been misused. It doesn’t mean God is finished with the Jewish people; Paul spends three chapters denying that, insisting “God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew” (Romans 11:2). And the parable is aimed at the tenants — the leadership standing before him. What changes hands is the stewardship: the care of God’s vineyard passes to others, who turn out to include Gentiles from every nation, as Peter told this same council: “This Jesus is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone” (Acts 4:11). It is also a warning to every church that assumes its position is permanent. A lampstand can be removed (Revelation 2:5).

“Have you not read?” A sting, put to professional scribes. And the text is Psalm 118:22–23 — the psalm the crowd sang at him on the road (11:9). They sang him verse 26; now he reads them verse 22.

From vineyard to building. The change of image is the gospel in one move. The story ended with a dead son thrown out of a vineyard; the psalm ends with a rejected stone holding up a building. The builders — the professionals whose job is to judge stones — throw this one on the spoil heap, and God makes it the cornerstone that sets the line of every wall. So the parable doesn’t end at verse 8. It ends in resurrection, told in the language of masonry.

The Lord’s doing. “This was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes.” The builders weren’t thwarted by accident; what they meant as rejection was what God was doing — and Peter, standing there, quotes the verse in his preaching and his letter (Acts 4:11; 1 Peter 2:7). A test: is the stone the world rejects the one your life rests on?

verseByVerse.quote: And they were seeking to arrest him but feared the people, for they perceived that he had told the parable against them. So they left him and went away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They understood exactly, and rejected him anyway — the problem was never lack of information but an unwilling heart.

They perceived. No misunderstanding. They knew they were the tenants, who the beloved son was, and what was said about their future. That removes the most convenient excuse ever offered for rejecting Christ. These men weren’t confused.

They acted out the parable. Told they are the men who murder the heir, they go away to arrange the murder of the heir. The warning becomes the occasion of the crime it warns about. That is what a hardened heart does with truth: it doesn’t soften; it uses the light to see by while it does what the light exposed.

Fear of the crowd. “But feared the people” — not conscience, not doubt whether he might be right, but crowd management. The city is full for Passover, the throng hears him gladly (v. 37), and a public arrest could start a riot. So fear of the crowd sets the timetable, which is why it will happen at night, in a garden, with a guide who knew where he prayed.

They walked away. “So they left him and went away” — the saddest clause in the chapter. They stood before the Son of God, who had told them, plainly enough to be understood perfectly, who he was, what they would do, and what it would cost. Nobody dragged them off; they lost no argument. They turned round and walked, and the next time they are in a room with him it will be at night with false witnesses.

The ordinary way of being lost. It is possible to understand the gospel completely — what it claims and what it requires — and walk away, not in rage or confusion but because it costs too much. That is the most ordinary way in the world of being lost. A test: is there something you know Christ is asking of you that you have walked away from because of the cost?

verseByVerse.quote: And they sent to him some of the Pharisees and some of the Herodians, to trap him in his talk. And they came and said to him, "Teacher, we know that you are true and do not care about anyone's opinion. For you are not swayed by appearances, but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? Should we pay them, or should we not?" But, knowing their hypocrisy, he said to them, "Why put me to the test? Bring me a denarius and let me look at it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sees through flattery and malice, and calmly takes control of a question designed to destroy him.

An unlikely alliance. The alliance from chapter 3 again (3:6): strict Pharisees, who resented Rome, and the party of Herod, whose power depended on it — agreed on nothing but this. Mark’s word for trap is a hunting word, to catch as with a snare. And they are sent: the council working through others, having found that direct confrontation failed.

Flattery as a technique. “We know that you are true and do not care about anyone’s opinion… you are not swayed by appearances.” They praise him for independence and fearlessness — exactly what they need him to display in the next thirty seconds. They aren’t complimenting him; they are pointing him at a cliff. And every word is true. Flattery is rarely a lie. It is a true thing said by someone who wants something, and the tell isn’t the content but the timing: it arrives just before the request. A test: when someone praises you, do you notice what they want next?

Two lethal jaws. They ask twice — “Should we pay them, or should we not?” — to shut off any escape into generality. Say yes, and he loses the crowd: this was the tax imposed when Judea became a Roman province in AD 6, which provoked an armed revolt under Judas the Galilean and was hated as the badge of occupation. A Messiah who endorsed it was no Messiah. Say no, and the Herodians have a charge of sedition to carry to Pilate — which is what they will allege anyway: “We found this man… forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar” (Luke 23:2).

He names it. “Knowing their hypocrisy, he said to them, ‘Why put me to the test?’” He isn’t taken in and says so aloud. He doesn’t pretend the flattery was sincere — a small lesson in dealing with people who come at you sideways.

“Bring me a denarius.” With that he takes control. He has no coin himself; he asks them for one — and they produce it. Someone among these scrupulous men has the emperor’s coin in his pocket, in the temple. The trap is already sprung on them, and they haven’t noticed.
verseByVerse.note: The Herodians supported Herod’s family and so Roman rule; the Pharisees resented Rome. The poll tax was paid directly to Rome and bitterly resented. The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage.

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought one. And he said to them, "Whose likeness and inscription is this?" They said to him, "Caesar's." Jesus said to them, "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." And they marveled at him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christians owe government real obedience, including taxes, but God alone owns the whole person, because we bear his image.

The coin. A silver denarius of Tiberius carried the emperor’s head and an inscription calling him son of the divine Augustus; the reverse called him high priest. A coin, and a small metal blasphemy. Mark’s word for “likeness” is eikōn, image — and the second commandment forbade graven images. They produce one, in the temple courts, on request.

“Caesar’s.” There is only one answer, and by giving it they concede that they use his currency, travel his roads and live under his protection.

Give back what is owed. “Render” means to pay back, to return what is owed. The coin has his face on it; hand it back to him.

What bears God’s image. Then the second half, where the sentence detonates. If what bears Caesar’s image belongs to Caesar, what bears God’s image belongs to God — and that isn’t a coin: “God created man in his own image” (Genesis 1:27). He answers the tax question and then puts the questioners on the scales. Caesar gets the coinage; God gets the person — all of him, because no part of a human being is unstamped. And he doesn’t say how much belongs to Caesar; that varies with the government you live under. He fixes only the limit.

A real duty. The verse works in two directions, both legitimate. It establishes an obligation. Jesus doesn’t call the tax illegitimate or license defiance of government. Paul says the authority is God’s servant for ordering society, so pay taxes and honour the office (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17). A faith that despises all earthly authority hasn’t read this verse. A test: do you pay what you owe — and speak of those in authority — as someone answerable to God?

A firm limit. It also bounds the obligation absolutely. Caesar may claim the coin, never the soul. When the state demands what belongs to God alone — worship, or breaking God’s plain command — the answer is no: “We must obey God rather than men,” the apostles told this council (Acts 5:29). The martyrs died on that line. They paid Rome’s taxes and prayed for its emperor, and wouldn’t burn the pinch of incense that called Caesar Lord, because that title was God’s.

They marveled. They came to trap him and went away astonished — the only recorded outcome.
verseByVerse.note: The coin bore the emperor’s head — probably Tiberius — and an inscription calling him son of the divine Augustus.

verseByVerse.quote: And Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection. And they asked him a question, saying, "Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man's brother dies and leaves a wife, but leaves no child, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother. There were seven brothers; the first took a wife, and when he died left no offspring. And the second took her, and died, leaving no offspring. And the third likewise. And the seven left no offspring. Last of all the woman also died. In the resurrection, when they rise again, whose wife will she be? For the seven had her as wife."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They try to make the resurrection look absurd by imagining the next life as this one continued.

The Sadducees. Mark explains them for his Roman readers. They were the temple party — the priestly aristocracy, wealthy, conservative, politically pragmatic, running the establishment Jesus had just disrupted. They gave the five books of Moses the highest authority and denied the resurrection, angels and spirits (Acts 23:8). A different opponent with a different objection, and the only time they appear in Mark.

Their ground. “Teacher, Moses wrote for us” — Moses, because his is the authority they accept. The question is designed to be argued on their own ground.

A mercy turned into a weapon. This is the law of Deuteronomy 25:5–6, and it was a kindness. In a world without pensions, where women seldom inherited, a childless widow was destitute and her husband’s name and land died with him. The brother married her so she was provided for and the first son carried the dead man’s name. A related duty of a near kinsman lies behind the book of Ruth. The Sadducees are about to make a joke of it.

A debating exercise. Seven brothers isn’t a real case but a puzzle built to make the resurrection ridiculous, with seven chosen for maximum absurdity. And notice the woman: seven men take her; she is passed along, widowed seven times, childless — and nobody in the conversation gives her grief a thought. A test: do you ever argue about doctrine in a way that forgets the people in it?

The joke. “Whose wife will she be?” isn’t really a question but a joke, the sort clever men use to embarrass a doctrine they have already dismissed. The logic: if the resurrection is real, heaven holds an insoluble domestic problem, so the resurrection is absurd.

The hidden assumption. Underneath lies the assumption Jesus will go straight for: they picture the life to come as this life continued — the same institutions, the same property law, running on forever. A great many people who have never heard of a Sadducee make the same mistake.
verseByVerse.note: The Sadducees, the priestly party, denied the resurrection. Levirate marriage kept a dead man’s name alive.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "Is this not the reason you are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God? For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The life to come isn’t this life extended but transformed by God — and nothing good in this life will be lost there.

Two failures. He answers the joke with a blunt diagnosis, delivered to the professional custodians of both. They don’t know the Scriptures — not that they hadn’t read them, but they didn’t know what was in them, as verse 26 will show. Nor the power of God — the deeper failure. They had quietly settled that God couldn’t do what they couldn’t imagine. Unable to picture a resurrection life that isn’t this life extended, they concluded there is none.

Unbelief that sounds like realism. That second failure is common among religious people, and it doesn’t announce itself as unbelief. It sounds like realism: the settled assumption that God won’t act, that this marriage won’t change, this person won’t be converted, nothing much will happen — formed from experience, not Scripture, and then read back into Scripture. A test: what have you decided God cannot or will not do?

Not this age with the same furniture. “When they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven.” He denies their premise.

For the bereaved. This verse needs gentle handling, because many live inside it. If you have buried a husband or wife and felt this sentence close on your chest, take the whole of it. He doesn’t say we become angels but are like them, in the point at issue: those who can no longer die no longer marry and bear children. He doesn’t say love ends, or that we won’t know one another. The fear that resurrection means less — thinner relationships, an impersonal eternity — is the Sadducees’ mistake in reverse, and the Bible never suggests it. Paul expects to see the Thessalonians as his joy and crown (1 Thessalonians 2:19); the disciples recognised Moses and Elijah on the mountain.

A signpost taken down. Marriage ends as an institution not because it was too small but because it was a signpost, and you take down the signpost when you arrive. Paul says the mystery of marriage refers to Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:32). What you had was a picture of the union about to be consummated in fact. So the honest word to a widow or widower is that nothing good will be lost — not the years, the knowing, or the love. It will be taken up into something larger, at the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9).

verseByVerse.quote: And as for the dead being raised, have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush, how God spoke to him, saying, 'I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob'? He is not God of the dead, but of the living. You are quite wrong."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s covenant bond with his people can’t be broken by death, so those who belong to him live to him and will be raised.

Their own ground. He could have quoted Daniel — “many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake” (Daniel 12:2) — or Isaiah — “Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise” (Isaiah 26:19). But the Sadducees gave Moses the highest authority, so he goes to the Torah, to the burning bush in Exodus 3, a passage every priest there knew well. “Have you not read?” — the second time in this chapter he asks professional readers that (v. 10).

The God of the patriarchs. “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (v. 26, quoting Exodus 3:6). When God speaks at the bush, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob have been dead for centuries, their bones in the cave at Machpelah. Yet God still names himself by them.

Not grammar but covenant. “He is not God of the dead, but of the living.” The argument doesn’t hang on a verb tense; it rests on what a covenant is. God had bound himself to Abraham personally, “to be God to you and to your offspring after you” (Genesis 17:7). A bond like that can’t be ended by the death of one party without God’s own word failing. If Abraham had simply ceased to exist, God would be naming himself by a relationship with no one — the God of a memory. He isn’t. He is their God still, which means they live to him, and the God who keeps covenant with the whole person will raise the body too. “God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city” (Hebrews 11:16). He put their names into his own title, and he isn’t the God of dust.

“You are quite wrong.” He began with “you are wrong” (v. 24) and ends more strongly — badly mistaken. Mark doesn’t soften it.

Hidden in a familiar text. The resurrection isn’t a late invention; it lay in the books of Moses, in one of the most familiar passages, and the men who read it constantly had never seen it. If you belong to Christ, the God who calls himself yours won’t let death end that. And there is more in your Bible than you have got out of it. A test: which passage do you think you know that you have never really read?
verseByVerse.note: “The passage about the bush” is how a passage was located before chapter and verse numbers existed. Jesus answers from the books of Moses, which the Sadducees accepted.

parallels.desc: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–44 — The Great Commandment, David’s Lord, and the Widow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The one honest question (vv. 28–34). After a day of traps, a scribe asks something he actually wants to know — which commandment is the most important. He gets the Shema and Leviticus 19, agrees warmly, and is told he is not far from the kingdom of God. And after that, nobody dares ask anything at all.

The question he asks them (vv. 35–37). So Jesus asks one instead, and it is the deepest thing he says in public. If the Christ is David's son, why does David call him Lord?

The warning (vv. 38–40). Then a warning about the men in the long robes who love the greetings and the best seats, say long prayers for show, and devour widows' houses.

The widow (vv. 41–44). And he goes and sits down opposite the treasury and watches people give — and the last thing he does in this temple before he leaves it forever is point out a woman putting in two of the smallest coins in circulation.

Mark has put her immediately after devour widows' houses, and that is not an accident.
verseByVerse.theology:
Psalm 110 and the deepest disclosure in the Gospel. Jesus takes the most quoted psalm in the New Testament and asks a question nobody could answer.

Everyone agreed the Christ would be David's son — the promise ran through the whole Old Testament (2 Sam. 7:12–16; Isa. 11:1). And in Psalm 110, David writes: The LORD says to my Lord: "Sit at my right hand. The first LORD is God; the second is somebody David calls my Lord.

In that culture the point is unanswerable. Honour ran upward from son to father, never downward. A man does not call his own descendant his lord.

So: how can the Christ be David's son and David's Lord at once? Mark records no answer, and the crowd hears him gladly, and nobody says a word.

The answer is that both are true, and it takes the whole New Testament to say it. Concerning his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh and was declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection (Rom. 1:3–4). David's son by birth; David's Lord from eternity.

And notice which verse of the psalm he quotes: sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet. He asks this in the temple, on the Tuesday, surrounded by the men who will have him killed on the Friday. They are the enemies in the sentence, and he quotes it to their faces.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: You are not far from the kingdom of God.

The scribe has answered magnificently. He has the doctrine of God right, the summary of the law right, and the priorities right — he even says out loud, as a temple professional, that love of God and neighbour outweighs the whole sacrificial system, which is a remarkable thing for such a man to concede.

And Jesus does not say you are in. He says not far.

Now: that is the most uncomfortable commendation in the Gospel, because not far is still outside, and it is the address of a great many people who have been in church all their lives.

The gap between near and in is not a gap in knowledge. This man's theology was better than the Twelve's. The gap is a Person. He was standing three feet away, and the question was never whether the scribe could give the right answer about the law but whether he would follow the man who was about to keep it for him.

So it is worth asking plainly: could you give the right answers, and never have come? Right doctrine is the beginning and it is not the destination. Being able to describe a door is not the same as walking through it — and Mark never tells us whether this man did.

verseByVerse.quote: And one of the scribes came up and heard them disputing with one another, and seeing that he answered them well, asked him, "Which commandment is the most important of all?" Jesus answered, "The most important is, 'Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.' The second is this: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself.' There is no other commandment greater than these."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love for the one true God, with the whole self, and love for others are the heart of God’s law, and no one has kept them except Christ.

At last, someone honest. Mark gives the man’s motive, unlike anyone else’s in this chapter: he has been listening, was impressed, and asks because he wants to know. Matthew’s account has a sharper edge — he asked “to test him” (Matthew 22:35) — so perhaps his motives improved as the conversation went on. Either way, Mark presents him as the one man all day who came to learn.

A live question. Later rabbis counted 613 commandments in the Law and debated which were heavy and which light. Asking a teacher to name the first was a way of finding out how he thought.

He begins with who God is. Jesus starts one line earlier than he needed: “Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4) — the Shema, recited by devout Jews morning and evening. He doesn’t begin with what you must do but with who God is. Because there is one God — not one among many, not a department of life — the love owed him can’t be partial. A rival would deserve a share. He has none.

All of you. Heart, soul, mind and strength aren’t a division into parts but a way of leaving nothing out. The heart is the control room: what you decide and want. The soul is your very life. The mind — added to Deuteronomy’s list — means God is loved with the intellect, and lazy thinking about him isn’t humility. Strength is the body, energy, money and hours. So it is concrete. Loving God with your strength is a question about your diary and bank statement; loving him with your mind, about whether you have taken the trouble to understand what you believe. A test: which of the four does God get least of from you?

And your neighbour. Asked for one, he gives two, and they can’t be separated: Leviticus 19:18, lifted from a chapter full of practical instructions about wages, gleanings, the deaf and the blind, and honest scales. “As yourself” isn’t a command to love yourself first; it takes the self-interest everyone already has as the measure. As carefully as you consider your own comfort, reputation and future — that much, for them. John draws the conclusion: “If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar” (1 John 4:20).

The command that convicts. No one has kept this for a single hour. It is the commandment that convicts everyone — and the man who quoted it is on his way to keep it perfectly for us, and to die for those who didn’t.
verseByVerse.note: “Hear, O Israel” (the Shema) was recited daily by devout Jews.

verseByVerse.quote: And the scribe said to him, "You are right, Teacher. You have truly said that he is one, and there is no other besides him. And to love him with all the heart and with all the understanding and with all the strength, and to love one's neighbor as oneself, is much more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices." And when Jesus saw that he answered wisely, he said to him, "You are not far from the kingdom of God." And after that no one dared to ask him any more questions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Right understanding brings a person close, but entering the kingdom means coming to Christ himself.

It went in. “You are right, Teacher.” He doesn’t argue; he repeats the answer back in his own words, which is what someone does when a thing has really gone in. And he adds a phrase of his own from Deuteronomy 4:35, “there is no other besides him.” He isn’t parroting; he is thinking.

A costly admission. Notice who is speaking and where: a scribe, in the temple courts, in Passover week, with the altar smoke rising nearby and the whole machinery of sacrifice running around him — saying that loving God and neighbour matters more than all of it. Not novel; the prophets had said it for centuries: “I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6); “to obey is better than sacrifice” (1 Samuel 15:22). He had read his Bible and believed it, and said so in the one place where it cost something.

Not far. “You are not far from the kingdom of God” — genuine praise, and one of the most searching sentences in the Gospel. The man has the doctrine of God, the summary of the law and the priorities right, and is told so. And not far is still outside. Near the kingdom isn’t in it, and there is no third category.

The gap is a Person. The gap isn’t information; he knows more than many. The gap is a Person standing a few feet away. This whole chapter asks who Jesus is — the beloved son, the rejected stone, David’s Lord. The scribe can recite the greatest commandment; the question is whether he will follow the man about to keep it in his place. Mark never tells us. The account stops, and the man walks out of the Gospel one step from home.

Near or in? That leaves the question with the reader. You can give the right answers and never have come: hold sound doctrine, love a good sermon, defend the faith well — and be near. Being able to describe a door isn’t the same as walking through it. A test: have you only admired Christ, or have you come to him and trusted him yourself?

Silence. “After that no one dared to ask him any more questions.” Three parties have tried and been dismantled; the silence is the verdict.

parallels.desc: to obey is better than sacrifice

verseByVerse.quote: And as Jesus taught in the temple, he said, "How can the scribes say that the Christ is the son of David? David himself, in the Holy Spirit, declared, 'The Lord said to my Lord, "Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet."' David himself calls him Lord. So how is he his son?" And the great throng heard him gladly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Messiah is both David’s descendant and David’s Lord — truly human and truly divine, enthroned at God’s right hand.

He asks them. No one dares ask him anything, so he asks. It isn’t an attack on the doctrine. The Christ is David’s son; the promise runs through the Old Testament (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Isaiah 11:1), and Bartimaeus shouted it on the Jericho road and received his sight (10:47–52). Jesus asks whether it is the whole truth.

Two authors, one text. “David himself, in the Holy Spirit, declared.” David himself — so the psalm is his; in the Holy Spirit — so it is also God’s. Two authors, one text, no tension. That is how Jesus read his Bible, and how he teaches us to.

Two Lords. “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet’” — Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse most quoted in the New. The first “Lord” is God’s own name, printed LORD in our Old Testaments; the second is a title of rank, “my master.” So David, under the Spirit, records God speaking to someone David calls his Lord.

A father doesn’t call his son lord. In that culture the difficulty is total. Honour flowed upward: a son honoured his father, a descendant his ancestor, never the reverse. Yet Israel’s greatest king looks down the centuries at his descendant and calls him Master. Mark records no answer; nobody had one.

Both true. The answer is that both are true at once: God’s Son, “who was descended from David according to the flesh and was declared to be the Son of God in power… by his resurrection from the dead” (Romans 1:3–4). David’s son by birth, David’s Lord from eternity; the one who came from David’s line existed before David — “before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58). This is the deepest thing Jesus discloses about himself in public in Mark, given as a riddle, days before the cross, because stated flatly in the temple it would end the week early.

His enemies under his feet. Notice the line he chose: “until I put your enemies under your feet,” quoted to the faces of men who have resolved to kill him. The one they will crucify is the one God will enthrone. A test: do you treat Jesus as a great teacher of David’s line, or bow to him as Lord?

Heard gladly. “The great throng heard him gladly.” The professionals have gone silent; the crowd is delighted. Within days that same city will shout for his execution.
verseByVerse.note: Psalm 110:1 is among the Old Testament verses most often quoted in the New.
